An AI engineer builds products on top of AI models they did not build themselves.

That one sentence lets you skip most of what people think they must learn. You are not becoming a researcher. You are becoming the person who takes a model that already exists and turns it into something that works: reliable, fast, cheap, safe and, most important, measurably good.

How this course teaches

Read a little. Recall a lot. Build every day.

Small chunks

Each round teaches one or two ideas, with a picture, in plain words. You stop before you feel completely comfortable. That is on purpose.

Pull it out of your head

Every round starts with questions from earlier days and asks you to close the page and rebuild what you just read. That is what makes it stick.

Try it hard, then study the mistakes

You build before you read the steps. When something breaks, you write down why, in four short lines, and you get better at spotting it.

The whole method is on one page: How to learn. Read it once before Day 1. It takes about ten minutes.

The split

What stays in, and what gets cut

The 20% that does the work
  1. Talking to modelsEverything sits on top of this: tokens, cost, speed, streaming, and getting answers back in a fixed shape.
  2. Giving the model the right facts (RAG)Most of a product’s value comes from putting the right information in front of the model, not from a fancier model.
  3. Tools and agentsThe difference between a chatbot and something that does real work.
  4. Testing quality (evals)The real advantage. Most people ship on gut feeling. People who can measure quality get hired.
  5. Making it hold up in the real worldWatching it, controlling cost, keeping it fast, defending it against tricks, and failing gracefully.
  6. One real, shipped productProof. Nobody hires from a certificate. They hire from a repo and a write-up.

Skipped on purpose

  • The math of how models learn, and building a transformer from scratch
  • Training models: GPUs, CUDA, big clusters
  • Fine-tuning as a first move (you get exactly one day of it, on purpose)
  • Older machine-learning pipelines and feature engineering
  • Building your own vector database or embedding model
  • Reading every new research paper
  • Comparing six agent frameworks before writing any code

None of this is worthless. All of it is a worse use of your next three months. Come back to it after the course, when a real project shows you which gap actually hurts.

Day 0

The check before you start

Do this before Day 1, and be honest. Everything on the list is taught in Week 0, so you only take the days you are missing. Starting without Python is the most common way this course fails.

How you work

Ground rules — these matter more than the lessons

  • 01Mostly building. Learn a little, then spend the rest of the round trying, breaking and fixing.
  • 02Close the page before you build. Say the idea out loud from memory first. If you cannot, read it once more, then close the page again.
  • 03Every day ends with a commit. No exceptions, even when the day went badly.
  • 04Stuck for 10 minutes? Open a hint. Stuck for 45? Ship the ugly version. Write down what is missing and move on.
  • 05One public repo per weekly project. Four of them by the end.
  • 06Write down numbers. Cost per request, p95 latency, eval score. Numbers are what make you believable.
  • 07No framework until you feel the pain it solves. Use the plain SDK for a whole week, then you understand every tool you add later.
  • 08Keep the error log. Four short lines for every mistake. It becomes your Day 29 write-up.

The work

Every day, in order

Each day is a few rounds. Each round is 90 minutes: warm up from memory, learn one small chunk, close the page, try something hard, then study your mistakes. Week 0 is optional. Take the check on the Overview and do only what you are missing. Your progress saves in this browser.

No day matches that.

The method

Read less. Pull more out of your head.

Most people learn by reading, watching, and reading again. It feels smooth, and it works badly. This course flips it. You take in a little, then you spend most of your time pulling it back out, trying it, and using it. The struggle is not a sign that something is wrong. It is the learning.

Here is why. Re-reading gives you the feeling of knowing. Trying to remember gives you the knowing itself. Your brain keeps what it has to work to find. So every part of this course is built to make you find things, not just look at them.

The loop

Eight moves, in a circle

This is the whole method. Every day in the course is built from it, so you never have to remember to do it yourself.

  1. Draw a rough map first.Spend 20 to 30 minutes seeing what a subject contains: the big ideas, the words, and how the pieces connect. Don’t try to learn any of it yet. Every week starts with a map page.
  2. Learn one small chunk.Read just enough to understand one idea. Stop before you feel completely comfortable. That is on purpose.
  3. Close it, then rebuild it from memory.Write what you remember, say it out loud, draw the system, retype the code. This is called retrieval practice, and it beats re-reading by a lot.
  4. Do something hard with it, right away.Solve a problem, build something, debug an example. If you succeed every time, the task is too easy. Make it harder.
  5. Study your mistakes.Don’t just fix them. Ask what you got wrong, why, which idea you were missing, and how you will spot it next time.
  6. Explain it simply.Teach it to a smart person who doesn’t know the subject. Every “basically” or “something happens here” is a gap you just found.
  7. Come back after longer and longer gaps.Same day, next day, three days, a week, two weeks, a month. Test yourself each time. Don’t just look again.
  8. Mix related problems.Don’t do thirty of the same kind. Mix kinds, so you have to decide which method fits. That decision is most of what expertise is.
Your sitting

One round: 90 minutes

Every day in the course is cut into rounds, and every round has the same five parts. At 3 hours a day you do two rounds. That is one study day.

MinutesPartWhat you do
10Warm-upAnswer questions from earlier rounds, from memory. The page picks them for you. Write an answer before you open the check.
25LearnOne or two small ideas, with a picture. Read once. Then close the page and say it back: that takes two minutes and is worth ten of re-reading.
40TryBuild the thing before you read the steps. Three hints wait, and you open them one at a time. Being stuck here is the point.
10MistakesFour questions in your error log. Check your work against the traps listed for the round.
5TomorrowRead the one sentence that says what you must be able to rebuild tomorrow, then stop.

Between round 2 and round 3, you sleep. That is not a break from the method. It is part of it, because sleep is when your brain files things away.

Four rungs

Recognition is not understanding

A common mistake is to stop at “I’ve seen this before” and believe that means you know it. It doesn’t. There are four rungs, and each day ends by asking which one you are on.

The error log

Study your mistakes. Don’t just fix them.

Every round has four boxes. When something goes wrong, write one line in each. It takes two minutes. It is where a lot of your progress comes from, because one understood mistake removes a whole family of them.

  1. What did I get wrong?
  2. Why did I get it wrong?
  3. What idea was I missing?
  4. How will I spot this next time?

A real example

  • Wrong: my summary got cut off in the middle of a sentence.
  • Why: I set max_tokens to 100 and thought that meant 100 words.
  • Missing idea: a token is a chunk of text, roughly three quarters of a word.
  • Next time: whenever I see a limit, I ask what it counts, and I check the stop reason.

Your entries live in the Error log tab. They stay in this browser.

Coming back

Test yourself again, on a schedule

The warm-up at the top of every round pulls one question from the round you finished last, one from the round before, and others from about three days, a week, two weeks and a month back. It only asks about rounds you have ticked as done. Try to answer each one before you open the check.

If you get a warm-up question wrong, that is good news. You just found something to fix while it is still cheap. Write it in the error log.

Why it is built this way

Courses give you ingredients. Projects make you cook.

Pick something slightly too hard

Each week ends with something you ship. It is a little beyond what you can do on Monday. That gap is what makes the ideas connect.

Getting stuck is allowed

Research the one thing you are stuck on, fix it, keep going. Afterwards, explain the whole thing from start to finish without looking anything up.

Too easy means too easy

If you answer everything right, make the task harder. Change the input, remove a hint, add a limit. Success every time means you are not learning.

    Interview practice

    Fifteen questions to answer cold

    If one of these makes you uncomfortable, that is your next study session. Try answering each one out loud, with the page closed.

    1. RAG, fine-tuning, or a longer prompt: how do you choose?
    2. How do you split documents into chunks, and why that size?
    3. What does hybrid search fix that plain vector search cannot?
    4. What is a reranker, where does it sit, and what does it cost in speed?
    5. How do you test a RAG system, and how did you build the golden set?
    6. LLM-as-judge: how do you know the judge itself is any good?
    7. How do you stop prompt injection that arrives through retrieved documents?
    8. What is your p95 latency, and where exactly does the time go?
    9. Break down your cost per request.
    10. When is an agent the wrong design?
    11. What happens when the model returns invalid JSON?
    12. What does prompt caching change about how you write a prompt?
    13. How do you version prompts and roll back a drop in quality?
    14. What breaks when you switch model providers?
    15. How do you decide something is good enough to ship, without going on gut feeling?

    Change the pace, not the order

    If 3 hours a day is not your situation

    1–2 hours a day

    One round a day. Same order, same rounds, about twice as many weeks. Keep the warm-ups and protect the ship days (7, 14, 21, 25–27); that is where the learning locks in.

    5–6 hours a day

    Three or four rounds a day. The whole course fits in about seven weeks. Do not skip the sleep between rounds. Put the second half of the day after a real break.

    Only ten days

    Days 1, 2, 3, 5 → 8, 9, 10, 11 → 15, and 18–19 merged. You get structured output, a measured RAG system, tool use and a test harness. Ship one project instead of four.

    Already a backend developer

    Squeeze week 1 into days 2, 3 and 5, and spend the time you saved on days 11, 18 and 19. Testing and retrieval quality are where experienced engineers still have the biggest gap.

    Honest expectations

    Three focused months gets you to junior-to-mid AI engineer, employable, with proof: someone who can own an LLM feature from start to finish. It does not make you senior. That comes from real incidents, real users and real scale, which take time you cannot squeeze. Anyone selling the second outcome in three months is selling something.

    What the course really gives you is the part that compounds: four systems shipped, measured, and broken on purpose. After that, every new model release is a small change on top of a foundation you own, instead of one more thing you feel behind on.

    terminal
    a window where you type commands and see text output
    environment
    a folder with its own set of packages so projects do not interfere with each other
    exception
    an error message that stops your code and says why
    HTTP request
    a message your code sends to a web server, in a format the server understands
    repository

    Before Day 0.1 (25 minutes): read this map once. Then close it and draw the week on paper from memory: the big ideas, the words, and arrows for how they connect. Open it again and fix what you missed. Do not try to learn anything yet.

    The terminal looks like a puzzle, but it is one small machine following five rules. Once you know the rules, error messages turn from noise into instructions. Today you learn the rules — and you break an install on purpose so the first real failure doesn't scare you.

    The shell is a loop that runs programs

    The shell is not the computer. It is one program. It sits in a loop all day, doing the same thing over and over until you close the window.

    The loop goes like this. Print a prompt. Wait for you to type a line. Split that line into words at the spaces. Take the first word as the name of a program, and every word after it as an argument. Start the program. Wait for it to finish. Show what it printed. Print the prompt again. Loop.

    Nothing you type is understood more deeply than this. The shell is not reading your intent. It is splitting a line into words and launching the first one.

    When you use tools like find, you give it a starting directory and then filters. For example, find drill -name "*.py" searches from the drill folder for files matching a pattern. Or find drill -type f -size +1k finds regular files larger than one kilobyte.

    One thing the shell holds in its head is the working directory — where you are standing. pwd prints it. cd changes it. ls lists what is there.

    Every path you type is resolved from that spot. A path starting with / is absolute — the same thing no matter where you stand. Anything else starts from where you are, where . means here, .. means the directory above, and ~ means your home.

    So: the shell cuts your line into words at spaces and runs the first word, starting from wherever you are standing.

    shell
    a program that reads your lines and runs other programs
    working directory
    where you are standing — where relative paths start
    absolute path
    a path starting with / that means the same thing everywhere

    Spaces and quotes: why filenames matter

    A file is called my notes.txt. You type that at the shell. The shell splits on spaces and sees four words: my, notes.txt, and two others. It runs the program my and hands it the rest as arguments.

    The program looks for a file called my. It doesn't exist. The program reports an error. The filename was never split into words by the program. The shell did the splitting before the program even saw the line.

    So you quote it: "my notes.txt". Now the shell sees one word and hands it as one argument. The program gets the whole name.

    Here is the rule: the shell splits on spaces. No program can fix that for you after the fact. Quoting happens before any program runs.

    So: quote any filename with a space in it, and the program gets it whole.

    quote
    wrap text in " to treat it as one word even if it has spaces
    space
    the character the shell uses to split words

    Close the page. Answer out loud, then write one sentence for each.

    1. What does the shell do in its loop, word by word?
    2. A file is called my notes.txt. If you type that without quotes, how many arguments does the program see?
    3. What is the difference between /home/user/file and ~/file?

    Your goal: navigate around the filesystem using pwd, cd, and ls. Create a folder with files in it. List those files. Try one command without quoting and one with quoting a filename that has a space.

    Hint 1 — a nudge

    Open a terminal. Start with pwd. Then cd to a few places. Then mkdir to make a folder, and touch to make some files. Use both relative paths (like ./folder) and absolute paths.

    Hint 2 — the shape of the answer

    Make a folder called drill. Inside it, create a few files with names that have spaces in them. List them with ls, then try to run a command on one filename without quotes, watch it fail, then quote the filename and watch it work.

    Still stuck after 10 minutes? The step by step
    1. Open a terminal. Run pwd, then cd ~.
    2. Run mkdir -p drill/src drill/data to create a folder structure with subdirectories.
    3. Run cd drill, then pwd again to confirm where you are.
    4. Create a file with a space in the name: touch "my notes.txt".
    5. Run ls. You see the file listed.
    6. Run file my notes.txt and watch it fail because it looks for my.
    7. Run file "my notes.txt" and watch it work. That is how quoting saves you.
    • Typing a filename with spaces and no quotes, then blaming the program for not understanding you.
    • Using relative paths and forgetting where you are standing. Run pwd anytime you are unsure.

    • What does the shell do in its loop?

      It prints a prompt, reads a line, splits it into words at spaces, runs the first word as a program with the rest as arguments, shows the output, and loops.

    • A program named open receives two arguments. You type open my file.txt without quotes. How many arguments does it actually see, and what are they?

      Three: my, file.txt, and nothing else. The space split the filename. Quote it as open "my file.txt" to fix it.

    • What is the difference between /home/user/file and ~/file?

      /home/user/file is absolute — it means the same thing from anywhere. ~/file means file in your home directory, also absolute but shorter.

    By tomorrow you can reproduce: the shell loop, why spaces matter, and the difference between relative and absolute paths, all from memory.

    Every program has three streams

    Every program that runs gets three flows: one to read from, and two to write to. They have names: standard input, standard output, standard error.

    Normally, input comes from your keyboard. Output and error both print to the screen. But the split is deliberate. It means you can keep the results and throw away the noise, or read the noise and ignore the results, without either one getting mixed up.

    Think of a restaurant with two separate doors out: one for dishes and one for complaints. The kitchen can send clean dishes out the first door and broken plates out the second. A diner can pick up only good dishes and ignore the complaints, or read the complaints and ignore the dishes.

    Redirection changes where those streams go. > sends output to a file, replacing what was there. >> appends to a file. 2> sends error to a file — the 2 is just that stream's number. No redirection for input is rare, but < reads from a file instead of the keyboard.

    So: output and error leave through different doors, and you can send each where you want.

    standard input
    where a program reads from, usually the keyboard
    standard output
    where results go, usually the screen
    standard error
    where complaints go, usually the screen but separate from output

    The pipe: connecting programs

    A pipe is a hose from one program's output into the next one's input. It is the character |. Data flows through the chain without ever touching the disk.

    Errors stay out of the pipe. They take a separate road to your screen. That is why a broken stage in a pipeline prints to you instead of poisoning the data downstream.

    You build a pipeline one stage at a time. Start with one program. Run it. See the output. Pipe that into a second program. Run it. Keep adding until you have what you want.

    So: the pipe connects programs so data flows through without touching the disk.

    pipe
    the | character that connects one program's output to the next program's input
    chain
    multiple programs connected by pipes

    Close the page. Answer out loud, then write one sentence for each.

    1. Why are stdout and stderr separate?
    2. What does > do, and what does >> do?
    3. In a chain of commands connected by pipes, where do errors go?

    Your goal: build a pipeline that searches files, sorts the results, counts them, and keeps only the top five. Use redirection to save the results to a file, and errors to a different file. Confirm that errors never reached the results file.

    Hint 1 — a nudge

    Start simple. Use grep with --recursive to search a folder and all subdirectories. Then add sort. Then uniq -c to count. Then head -5 to take the top five. Run after each addition to see what each stage does.

    Hint 2 — the shape of the answer

    Search for lines with a word like TODO in a folder of files. The command looks like grep -rn TODO . | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5 > report.txt 2> problems.txt. Open both files and confirm the errors never reached the results.

    Still stuck after 10 minutes? The step by step
    1. Create a folder with a few text files, each with some lines containing TODO and some not.
    2. Run grep -rn TODO drill. The flags -r means recursive (search all subdirectories) and -n shows line numbers.
    3. Try grep -rho "TODO.*" drill where -o prints only the matching parts. See all the TODO lines extracted.
    4. Pipe that into sort: grep -rho "TODO.*" drill | sort. See the lines sorted.
    5. Pipe that into uniq -c: grep -rho "TODO.*" drill | sort | uniq -c. See counts of identical lines.
    6. Add sort -rn | head -5 to see the top five. Use -l with ls to show a long listing with all file details.
    7. Redirect both streams to files: ... > report.txt 2> problems.txt. Open both files and verify errors never reached the results.

    Mix it in. From Round 1: does your pipeline still work if one of your filenames has a space in it? Try it. What happens if you do not quote the filename?

    • Building a pipeline all at once and not testing each stage. Build one stage, run it, see the output, then add the next.
    • Piping data and errors together by mistake, so errors contaminate the data stream.

    • Why are stdout and stderr separate?

      So you can keep results and throw away noise, or read noise and ignore results, without them mixing. You can save them to LOG.md or separate files for later review.

    • You run a command that sends results to output.txt and errors to errors.txt. The command fails partway through. Where are the partial results and the error message?

      Partial results are in output.txt because that file captures stdout before the program stops. The error is in errors.txt.

    • In a pipeline, where do errors go?

      Errors do not flow through the pipe. They skip the whole chain and print to your screen.

    By tomorrow you can reproduce: how to build a pipeline one stage at a time, why >, >>, and 2> do different things, and where errors go.

    PATH and finding programs

    Every running process carries a dictionary of names and values called its environment. env prints yours. There is nothing mystical in there, just names like HOME and values like /home/yourname.

    One of those names is PATH. Its value is a list of directories separated by colons. When you type python, the shell walks that list from left to right, looking for a file named python in each directory. It runs the first one it finds and stops looking. It does not search your whole disk. which python tells you which one won.

    You can set an environment variable for one command by putting it in front: DEBUG=1 python app.py. Or for the rest of the session with export DEBUG=1. Here is the rule that catches people: environments pass from parent to child, never sideways. Set a variable in one window and a second terminal window knows nothing about it, because that window is not the first one's child.

    So: a program is findable only if its directory is on PATH, and the leftmost match wins.

    environment
    a dictionary of named values that a process carries and passes to its children
    PATH
    an environment variable holding a colon-separated list of directories to search for programs
    which
    a command that shows which file matched when you typed a program name

    Reading an error message from the top

    A failed install prints hundreds of lines. The last one is almost always useless: command failed with exit code 1. That is the symptom, not the cause.

    The cause is higher up. Scroll back to the first line containing error, fatal, No such file, or Permission denied. Read that line literally, word by word. It names a file, a version, or a missing piece. That name is usually the whole answer. Everything after is wreckage.

    Programs also report success with a plain number. Zero means it worked. Anything else means it didn't. echo $? prints the number from the last command.

    Most install failures fall into one of three kinds. The thing isn't on PATH. You're writing to a directory you don't own. Or something needs a version you don't have. Before you type a fix, name which of the three it is.

    So: the last line tells you it broke, the first error line tells you why, and there are only three usual whys.

    exit code
    a number a program reports: zero means success, anything else means failure
    error line
    the first line in a log containing error, fatal, or denied — this is the cause, not the symptom

    Close the page. Answer out loud, then write one sentence for each.

    1. Why does command not found happen, and what is which for?
    2. You set export DEBUG=1 in one window. Why doesn't a second window see it?
    3. An install prints 500 lines and fails. Where do you look first?

    Your goal: break an install on purpose and read the error message top to bottom. Name which of the three kinds of failure it is. Fix it using only what you learned — no sudo, no guessing.

    Hint 1 — a nudge

    Use a tool you can install that has a simple name, like a text utility. Introduce a failure on purpose — like removing a directory from PATH or trying to install into a directory you don't own. Watch the install fail. Scroll to the first error line. Read it literally.

    Hint 2 — the shape of the answer

    Export a broken PATH: export PATH=/usr/bin:/bin. Try to run a command that is in ~/.local/bin. Watch it fail with command not found. Understand why. Fix it by restoring the PATH. Then run --help on a command and read a flag you never used.

    Still stuck after 10 minutes? The step by step
    1. Open a terminal and run echo $PATH to see the current PATH.
    2. Run export PATH=/usr/bin:/bin to break the PATH.
    3. Try to run a command that is in ~/.local/bin, like uv. Watch it fail with command not found.
    4. Run which uv — it returns nothing, confirming the directory is not on PATH.
    5. Run export PATH=/usr/local/bin:~/.local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin to fix it.
    6. Run the same command again. It works. That was a PATH failure.
    7. Run man ls and --help on two other commands. Find a flag you didn't know existed.

    Mix it in. From Round 2: when you broke the PATH and ran a command, where did the error message go — stdout or stderr? Check with redirection.

    • Reading only the last line of a long failure and never scrolling up to the first error line.
    • Reaching for sudo at the first permission error. It writes files as the administrator, so the next command fails in a stranger way because those files aren't yours.
    • Setting an environment variable in one window and expecting another window to see it. Environments are inherited by children, not siblings.

    • Why does command not found happen?

      The program is not in any of the directories on PATH. which shows you which one matched, or nothing if it isn't found.

    • You export PATH=/usr/bin. Now you cannot run ls even though it is installed. Why?

      ls is in /bin, not /usr/bin. Your new PATH does not include /bin, so the shell cannot find it.

    • An install prints 500 lines and fails. Where do you look?

      Scroll back to the first error line, not the last line. The first error line names the cause. Everything after is wreckage.

    By tomorrow you can reproduce: how PATH works, why environments pass to children, and how to read an error message from the cause instead of the symptom.

    Teach it back

    Explain this to a smart friend who has never used a terminal. What happens when you type a command and press Enter? How do the three streams work? Where do errors go in a pipeline? Start from the moment you type and use five to seven sentences. Say it out loud, or write it down.

    Watch for the words "basically", "something happens here" and "you just". Each one marks a gap. Go back to that spot in the page, fill the gap, and explain again.

    Where are you on the ladder?

    Being able to say "I've seen this" is only the first rung. Climb all four.

    1. I have seen a shell loop and streams before.
    2. I can say what the shell does when you type a line, why spaces matter, what the three streams are, and where PATH comes in, without looking.
    3. Given a new command with flags and a new filename with spaces, I can use redirection and pipes without getting mixed up.
    4. I can read a long install error from the top and identify which of the three kinds of failure it is, then fix it.

    Today you learn the third of Python this course actually types. You learn how code is organized into pieces you can test, what to keep in a container and what to throw out, and why one simple annotation saves hours later. By tonight, one command should rebuild your project environment from nothing, and your own program should run on the first try.

    Functions that do one thing

    A function takes named inputs and hands back one value. Think of a kitchen tool: a grater has one job, and it does it well. A function that tries to grate and also mix is a tool nobody wants to use.

    Keep each function small enough to describe in a single sentence. Give it exactly one job. The reason is not tidiness. A function that does one thing is a function you can test on its own — test one thing, know one thing worked. Next week you will be writing tests, and every function that does three things makes testing harder.

    A module is just a file. There is no registration, no manifest. A file named counter.py is a module named counter.

    So what does import counter actually do? Three things happen. Python finds the file counter.py. It runs that file from top to bottom, exactly once. It stores the result in a table of loaded modules. A second import counter anywhere else in your program hands back the cached one without re-running a single line.

    That one fact explains why code at the top level of a file runs when somebody imports it. Importing is running.

    One guard stops that. The variable __name__ holds "__main__" only inside the file you actually ran. Anything under if __name__ == "__main__": fires when you run the file and stays quiet when someone imports it. This is where you usually put the command-line entry point, where you parse argparse arguments and call your functions.

    So: keep functions small, one file is one module, and importing runs it exactly once.

    function
    a piece of code with a name, inputs, and one output
    module
    a file of Python code that can be imported
    import
    the command that finds and runs a module exactly once, then shares the result

    Close the page. Answer without looking.

    1. You import a file twice in different places in your code. How many times does the file run?
    2. Why should a function have exactly one job, not three?

    Your goal: write two small functions in one module file, import that module in a second file, and use both functions. Nothing fancy — just separate them and call them.

    Hint 1 — a nudge

    One function counts words in text. Another counts lines. Write them in a file called counter.py. Then write a second file that imports and calls them both. Start with function signatures like def read_text(path: str) -> str: for reading and def tokenize(text: str) -> list[str]: for splitting.

    Hint 2 — the shape of the answer

    Each function takes one argument and returns one number. Name them clearly: count_words and count_lines. The second file imports the module and calls both functions on a piece of text you write. Add from counter import count_words for selective imports too.

    Still stuck after 10 minutes? The step by step
    1. Create a file called counter.py with two functions. The first takes text and returns the word count; the second takes text and returns the line count.
    2. Create a second file that imports counter and calls both functions on the same text.
    3. Run the second file. Both functions should produce numbers.
    • Code at the top level of a module runs when you import it, which breaks your other imports if it tries to do something that needs setup.
    • A function that takes three arguments, does three things, and is impossible to test in isolation.

    • What happens when you import the same module twice in your code?

      The file runs once the first time. Every other import returns the cached result without running anything.

    • You write a function that counts words, removes duplicates, and converts to lowercase. Should this be one function or three?

      Three. Each one does one job and can be tested separately. Build each one, test it, then chain them together.

    By tomorrow you can reproduce: two simple functions in a module, and why they run once when you import them.

    Lists, dicts, and the loop that builds them

    Four containers hold almost all the data you will write. A list is an ordered sequence you can change. A dict maps keys to values, and it is the shape almost all API data arrives in. A set holds unique items and answers the question "is this in here?" instantly. A tuple is a small fixed record.

    Most of the time, you build a container from existing data. A comprehension is a loop that builds a container on one line: [w.lower() for w in words if w.isalpha()]. Read it left to right: what to keep, what to loop over, what to skip.

    One extra tool counts things. collections.Counter is a dict that keeps score. Counter(words).most_common(10) is your entire "ten most common items" feature, finished in one line.

    Here is where it gets useful. (w.lower() for w in words if w.isalpha()) swaps brackets for parentheses. You get a generator instead of a list. It builds nothing. It produces one item, waits, and produces the next when asked. That is the difference between streaming a two-gigabyte file through your program and running out of memory.

    So: dicts and lists carry your data, a comprehension builds one in a line, and a generator hands items over one at a time without building them all.

    list
    an ordered, changeable sequence
    dict
    a mapping from keys to values
    comprehension
    a one-line loop that builds a container
    generator
    a comprehension with parentheses that produces one item at a time

    Close the page. Answer from memory.

    1. You need to check if a name is in a list of ten thousand names. Should you use a list or a set?
    2. Write a one-line comprehension that keeps only words that are longer than three letters.

    Your goal: a function that takes a list of words and returns the ten most common ones, using Counter and a comprehension to filter out short words. Use from counter import top_words to test it.

    Hint 1 — a nudge

    You already learned Counter. It counts words for you. Now filter the input with a comprehension before you send it to Counter — keep only words longer than 2 letters.

    Hint 2 — the shape of the answer

    A comprehension is one line. One for-loop to filter, one Counter to count, one call to most_common(10) to rank them. Chain them together.

    Still stuck after 10 minutes? The step by step
    1. Write a one-line comprehension: [w for w in words if len(w) > 2].
    2. Pass that to Counter: Counter(...).most_common(10).
    3. Test it on a real list of words from the Round 1 function.

    Mix it in. Your Round 1 function returns a word count and a line count. Store them in a dict with keys "words" and "lines". Then print the dict.

    • Nesting comprehensions too deep. If you can't read it aloud in one breath, write the loop on separate lines.
    • A mutable default argument like def f(items=[]): — the list is created once at function definition and shared by every call forever. Use None instead and create the list inside the function.
    • Building the entire list with brackets when you only need one item at a time — a generator with parentheses is faster and uses less memory.

    • You need to check if a value is in a collection of one million items. Use a list or a set, and why?

      Use a set. Lists check every item one by one. Sets check in one step, no matter the size.

    • You have a list of sentences and want to count how many words appear in all of them. What data structure do you reach for first, and why?

      Sets. Convert each sentence to a set of words, then use set operations to find words that appear in all of them.

    By tomorrow you can reproduce: a one-line comprehension and a one-line dict lookup, from memory.

    Type hints that other tools enforce

    Write def top_words(path: str, n: int = 10) -> dict[str, int]: and Python stores those annotations as data — then ignores them completely at runtime.

    Pass a list where you promised a string and nothing stops you. Your program runs on happily until something further down tries to use it and crashes, usually somewhere that looks unrelated. Python does not check types when your code runs. Say that out loud once, so you never expect it to at two in the morning.

    So why write them? Because other tools read them, and those tools do check. Your editor reads them and flags the mistake as you type. A tool called mypy reads them and flags mistakes before you run anything.

    The real payoff arrives later. Pydantic is a library that reads these same annotations and enforces them at runtime: when data arrives from the internet, Pydantic checks it against your declared types and raises an error if anything doesn't fit. Every annotation you write now is a contract you get to enforce later, at the exact boundary where untrusted data walks in. When you need a typed record and nothing more, use @dataclass, which writes the boilerplate for you.

    So: the annotation does nothing by itself, but three different tools read it and catch mistakes you would otherwise spend hours finding.

    type hint
    an annotation saying what type a function expects and returns
    mypy
    a tool that checks type hints before you run code
    Pydantic
    a library that enforces type hints at runtime when data arrives

    One environment per project

    Installing a package copies files into a directory called site-packages. That is all an install is — a copy. If there is one such directory for the whole machine, every project shares one copy of everything. The day project A needs version 1 of a library and project B needs version 2, one of them breaks — usually the one you are not looking at.

    A virtual environment fixes that by being simple. It is a directory, conventionally .venv, holding its own site-packages and its own python inside it. Activating it does not enter a magic mode. It puts .venv/bin at the front of your PATH, so the word python resolves there first. Run which python to see which one you're using.

    The tool uv makes this routine. uv init starts a project. uv add httpx installs a package and records that you depend on it. Then you can import httpx in your code. uv run script.py executes your code inside the environment without activating anything. The lockfile it writes pins exact versions, so a fresh machine reproduces yours instead of approximating it.

    Here is the habit: treat the environment as disposable. Deleting one is rm -rf .venv and rebuilding takes seconds. Once that round trip is routine, a broken environment stops being a crisis. The uv docs are short; read the project section properly once.

    So: one package directory per project, one shared interpreter, and a rebuild cheap enough that you delete rather than debug.

    type hint
    an annotation saying what type a function expects and returns
    mypy
    a tool that checks type hints before you run code
    virtual environment
    a private folder holding packages for one project
    uv
    a tool that makes and installs packages into environments

    Close the page. Say or write the answer.

    1. You put type hints in your code but Python ignores them. Where else do they get read?
    2. You delete your .venv folder and rebuild it. Should you need to write uv init again?

    Your goal: the command line tool from Rounds 1 and 2, now with full type hints on every function. Run mypy on it and fix every warning. Then delete .venv and rebuild it in one command to confirm your environment is reproducible.

    Hint 1 — a nudge

    Add type hints to the functions you wrote in Rounds 1 and 2. Every input gets a type, and every function declares what it returns. For example: def summarize(tokens: list[str], n: int = 10) -> dict[str, int]:.

    Hint 2 — the shape of the answer

    Use dict[str, int] for a dict of words and counts, list[str] for a list of words. Create a project with uv init wordstat, then uv add typer for the CLI (or use argparse from the standard library). Run uv add mypy, then uv run mypy wordstat.py. Fix whatever it finds.

    Still stuck after 10 minutes? The step by step
    1. Run uv init wordstat. Add any packages you need with uv add typer.
    2. Write the functions with full type hints. Every input argument and the return value get a type.
    3. Add the entry point: parse one file argument and an optional --top flag. Guard it with if __name__ == "__main__":.
    4. Run uv run mypy wordstat.py to check them. Fix every error.
    5. Delete .venv entirely: rm -rf .venv.
    6. Rebuild with uv sync. Run mypy again. If it works, your environment is reproducible.
    7. Run your CLI on a test file: uv run wordstat.py somefile.txt --top 5. It should work on the first try.

    Mix it in. Look at your type hints. Which function would be hardest to use wrong? Which is most likely to break because of a type mistake?

    • Type hints that do not run. Only mypy and your editor read them. Never expect Python to catch a type mistake at runtime without a separate tool.
    • Naming your file json.py or types.py in the project root, which shadows the standard library and produces an error message that names neither file.

    • Python ignores type hints when your code runs. Where do they actually get read?

      Your editor reads them as you type. A tool like mypy reads them before you run. Later, Pydantic reads them and enforces them at runtime when data arrives.

    • You wrote a function that takes a dict and returns a list. Write the type hint for the function signature.

      def myfunction(data: dict[str, int]) -> list[str]: (or with your own types, but every argument and return gets a type).

    By tomorrow you can reproduce: the full typed tool, running mypy without errors, from a fresh environment built in one command.

    Teach it back

    Explain today to a smart friend who has never written Python. What are functions for, what's a dict versus a list, and why would you write type hints if Python ignores them? Start from a real example: reading a text file and counting words. Use three to four sentences.

    Watch for the words "basically", "something happens here" and "you just". Each one marks a gap. Go back to that spot in the page, fill the gap, and explain again.

    Where are you on the ladder?

    Four rungs: from seeing it to building it.

    1. I have seen functions, dicts, and type hints before.
    2. I can explain what a module is and why a dict is faster than a list for lookups.
    3. Given a blob of text, I can write a comprehension to filter and count words.
    4. I can write a full typed CLI tool that reads files and counts, with mypy passing and the environment reproducible.

    Three things separate code that talks to the internet from code that doesn't: what happens when a call fails, how one thread does ten things at once, and how you prove that it all still works. Today you build a downloader that does all three, and you time it — because the timing is the whole lesson.

    Exceptions are a second way out

    A function has two exits. One is return. The other is raise, and it does not go back the way it came.

    When something raises, Python stops mid-function and unwinds the call stack. It discards the current frame and looks in the caller for an except clause that matches the error type. If there isn't one, it discards that frame too and looks in the caller's caller. And so on, upward. If nobody catches it, the program stops and prints the traceback.

    Read a Python traceback from the bottom: the bottom line is the actual error (like NameError or TimeoutException), and the lines above it show the route it took. That is the opposite of an install log, where the cause is at the top.

    Now the rule that saves hours: catch narrowly. except httpx.TimeoutException: says you thought about one specific failure and decided what to do. except Exception: catches your own typos and bugs, turning a five-second fix into an hour of debugging. Bare except: is worse: it also swallows the interrupt you press to stop the program.

    Catch only where you can act: retry, substitute a default, record the failure and move on. Anywhere else, let the error travel up to code that can handle it. When you re-raise something wrapped in your own error, write raise MyError(...) from err so the original cause stays attached.

    So: a raise unwinds upward until a matching except stops it. Catch the specific error you named, where you can actually act on it.

    exception
    an error that stops the normal flow and travels up the call stack
    raise
    the command that throws an exception
    except
    the clause that catches an exception and decides what to do

    Context managers guarantee cleanup

    Write with open(path) as f: and two things happen for you automatically: one on the way into the block, one on the way out.

    Here is the part that matters: the way out includes the exception path. The file closes whether the block finishes normally or crashes in the middle. You don't have to remember, and you can't forget.

    This matters more for network clients than for files. A network client holds open sockets. If an exception skips your cleanup, that socket leaks. Do it ten thousand times in a loop and you exhaust the operating system's file handles. The error message will mention handles or descriptors — it will not mention the raise three functions away that actually caused it.

    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client: costs one line and removes the whole category of bugs. try/finally is the same guarantee written out by hand.

    So: with is a promise that cleanup runs even when the code inside it fails — which is exactly when cleanup otherwise gets skipped.

    context manager
    a with statement that guarantees setup and cleanup, even if an exception happens
    async with
    a context manager for async code that sets up and cleans up around an await

    Close the page. Answer without looking.

    1. An exception raises three levels deep. How does Python find the code that catches it?
    2. You open a file without a with statement and an error happens. What happens to the file?

    Your goal: a function that fetches a URL and returns the status code and byte count. It catches the specific error (timeout), returns a record with the error set, and does not let the exception escape. One dead URL must not crash the whole program. Use uv add httpx pytest pytest-asyncio to set up.

    Hint 1 — a nudge

    Use httpx.get(url, timeout=10) inside a try/except. Catch httpx.HTTPError narrowly. Return a small record: url, status, bytes, error.

    Hint 2 — the shape of the answer

    The function returns the same record structure whether it succeeds or fails. Success has status and bytes. Failure has the error message and None for status and bytes. Then call it on a list of five URLs, some good and some broken.

    Still stuck after 10 minutes? The step by step
    1. Write def fetch(url: str) -> dict: that returns a record with url, status, bytes, and error.
    2. Call httpx.get(url, timeout=10) inside try/except. Catch httpx.HTTPError and set the error field.
    3. Call it on five URLs: a real site, a slow site (set timeout to 0.5), and three URLs you make up.
    4. Print the records. No exception should escape.
    • Catching except Exception, which swallows your own typos and bugs. Catch the specific error you named.
    • No timeout on a request. The default in some clients is to wait forever, so one unresponsive server hangs your whole program with no error.

    • When an exception raises, how does Python know where to catch it?

      It travels up the call stack, frame by frame, until it finds an except clause whose type matches. If none matches, the program stops.

    • You have a function that opens a file and parses it. An error during parsing leaves the file open. What do you add to fix it?

      Wrap the code in a with statement. The file closes even if an exception happens inside the block.

    By tomorrow you can reproduce: a try/except that catches one specific error, and why broad catches hide bugs.

    One thread, ten downloads

    Downloading is mostly waiting. You send a request and for the next 300 milliseconds your program does nothing while bytes travel. Do that ten times in a row and you spend three seconds being almost entirely idle. No amount of faster code fixes it, because your code was never the bottleneck.

    async def defines a coroutine: a function that can suspend itself in the middle. await on an I/O operation means "register interest with the operating system, then hand control back." Hand it back to what? The event loop.

    The event loop is one thread holding a queue of tasks ready to run. It runs one until that task awaits, parks it, and picks up the next. When the operating system reports that bytes have arrived, the parked task goes back in the queue.

    That is why ten downloads started with asyncio.gather finish in about the time of the slowest one, not the sum of all ten. Nothing got faster. The waiting just happened at the same time.

    Math gets nothing from this. A loop multiplying numbers never awaits, so it never yields. The single thread stays occupied and every other task waits behind it. Heavy computation belongs in separate processes.

    One trap looks innocent: a blocking call inside a coroutine — time.sleep, or the old synchronous requests library. It freezes the entire loop and every task in it, and nothing warns you.

    So: one thread does many things by never standing still while waiting — and one blocking call takes all of that away.

    coroutine
    a function that can suspend itself with await
    await
    a command that suspends the coroutine until the I/O is ready
    event loop
    the queue of tasks, running one at a time and switching when they await

    Close the page. Say or write each answer.

    1. You have ten downloads to make, each taking one second. Sync takes ten seconds. How long does async take, roughly?
    2. A math loop in an async function. Will the other tasks get a turn to run?

    Your goal: rewrite your Round 1 function to use async. Fetch the same five URLs concurrently with asyncio.gather. Time both versions with time.perf_counter. The async version should be much faster.

    Hint 1 — a nudge

    Change httpx.get to httpx.AsyncClient and await. Wrap the fetch call in asyncio.gather. Time the whole thing.

    Hint 2 — the shape of the answer

    Write a sync version first and time it. Then: async def fetch(client, url) inside async def main(), then asyncio.run(main()). Use async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client and await asyncio.gather(...).

    Still stuck after 10 minutes? The step by step
    1. Write the sync version first: loop calling httpx.get(url, timeout=10). Time it with time.perf_counter.
    2. Write an async version: async def fetch(client, url) using client.get(url) with await.
    3. Use async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client: and await asyncio.gather(*[fetch(client, u) for u in urls]).
    4. Time it. Compare.

    Mix it in. Look at both timings in your LOG.md. If sync took 3.1 seconds and async took 0.42 seconds, what does that tell you about which URL was slowest?

    • A blocking call inside a coroutine, like time.sleep or the old requests library. Everything still works and nothing is faster, which is the most confusing outcome.
    • Firing all ten thousand URLs at once with gather. Concurrency needs a ceiling — a semaphore or bounded pool — or you get rate-limited and blocked.

    • One thread runs ten concurrent downloads. The slowest takes 1 second, the fastest 0.3 seconds. How long does the async version take?

      About 1 second, the time of the slowest. The waiting all happens at the same time, so total time is the maximum, not the sum.

    • You write an async function that has a tight loop multiplying numbers. Will other tasks get a turn?

      No. The loop never awaits, so the thread stays occupied and other tasks wait. Concurrency only helps when tasks await (usually on I/O).

    By tomorrow you can reproduce: the shape of an async function, asyncio.gather, and why the async version is faster than sync.

    Pytest finds tests by name

    pytest finds your tests by looking for files called test_*.py and functions called test_*. No base class, no registration. Just name them and write the function.

    You assert with the plain assert keyword. When an assertion fails, pytest rewrites the statement and shows you both sides of the comparison instead of just "false". That display is most of the reason to use pytest.

    Run everything with pytest. Run one file with pytest tests/test_fetch.py. Run one test by name with pytest -k name. Add -x to stop at the first failure, which is what you want while you're fixing something.

    Here is the test worth writing first, though: the failure path. with pytest.raises(TimeoutException): asserts that bad input produces the right error instead of a crash or a silent wrong answer that looks fine.

    One rule about the network. Don't test against the live internet. A test that fails when the wifi drops teaches you nothing and trains you to ignore red, which is expensive. Point it at a local server, or use a fake (stub or mock).

    Async tests need a plugin, because pytest itself is synchronous. Install pytest-asyncio, and mark your test with @pytest.mark.asyncio. See the pytest docs for more.

    So: name the file and the function so pytest finds them, assert plainly, and test the failure you are afraid of.

    pytest
    a tool that finds and runs tests by name and shows clear failure messages
    assert
    a plain keyword that checks if something is true; pytest rewrites it for clarity
    pytest.raises
    a context manager that asserts an error is raised with the right type

    Close the page. Without looking, answer this.

    1. You write a test function called my_special_test. Will pytest find it?
    2. Your test checks that a function raises a TimeoutError when given bad input. Write the line that asserts this.

    Your goal: write two tests for your async fetch function: one that checks the success path (url, status, bytes all present) and one that checks the failure path (error is set and no exception escapes).

    Hint 1 — a nudge

    Create a test_fetch.py file. Import pytest and your fetch function. Write test_fetch_success and test_fetch_timeout.

    Hint 2 — the shape of the answer

    For success: call fetch on a real URL and assert the status code and bytes. For timeout: call fetch with timeout=0.001 or a fake that raises, and assert the error field is set and the result is a dict, not an exception.

    Still stuck after 10 minutes? The step by step
    1. Create test_fetch.py. Install pytest-asyncio with uv add pytest-asyncio.
    2. Write @pytest.mark.asyncio async def test_fetch_success(): call fetch on a real URL, assert the status and byte count.
    3. Write @pytest.mark.asyncio async def test_fetch_timeout(): call fetch with timeout=0.001 on a slow URL, assert error is set.
    4. Run pytest -x. Both should pass. Break an assertion on purpose and read what pytest prints.

    Mix it in. Look at your two tests. Which one tests the happy path and which tests what happens when things go wrong? Why do you need both?

    • Testing against the live internet, which fails when the wifi drops and trains you to ignore red.
    • Naming your test file something other than test_*.py, so pytest never finds it.

    • What does pytest look for when searching for tests in your code?

      Files named test_*.py and functions named test_* inside them. No registration or base class needed.

    • You write a test that checks a function raises a ValueError on bad input. How do you write the assertion?

      with pytest.raises(ValueError): followed by the call that should raise. If the error is raised, the test passes.

    By tomorrow you can reproduce: the names pytest looks for, and why testing the failure path matters as much as testing success.

    Teach it back

    Explain today to a smart friend who has never written code that talks to the network. What do you do when a request fails, how does async make ten downloads fast, and why would you write a test for something you expect to fail? Use three to four sentences, starting from a real example.

    Watch for the words "basically", "something happens here" and "you just". Each one marks a gap. Go back to that spot in the page, fill the gap, and explain again.

    Where are you on the ladder?

    Four rungs: from seeing it to building it.

    1. I have heard of exceptions, async, and pytest.
    2. I can explain why a narrow except is better than a broad one, and why async makes I/O faster.
    3. Given a sync downloader, I can rewrite it as async and predict how much faster it will be.
    4. I can write a downloader with error handling, tests for both success and failure, and know why the async version is faster.

    Every call to a model is one HTTP request with a secret in a header. Today you see what that request looks like as actual text, learn what each status code means, and put your key where it cannot leak.

    What an HTTP request looks like

    Strip away any library and an API call is plain text sent down a wire. Your program opens a connection to a host and writes characters into it.

    Think of a letter. You write the address line, then details, then a blank line to signal the headers are done, then the message itself.

    First comes a request line: the method (the verb), the path (the mailbox at that address), and the protocol version. Then headers, one per line. Headers are metadata: they say what the body contains, who you are, and what you understand. Then comes a blank line — that blank line is the whole point, because it tells the server the headers have ended. Then optionally a body.

    The server replies in the same shape: a status line, its own headers, a blank line, a body.

    So: text, then headers, then a blank line that matters, then optionally a body. Nothing magic.

    HTTP
    the protocol that web and API clients use to talk to servers
    method
    the verb that names what you want to do: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE
    header
    one line of metadata about the request or response

    Methods: the verbs of HTTP

    Each method is a promise about what the request does.

    GET fetches data and comes with no body. Running it twice is supposed to give the same answer both times, which is why it is safe to repeat if the network fails.

    POST sends a body and may change something on the server. PUT and PATCH update; DELETE removes.

    The server trusts the method name. If you send a DELETE to fetch data, the server will probably comply, but you have broken the promise. A good test always respects the method.

    So: the method is a contract. GET is safe to retry. POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE are not.

    GET
    fetch data; safe to repeat
    POST
    send a body; may create something new
    safe
    repeating the request does not change anything on the server

    Close the page. Answer without looking.

    2. Why is GET safe to repeat but POST is not?

    • What are the four parts of an HTTP request?

      The request line (method, path, version), headers, a blank line, and optionally a body.

    • You want to fetch data from an API without changing anything. Should you use GET or POST?

      GET. It is safe to repeat, and it says to the server "I am only reading."

    By tomorrow you can reproduce: running curl -v and reading the request line, headers, blank line, and body in both directions.

    The three-digit status code

    Every response starts with a three-digit number. The first digit is the family, and the family is the whole story. The other two digits are detail.

    2xx means success. 200 means "here is something." 201 means "I created it." 204 means "I succeeded but have nothing to return."

    3xx means "go somewhere else." Clients follow these redirects automatically, which is why a POST sometimes arrives as a GET.

    4xx means your request is wrong. Sending it again unchanged gets the same answer forever. 400 is malformed. 401 means the credentials are missing or bad. 403 means the credentials are valid but not allowed here. 404 means no such path. 429 means too many requests, and it is the only 4xx worth retrying, after waiting the time the server names.

    5xx means the server broke. 500 is internal error, 502 is a proxy that could not reach the real server, 503 is overloaded. These are worth retrying with a growing delay.

    So: the first digit tells you which of three things to do. Retrying a 400 forever turns a typo into five slow failures.

    2xx
    success: the server did what you asked
    4xx
    your mistake: the request is wrong
    5xx
    server mistake: something broke on their end

    JSON, and what Python turns it into

    JSON is text written in six kinds of value. An object is a key-value pair (like a Python dict). An array is a list. Then string, number, boolean, and null.

    Python maps them straight across: dict, list, str, int or float, bool, and None. There is no cleverness in the translation, which is why it almost never surprises you. With httpx you call r.json() to parse what came back.

    The format is strict: double quotes only, no trailing commas, no comments. A parser will refuse an entire response over one stray comma. That is why "the API returned invalid JSON" happens in production. Libraries like json.dumps and json.loads handle serialization and deserialization, but httpx handles it with json=payload in requests and r.json() in responses.

    With httpx you call r.json() to parse what came back. The library handles the string conversion for you.

    So: JSON has six value types, they map directly to Python, and the parser has no tolerance for mistakes.

    JSON
    a text format for structured data, with objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, and null
    parse
    turn text into Python objects
    r.json()
    a method that parses the response body from JSON into Python

    2. A response body is JSON. What does r.json() return?

    • You get a 429 status code. Should you retry immediately or wait?

      Wait. 429 means too many requests. Retry immediately and you will hit the same limit again. Read the retry-after header.

    By tomorrow you can reproduce: branching on a status code to decide whether to retry, and parsing r.json() from the response.

    Where the auth goes

    HTTP is stateless. The server remembers nothing about you between requests, so every single request has to prove who you are.

    Usually that proof is a header. authorization: Bearer sk-... is the common shape. Some providers use x-api-key. Same mechanism — a secret string, sent every time, over HTTPS so it is encrypted before it leaves your machine.

    Never put a key in the query string or the URL. URLs get written to browser history, server logs, proxy logs, and error trackers. A key in a log has leaked whether anyone has read it yet or not.

    So: the secret rides in a header on every request. Keep it out of logs.

    authorization header
    a header that proves you are authorized to make this request
    Bearer token
    an authorization format where the header says "Bearer" then the secret
    HTTPS
    HTTP encrypted, so headers and body are secret before they leave your machine

    Secret hygiene

    An environment variable is a string your process inherited from the shell. Your code reads os.environ["API_KEY"] at startup and fails immediately if it is missing. For example, os.environ["WEATHER_API_KEY"] reads that specific key. Failing fast is the point: the alternative is a confusing 401 twenty seconds into a run.

    A .env file is a plain list of NAME=value lines. A loader reads it into the environment at startup, so you do not retype export all day. It is not encrypted and must never be committed.

    Before your first commit, add .env to .gitignore. Also check in a .env.example holding the names with no values, so the next person knows what to set up.

    If a key ever reaches a public repository, deleting the line does not fix it. Git history keeps every version, and scanners find keys within minutes. Rotate the key instead: replace it on your provider account. That takes a minute and actually works. Never use raise_for_status without handling non-2xx responses properly, as it hides the response body where error details live.

    So: read the key from the environment at startup, store it in a .env file that git ignores, and rotate it instead of deleting it if it leaks.

    environment variable
    a named value stored outside your code, which your program can read
    .env file
    a plain text file with KEY=value lines, loaded into the environment at startup
    .gitignore
    a file listing patterns of files git must never save

      No. Git history keeps the old version. Scanners will find it. You must rotate the key on the provider account.

    Explain this to a smart friend who has never used an API. What does an HTTP request look like? How do you know if it worked? Where does the secret go? Use four to six sentences and start from opening your terminal.

    Watch for the words "basically", "something happens here" and "you just". Each one marks a gap. Go back to that spot in the page, fill the gap, and explain again.

    Where are you on the ladder?

    Four steps, from seeing to doing.

    1. I have seen an HTTP request and a status code before.
    2. I can say what a request contains, what the first digit of a status code means, and where a key lives, without looking.
    3. Given a new API, I can predict what status code it will return and whether I should retry.
    4. I can write a script that calls an API, branches on the status code, parses JSON, and keeps the key secret.

    Git and reading documentation look like tools for grown-ups to master. They are not. Git is how you take risks cheaply because you cannot lose work you committed. Reading docs is how you stop needing tutorials. Both are skills with techniques.

    A commit is a snapshot, not a change

    Git does not store your changes. It stores your files — all of them, complete, at the moment you commit.

    Think of a photograph. Each photograph is a moment frozen. Git does not keep just the differences between photos; it keeps whole photos.

    Each file's contents get a name computed from the bytes themselves. Same bytes, same name. So a file that did not change between two commits is stored once and referenced twice. That is why a repository full of snapshots does not fill your disk.

    A commit records four things: that tree of contents, your name and the time, your message, and the identity of the commit before it. Diffs are not stored anywhere; they are computed when you ask, by comparing two snapshots.

    So: a commit is a full photograph with a parent attached, and diffs are calculated when you ask for them.

    commit
    a snapshot of all your files at one moment, with a message and a parent
    diff
    a comparison between two snapshots, computed on demand
    parent
    the commit that came before this one, stored as part of this commit's identity

    Branches are labels

    A branch is one of the simplest ideas in software, and it surprises people because it is so simple.

    A branch is a small file containing one commit's identity. That is the entire implementation. Creating a branch writes about forty bytes. Nothing is copied, no files move, and there is no branch folder anywhere.

    HEAD is a pointer to the branch you are currently on. Committing moves that label forward onto the new commit. Once you know that, "should I branch for this?" stops being a question worth asking.

    So: a branch is a label you can make for free, and it is how you work on one thing without touching another. To create one, you use git switch -c feature/greeting.

    branch
    a label pointing at one commit, so you can work on separate changes separately
    HEAD
    a pointer to the branch you are currently on
    main
    the default branch, where the stable code lives

    Close the page. Answer without looking.

    1. A file did not change between commit A and commit B. How many copies of it does git store?
    2. Creating a branch takes how much disk space?

    Your goal: a repository with three commits on main and one branch that has its own commits, using only the terminal and git commands.

    Hint 1 — a nudge

    Create a folder, git init practice, make a file, commit it. That is commit 1. Modify the file, commit. That is commit 2. Modify again, commit. That is commit 3. Now you have main.

    Hint 2 — the shape of the answer

    Make a new branch with git switch -c feature/name. Change the file, commit. Check git log. Switch back to main, check the log again. The branch goes away from main. Then run git log --graph --oneline --all.

    Still stuck after 10 minutes? The step by step
    1. Create a folder practice and run git init practice.
    2. Create a file README.md, add it, commit. Run git log. You see commit 1.
    3. Edit the README, commit again. Now you have two commits.
    4. Edit and commit once more. Three commits on main.
    5. Run git switch -c feature/greeting. You created a branch and switched to it.
    6. Edit the README, commit. Now feature/greeting is one commit ahead of main.
    7. Run git log and see your commit. Switch to main with git switch main. The file reverts. Log shows three commits, not four.
    8. Run git log --graph --oneline --all and see both branches diverge.
    • Editing files before committing them, then wondering which version is saved. Run git status constantly.
    • Creating a branch but forgetting to switch to it with git switch, so you commit on the wrong branch.

    • What is a branch? How much does it cost?

      A label pointing at a commit. About forty bytes. They are free to make.

    • You committed to main by mistake, but you meant to commit to a feature branch. How do you fix it?

      Create the branch now with git switch -c feature/name. It points to that commit. Then go back to main and undo the commit.

    By tomorrow you can reproduce: creating a branch, switching between branches, and viewing both on a log graph, all from memory.

    Merging works backward from the graph

    Git finds the most recent commit both branches share — the common ancestor — computes what each side changed since then, and combines the two sets of changes.

    Where only one side touched a region, that side wins with no ceremony. When both sides changed the same line, git refuses to guess. That refusal is the feature. You can see the merge happen with git push and git pull, or with local branches and git merge.

    The merge itself becomes a commit with two parents, which is why history is a graph and not a line. The origin label points to the remote copy of the repository on another machine.

    So: git merges by comparing, not by guessing, and refuses where both sides changed the same line.

    merge
    combine two branches into one by comparing their changes since they split
    common ancestor
    the most recent commit both branches share
    conflict
    a situation where two branches changed the same line and git cannot choose

    Conflicts are mechanical, not personal

    A conflict happens in exactly one situation: two branches changed the same lines of the same file since their common ancestor.

    What you get is the file with both versions left in it, wrapped in three marker lines: <<<<<<< HEAD, then your side, then =======, then their side, then >>>>>>> and the other branch's name.

    Your job is not to pick a winner. You edit the file into what it should actually say — frequently neither side word for word — delete all three marker lines, git add it, and commit.

    And if you want out, git merge --abort puts everything back exactly as it was. Nothing can be lost either way, because both versions still exist in their own commits. The fear is entirely about never having done it.

    So: a conflict is git telling you two people edited the same lines, and resolving it is editing the file and deleting three lines.

    conflict marker
    the three lines <<<, =======, and >>> that mark the two sides of a conflict
    resolve
    edit the file to the correct state, remove the markers, and commit
    merge --abort
    cancel the merge and return to the state before it started

    Close the page. Answer out loud.

    1. Your merge has a conflict. What are the three marker lines?
    2. You started a merge and changed your mind. What command undoes it?

    Your goal: cause a merge conflict on purpose, resolve it by hand, and commit the result. Then do it again and abort the merge instead.

    Hint 1 — a nudge

    Edit line 3 of the README on main. Commit. Go to the feature branch, edit line 3 differently. Commit. Merge main into feature. Conflict.

    Hint 2 — the shape of the answer

    Open the README. You see three marker lines. Delete them. Write what line 3 should actually say. Save. git add README.md. git commit. Done. Then try again and use git merge --abort instead of committing.

    Still stuck after 10 minutes? The step by step
    1. On main, edit line 3 of the README to say "main says this" and commit.
    2. Switch to the feature branch. Edit line 3 to say "feature says this" and commit.
    3. Now run git merge main. Git refuses because both sides edited line 3.
    4. Open the README. You see the markers and both versions.
    5. Edit line 3 to say what it should say (maybe combine them or pick the better one). Delete all three marker lines.
    6. git add README.md. git commit -m "merge main".
    7. Now create a second conflict. On main, edit line 5 and commit. Back to feature, edit line 5 and commit. Merge again.
    8. This time, run git merge --abort. Everything returns to before the merge. Check the log.

    Mix it in. Go back to main. Run git log --all --graph --oneline. Find the merge commit with two parents. Did the conflict branch become part of main?

    • "Resolving" a conflict by deleting the other side's work or by leaving a marker line in the file.
    • Committing a merge conflict without removing the marker lines. The code will not parse.
    • Watching another tutorial instead of causing a real conflict. The technique takes five minutes; the confidence only comes from doing it.

    • Git shows you a merge conflict. What are the three marker lines that wrap the two versions?

      <<<<<<< HEAD, then =======, then >>>>>>> branch-name.

    • You start merging and halfway through you realize you want to undo it. What happens to your commits if you use git merge --abort?

      They are not lost. Nothing changed. --abort puts everything back exactly as it was before the merge started.

    By tomorrow you can reproduce: causing a conflict and resolving it by hand, and using git merge --abort to undo a merge.

    Four shapes of documentation

    Docs come in four shapes, and they answer four different questions. Knowing which one you need is most of the speed.

    A tutorial walks you to a first success. A how-to guide solves one named task — "how to add a new column to a table." A reference lists every parameter, its type, its default, and the errors it can return. An explanation says why it is built that way.

    A reference is the one you will live in. The format is always the same: function name, parameters with their types and defaults, what errors it can throw, then an example last.

    Read a reference in this order: find the function, read the parameters and their types, read the defaults, read the errors and limits, and read the example last. Most people do the opposite. They read the example first and copy it, which is exactly why they can not change anything about it afterward — they have the shape without the meanings. Think of it like reading a recipe: reading the ingredient list and the timing first teaches you more than jumping to step 5. When you first use git switch feature/greeting, read the reference for what each flag does, not just the example.

    So: pick the shape that answers your question. Reach for the reference when you need to know what you are changing.

    reference
    documentation that lists every parameter, type, default, and error for a function or command
    tutorial
    documentation that walks you through one complete example from start to finish
    how-to
    documentation that solves one specific task in one specific way

    One check that costs ten seconds

    Before you believe anything you read in a doc, check two things. Check the version. Check the changelog.

    A video from eight months ago describes an API that has changed twice since then. A blog post from last year talks about a feature that was removed. The git reference describes the one running right now. When you run git push or git pull, you are using a specific version of git that matches the docs you should read.

    For anything dated — a video, a blog post, an article — go find the changelog and see what has changed since that date. Spend ten seconds. It saves thirty minutes of trying to follow steps that no longer work.

    That is why every day of the next four weeks starts with forty-five minutes in primary documentation. It is not discipline for its own sake; it is the cheapest way to stop guessing.

    So: pick the shape that answers your question, read the reference before the example, and check the date on everything else.

    changelog
    a record of what changed in each version of a tool
    version
    a released snapshot of a tool, numbered to show whether it is a patch, minor, or major change
    primary documentation
    the official docs maintained by the tool's creators, usually the most up-to-date
