    The map for this week

    Week 1 is the layer everything else sits on: one call to a model, and everything you can know about it. By Sunday you can look at any request your code makes and say four things out loud: what it cost, how long it took, where the time went, and what happens when it fails.

    You start with the raw SDK, no framework, because frameworks hide the numbers you came here to learn. Each day builds on the last. Day 2 pulls prompts out of code and into files with test cases. Day 3 replaces messy text parsing with typed objects. Day 4 makes long documents cheap with caching. Day 5 shows you where the seconds go. Day 6 breaks everything on purpose. Day 7 you deploy it and write down the numbers.

    token
    a chunk of text the model reads or writes; you pay by the token
    temperature
    a knob that controls how adventurous the model is when picking words
    structured output
    asking the model to return data in a specific shape like a typed object
    caching
    storing input the model has seen so it costs less to reuse the same context
    streaming
    getting the answer one word at a time as the model writes it
    latency
    how long it takes for an answer to arrive, measured in seconds

    Before Day 1 (25 minutes): read this map once. Then close it and draw the week on paper from memory: the big ideas, the words, and arrows for how they connect. Open it again and fix what you missed. Do not try to learn anything yet.

    Today you build the smallest program that talks to an AI model. Then you learn to describe that program in numbers. By tonight you should be able to point at one run and say: “That cost two cents. The first word showed up after 0.4 seconds. The last word after 2.1 seconds.” Being able to say that one sentence is the whole point of the day.

    A shelf of your own

    Before you write any code, you set up three things. A folder that git watches. An environment for your Python packages. And one package inside it: your model provider’s SDK, which is the toolkit that lets your code talk to their servers.

    The word to slow down on is isolated. Think of a garage with one shelf per project. Each shelf holds only the tools that project needs. If you install something new today, it goes on today’s shelf. It can’t reach back and break the project you finished last month, because the two never share a shelf.

    You make that shelf with a tool called uv. One command creates it. One command puts a package on it.

    So: one folder, one isolated environment, one package. Nothing leaks in and nothing leaks out.

    SDK
    a toolkit of ready-made code that makes calling a service easier than doing it by hand
    environment
    a private set of installed packages for one project
    uv
    a fast tool that makes environments and installs packages into them

    One secret that stays secret

    Now the secret. To use a model, you have an API key. It is a long password that says “this request is from me, so bill me.”

    Your key goes into an environment variable, which is a named value that lives outside your code. Your program reads it when it starts. It never becomes a string typed into a source file. Not for five minutes. Not in a branch you plan to delete.

    The reason is practical, not moral. Bots scan public code sites all day and all night, looking for anything shaped like a key. When one finds yours, it starts spending, usually within minutes. Someone else does the spending. You get the bill.

    Here is how to do it right. Put the key in a file called .env. Then tell git to ignore that file by listing it in .gitignore. Don’t pass keys on the command line either. Those get saved in your shell history, which is one more file you will forget about.

    So: one secret, and it never touches anything git can see.

    API key
    a secret password that proves a request is yours and tells the provider whom to bill
    environment variable
    a named value stored outside your code, which your program can read
    .gitignore
    a file that lists what git must never save

    Close the page. Without looking, say or write the answers to these two questions.

    1. Why can’t today’s install break last month’s project?
    2. Where does your API key live, and where must it never be?

    Your goal: a program that sends one message to the model and prints the reply. The key is read from an environment variable. Git is set up so it can never see the key.

    Hint 2 — the shape of the answer

    Only four lines really matter: read the key from the environment, build a client with the SDK, send one message, print the text of the reply. Find the “quickstart” page in your provider’s docs and match it to those four lines.

    Still stuck after 10 minutes? The step by step
    1. Create the repo and run uv init.
    2. Add your provider’s SDK with uv add.
    3. Create .env, put your key in it, and add .env to .gitignore before your first commit.
    4. Write a tiny script that loads the key, sends “say hi”, and prints the reply.
    5. Run git status. If .env shows up in the list, stop and fix that first.
    • A key pasted into a notebook cell, then committed. Once it is in git history, replacing the key is the only real fix.

    • Why can’t installing a package today break a project you finished last month?

      Each project has its own isolated environment. The packages live in that folder only, so the two never share a shelf.

    • A friend pastes their API key into a script and pushes it to a public repo “just to test”. What happens next, and what is the only real fix?

      Bots scan public repos and use keys within minutes. Deleting the file isn’t enough because the key is still in git history. The fix is to replace (rotate) the key.

    By tomorrow you can reproduce: the folder, the uv environment, the .env file and the four-line call, from an empty directory, without looking.

    Tokens: the unit you pay in

    A language model doesn’t read words. It reads tokens. A token is a chunk of text, and every chunk is really a number. The word “strawberry” might arrive as two tokens: straw and berry.

    Where do the chunks come from? A tokenizer cuts your text up using a fixed list built when the model was trained. Picture a phrasebook with a set number of entries. Common words earned an entry of their own, so they cost one token. Rare words, names, code and anything that isn’t English didn’t earn one each, so they get spelled out of smaller pieces.

    For ordinary English there is a rough rule: about four characters per token, or about 0.75 words per token. “Rough” is doing real work in that sentence. Don’t build a budget on it.

    Here is why any of this matters. The model reads every input token. Then it writes output tokens one at a time. You pay for both, at two different prices, and output usually costs four to five times more. The context window is the ceiling on input and output added together, for one call.

    Now the trap, and it catches everybody once. Tokenizers differ between model families, so a count from a generic library can be off by 10 to 30 percent for the model you are actually calling. Off by 30 percent is the difference between a budget and a wish.

    You never have to guess. Every provider hands you the real number twice: a counting endpoint you can call before the request, and exact usage in the response after it. See the token counting docs.

    So: tokens are the unit of both the bill and the clock, and you should never be guessing at them.

    token
    a chunk of text the model reads or writes; every chunk is a number
    tokenizer
    the piece that cuts text into tokens
    context window
    the most tokens, input and output together, that fit in one call

    The parts of a call

    A request is a list of messages. Each message has a role, either user or assistant. Next to the list sits a separate system prompt, which holds your standing instructions.

    Here is the part that surprises people. The API is stateless. That means the model remembers nothing between calls. Imagine texting a friend who forgets you the second they reply. The only way to hold a conversation is to paste the whole chat so far into every message. That is exactly why the tenth turn costs more than the first.

    Then come the knobs. Temperature controls how adventurous the model is when it picks its next token. At every step the model gives every token a probability. Near 0, it almost always picks the most likely one. That is close to repeatable, but never guaranteed. Turn it up and the model is more willing to pick unlikely tokens.

    max_tokens is a hard ceiling on the answer. Hit it and the model stops mid-sentence, with no apology. Stop sequences end the answer the moment a certain piece of text appears. That text isn’t included in what you get back.

    One portability note, and it is your first. Some newer reasoning models refuse the temperature setting entirely and give you an effort setting instead.

    The response also tells you how it ended, and you should read that field on every call. end_turn means the model finished. max_tokens means you cut it off.

    So: a call is a history you resend, a few knobs that change how the next token is picked, and one field that says whether the answer is finished.

    stateless
    remembers nothing between requests
    system prompt
    standing instructions that go with every request
    temperature
    a knob for how adventurous token picking is
    stop reason
    a field saying why the answer ended

    Close the page. Answer out loud, then write one sentence for each.

    1. What is a token, and why do we count tokens instead of words?
    2. Why does the tenth message in a chat cost more than the first?
    3. What does the stop reason max_tokens tell you?

    Your goal: a command-line tool. Give it a URL or a file path and it returns a tidy summary: a title, three bullet points and one open question. It counts the input tokens before it sends anything.

    Hint 1 — a nudge

    Split it in two. One function turns a URL or path into plain text. A second function sends that text to the model. Test each one alone before you connect them.

    Hint 2 — the shape of the answer

    The “title, three bullets, one question” rule belongs in the system prompt. Set temperature to 0 and max_tokens to 500. Choose a text cap on purpose, so one enormous web page can’t surprise you.

    Still stuck after 10 minutes? The step by step
    1. Write one input function: given a URL or a file path, return plain text. Fetch or read it, strip the markup, and stop at a token count you chose on purpose.
    2. Write one call. The system prompt states the contract: a title, three bullet points, one open question. Set temperature to 0 and max_tokens to 500.
    3. Ask your provider’s counting endpoint how many input tokens you are about to send, and print that number before the call.
    4. Print the stop reason after the call.

    Mix it in. Where does your program read the key from? Check that your new script still does it the safe way, and run git status once more.

    • Counting tokens with a library built for a different model family, then wondering why the bill doesn’t match your estimate.
    • Setting max_tokens too low and shipping silently cut-off answers. If you never read the stop reason, you never find out.

    • What is a token, and why do we count tokens instead of words?

      A token is a chunk of text, and every chunk is a number. The bill and the context window are both measured in tokens, and one word can be one token or several.

    • Your chat app’s tenth message costs more than the first, even though you typed the same amount. Why?

      The API is stateless. Every turn resends the whole history, so the input keeps growing.

    • What does the stop reason max_tokens tell you?

      That you cut the answer off. It isn’t finished. end_turn means the model finished by itself.

    By tomorrow you can reproduce: the two-function structure of the tool, and what each of temperature, max_tokens and the stop reason does, in one sentence each.

    Cost, to the cent

    Every reply comes back with usage numbers: input tokens, output tokens, and cached tokens. Cached tokens are input the provider already saw recently, so they get a discount. The arithmetic is one line. Put the two prices in your code as constants, multiply, and print the result next to the answer.

    Do it per call, not per month. A monthly number arrives far too late to change anything you did.

    Watch what the per-call number does for you. Three thousand input tokens and seven hundred output tokens, at $3 and $15 per million, come to $0.0195. That is about two cents. Twenty debugging runs cost 39 cents. Ten thousand users a day cost $195.

    One number answers two different questions. Can you afford to experiment this afternoon? And can this product exist at all?

    Two traps. The first is guessing from character counts, which you now know better than to do. The second is quieter: failures bill too. A call that produced 400 tokens before your program gave up still made 400 tokens, and you pay for all 400.

    So: print the cost of every call, in cents, right next to its output.

    usage
    the token counts a response reports about itself
    cached tokens
    input the provider recently saw, billed at a discount
    per million
    the way prices are quoted: dollars for each million tokens

    Close the page. Do this from memory.

    1. Three thousand input tokens and 700 output tokens, at $3 and $15 per million. What does one call cost?
    2. Why should a call that failed still show up in your cost log?

    Your goal: every run of your tool prints its own cost, to the cent, and its stop reason. Then you run it on five inputs of very different sizes and keep the results in a table.

    Hint 1 — a nudge

    The response object already contains the token counts. You don’t need to count anything yourself. You only need two prices and one multiplication.

    Hint 2 — the shape of the answer

    Keep two constants at the top of your file: dollars per million input tokens and dollars per million output tokens. Cost is input * in_price / 1_000_000 + output * out_price / 1_000_000. Write one row per run to LOG.md.

    Still stuck after 10 minutes? The step by step
    1. Print the usage numbers from the response. Compute the cost inline from your two price constants.
    2. Print the stop reason next to it. That is how you learn whether the answer is whole.
    3. Run the tool on five inputs of very different sizes: a tiny note, a short article, a long page, and two in between.
    4. Put one row per run in LOG.md: tokens in, tokens out, cost.

    Mix it in. Pick the largest of your five inputs. Predict its cost before you run it, using the token counting endpoint. How far off were you?

    • Guessing tokens from character counts, then being surprised by the real bill.
    • Leaving failed runs out of your log. They cost money too.

    • A call has 3,000 input tokens and 700 output tokens. Input costs $3 per million and output $15 per million. What does the call cost?

      $0.009 for input plus $0.0105 for output, so $0.0195. About two cents.

    • Why should a call that failed still show up in your cost log?

      Failures bill too. Tokens the model generated before your program gave up are still charged.

    By tomorrow you can reproduce: the cost formula, from memory, with your own two price constants.

    Two clocks

    There are two numbers, not one. Time to first token is the gap between sending the request and the first piece of the answer showing up. Total time runs until the last token.

    Think of a restaurant. The first clock stops when the first dish reaches your table. The second stops when the last plate is down.

    They move for different reasons, and that is the useful part. The first clock is queueing plus the model reading your input, so it grows with prompt length. The second is the writing, and it is roughly the number of output tokens divided by the model’s speed in tokens per second.

    Do that division once and it sticks. A 900-token answer at 60 tokens per second takes 15 seconds, no matter how fast the model started.

    So the split tells you what to fix. A long prompt with a short answer? Shrink the input. A short prompt with a long answer? Shrink the output, or stream it.

    One more fact, about people. They feel the first clock as speed. That is the whole reason streaming exists: the words appear as they are written instead of all at once at the end. You build it on Day 5.

    So: measure both clocks separately, because they have different causes and only one of them is yours to fix today.

    time to first token
    how long until the first piece of the answer arrives
    total time
    how long until the last piece arrives
    streaming
    sending the answer piece by piece as it is written

    Close the page. From memory.

    1. Which clock does a long prompt slow down? Which does a long answer slow down?
    2. A 900-token answer at 60 tokens per second: what is the least total time?

    Your goal: your tool now reports both clocks on every run. You add those two columns to yesterday’s table, and you have run one experiment on temperature.

    Hint 1 — a nudge

    To catch the first token you need to stream the answer. Otherwise everything arrives at once and both clocks show the same time.

    Hint 2 — the shape of the answer

    Start a monotonic timer right before the call, not at program start. Note the timer’s value when the first chunk arrives, and again when the last one does. Print both.

    Still stuck after 10 minutes? The step by step
    1. Wrap the call in a monotonic timer. Stream the answer so you can note the clock time of the first chunk and the last. Print both.
    2. Run the five inputs again and add two columns to your LOG.md table: first-token time and total time.
    3. Set temperature to 1.0 and run the same input three times. Write down what changed and what didn’t. That is the knob explaining itself.
    4. Commit. Every day ends with a commit, even if the day went badly.

    Mix it in. Look at your table. Which of your five inputs has the biggest gap between first-token time and total time? Use tokens and your division to explain why.

    • Timing the whole program instead of the request. Imports and file reads pollute the number, so start the clock right before the call.

    • Which clock does a long prompt slow down, and which does a long answer slow down?

      A long prompt slows the time to first token. A long answer slows the total time.

    • A 900-token answer streams at 60 tokens per second. What is the least total time?

      About 15 seconds, however quickly the first word appeared.

    By tomorrow you can reproduce: how to time the first token and the last one, and which one you would work on for a short prompt with a long answer.

    Teach it back

    Explain this to a smart friend who has never used an API. What happens, and what does it cost, when your tool summarizes one web page? Start from the moment you press Enter and use four to six sentences. Say it out loud, or write it down.

    Watch for the words “basically”, “something happens here” and “you just”. Each one marks a gap. Go back to that spot in the page, fill the gap, and explain again.

    Where are you on the ladder?

    Being able to say “I’ve seen this” is only the first rung. Climb all four.

    1. I have seen “token” and “API key” before.
    2. I can say what a token is, why the bill has two meters, and where the key lives, without looking.
    3. Given a new URL, I can predict about what one run will cost, then check my guess against the real number.
    4. I can design a small tool that reports its own cost and both clocks on every run, and defend each choice.

    A prompt that works on three examples is just a coincidence. Today you turn prompting into something measurable. You learn what actually changes the model's output, which is the whole difference between tweaking and engineering.

    An output contract, not a wish

    Say exactly what you want back. Not "summarize this well". Instead: "Return a title under 60 characters, then exactly three bullet points, then one sentence starting with ‘Unclear:’."

    A contract removes thousands of plausible shapes before any sampling happens. Think of the model as picking a continuation from a very wide cloud of possibilities. A loose request leaves the cloud huge. A tight contract cuts it down to a narrow column.

    Here is the trap people fall into. Negative instructions sound like they should help. "Don't apologize" puts apologizing into the context, and the phrasing you just banned sits right there in the model's attention.

    State the positive form instead. "Begin with the title, no preamble." Save sharp negatives for failures you have actually watched happen.

    So: describe the shape you want, not the shape you're afraid of.

    contract
    a precise description of what the output should look like: fields, order, length, what to do when data is missing
    positive instruction
    a statement of what to do, rather than what not to do

    Examples teach by showing

    Explanations describe a rule. Examples demonstrate it. The model learns the demonstrated pattern faster and more reliably than it learns a paragraph of rules.

    A few-shot prompt puts complete input-and-output pairs in front of the real input. They are just more tokens. What makes them work is that they show the mapping, not describe it.

    Choose your examples from the edges, not the middle. The ambiguous case. The empty case. The case that should return "unknown". The case with a trap in it. Three to five examples are usually enough. After that you are paying rent on those tokens forever.

    Here is the sneaky trap. If all four of your examples happen to be short, English, and cheerful, the model copies all three properties. Then your long German complaint comes back wrong, and nothing in your prompt can explain why.

    So: examples teach everything they have in common, including the parts you didn't notice putting there.

    few-shot
    a prompt that shows several input-and-output pairs before the real input, so the model learns by example
    accidental property
    a pattern in your examples that you didn't mean to teach but that the model copies anyway

    Close the page. Without looking, answer these.

    1. Why does a tight contract shrink the set of plausible answers?
    2. Why should your few-shot examples come from hard cases, not easy ones?

    Your goal: a prompt with a tight output contract and three carefully chosen examples, that returns consistent structure across five test inputs you have not seen before.

    Hint 1 — a nudge

    Start with one test case you know should work. Write the contract first, then add examples from the edges.

    Hint 2 — the shape of the answer

    A title under 60 characters, three bullets (each under 40 characters), and one "Unclear:" line. Pick three examples that cover empty input, ambiguous cases, and one with a trap.

    Still stuck after 10 minutes? The step by step
    1. Write the contract: exact fields, exact order, exact length limits for each field.
    2. Write one example: an input that should work and the output you want.
    3. Add an example with an empty field. Add an ambiguous case. Add a trap.
    4. Test the prompt on five different inputs. Do all five come back in the same shape?
    • Negative instructions that reinforce the thing you want to avoid.
    • All your examples being short, English, and optimistic when your real input is long, mixed language, and critical.

    • Why does a tight output contract help the model generate consistent structure?

      A contract removes thousands of plausible answer shapes before sampling starts. The model still picks from a probability distribution, but a narrower one.

    • You write four few-shot examples and they are all short, English, and positive. Your real input is long, mixed language, and critical. What will the model do?

      Copy the hidden pattern. The output will be short, English, and positive, even though your prompt doesn't say that. Examples teach everything they have in common.

    By tomorrow you can reproduce: one tight contract and three edge-case examples, from memory, for a prompt you care about.

    One call, one job

    A single call that has to extract facts, judge them, decide a tone, and hit a format will fail at one or more of those jobs.

    Think of why. Each requirement is another chance for the sampled continuation to drift. When you have four independent goals, the chance that all four land together is the product of four smaller chances. Products get small fast.

    So split when failures actually happen. Extract to a typed object in one call. Judge in a second. Write prose in a third.

    Now every step is separately testable and separately fixable. Each step often runs on a cheaper model. When something breaks, you know which step broke it.

    This is not free. You pay in extra calls and extra latency. So decompose where the failures actually are, not everywhere.

    So: one call, one job turns a single unexplainable failure into three you can inspect one at a time.

    decomposition
    splitting one big task into several smaller calls, each with one goal
    chaining
    running calls in sequence, where each call's output becomes the next call's input

    Reasoning is tokens, and tokens are money

    Step-by-step reasoning makes the model generate intermediate tokens. Those tokens become part of what it reads while producing the final answer. That is the whole mechanism: it gets to think on paper.

    It helps when the answer is not determined by the input alone. Multi-step math. Constraint satisfaction. A classification that needs a policy applied to an ambiguous case.

    It helps almost nothing when the answer already sits in the input. Pulling a date from an invoice. Mapping text to one of five obvious labels. Reformatting. There you pay for hundreds of extra tokens and added latency to get the same answer.

    Reasoning models make this explicit with an effort or thinking setting. Internal tokens are billed, and often not even shown to you.

    Do not argue about this. Measure it. Run twenty cases with reasoning on and off, and compare accuracy against tokens spent.

    So: if accuracy is equal, reasoning is a tax.

    step-by-step reasoning
    asking the model to show its work by generating intermediate tokens before the final answer
    token efficiency
    getting the same quality output for fewer tokens, or better output for the same tokens

    Close the page. Answer these from memory.

    1. When does decomposing a task into multiple calls make sense?
    2. Why does step-by-step reasoning sometimes waste tokens instead of helping?

    Your goal: take one case that fails, either as a single call or with reasoning on. Split it into two calls, or turn reasoning off. Prove it failed on one strategy and passed on the other.

    Hint 1 — a nudge

    Pick one test case where the output is wrong. Is it a single call trying to do too much, or reasoning burning tokens on an obvious answer? Fix the other way.

    Hint 2 — the shape of the answer

    Extract the facts in one call, then judge them in a second. Or turn off reasoning and run the same case without it. Count tokens and compare.

    Still stuck after 10 minutes? The step by step
    1. Find a case where the output is wrong.
    2. If it is one call with multiple goals, split it into two: extract, then judge.
    3. If it is reasoning burning tokens, run it without reasoning and check accuracy.
    4. Compare tokens and cost before and after.

    Mix it in. Look at your Round 1 examples. Do they still teach the right thing? Pick the case you fixed in this round and add it as an example if it was an edge case.

    • Decomposing everywhere instead of where failures actually are.
    • Using reasoning models on factual lookups that need no reasoning at all.

    • When does splitting one call into two make sense?

      When a single call has to satisfy multiple goals and one of them is failing. Each call can then be fixed separately.

    • You want to extract a date from an invoice using a reasoning model. What are you probably overpaying for?

      Reasoning. The date is already in the input. Step-by-step thinking does not help extract a fact that is already there.

    By tomorrow you can reproduce: when to decompose instead of asking for everything in one call, and when reasoning helps instead of burning money.

    Prompts live in files, versions matter

    A prompt copied into an f-string is scattered across your codebase. A prompt in a file is code. Move every prompt to prompts/summarize.v3.md, loaded and rendered by one small function that fills in the variables.

    Store the version string alongside every result you produce. Now a prompt change is a diff you can read. A rollback is a checkout. Any output you are holding can be traced back to the exact text that made it.

    The other half is the case file. Twenty real inputs in one .jsonl file, one object per line with an id and the raw text. Include three you expect to fail, so you have an edge case set. A runner that executes the prompt across all of them and writes results.v3.json with output, tokens, cost, and latency for each.

    Watch what that buys you. Changing a prompt now means diffing two result files and seeing which cases moved and in which direction. You can argue about accuracy objectively, not by reading three outputs and having a feeling.

    Why twenty cases, not five? Five is too small. A fix that breaks something can hide in five test runs. Five is also easy to remember by heart. Twenty is big enough that you catch the quiet breakage, small enough to eyeball in one sitting. This is the seed of the eval harness you will build in Week 3. By then you will have hundreds of cases and know why.

    So: once the prompt is a file and the inputs are a file, prompting stops being a feeling and becomes a diff.

    version string
    a label that travels with every result, so any output can be traced back to the exact prompt that made it
    runner
    a program that takes a prompt file and a case file and produces a result file with all outputs, tokens and cost

    Close the page. Answer these from memory.

    1. Why does storing the version string with every result matter?
    2. Why use 20 test cases instead of 5?

    Your goal: a prompt module, a case file with 20 real inputs, and a runner that executes any prompt across all of them and writes a result file with versions, outputs, tokens and cost.

    Hint 1 — a nudge

    Three files. One prompt. One case file. One runner. Keep it simple: the runner loops, calls the model, records the result and the version.

    Hint 2 — the shape of the answer

    Write a loader function that returns (version_string, prompt_text). Write the case file with 20 lines, one object per line, with an id and text field. The runner loops, calls, records, and writes to results.json.

    Still stuck after 10 minutes? The step by step
    1. Move your Round 1 prompt into prompts/summarize.v1.md with a placeholder.
    2. Write a loader: read the file, fill {{text}}, return the version string and the prompt text.
    3. Collect 20 real inputs into cases.jsonl. Include three you expect to fail.
    4. Write a runner that loops the cases, calls the model, and writes results.v1.json with version, output, tokens, and cost.
    5. Run it once. Diff the output by eye. Which cases changed from Round 2? Which broke?

    Mix it in. Look at the three cases you expected to fail in Round 1. Did they? Are they still in your test set, or would different edge cases teach better?

    • Editing a prompt and a case file in the same commit, so you cannot tell whether the score moved because of the prompt or the data.
    • Judging by reading three outputs. Twenty cases catch the fix that breaks two other things.

    • Why should the version string travel with every result?

      So any output can be traced back to the exact prompt and case file that made it. A change in output can then be diffed as a change in prompt.

    • You change a prompt and results.v1.json changes. How do you tell whether the change was good, and which cases moved?

      Diff results.v1.json against results.v2.json by case id. You see exactly which cases moved and in which direction.

    By tomorrow you can reproduce: the prompt loader, the case file format, and the runner that diffs two result files by case id.

    Testing and versioning

    You now have a measurable system. A prompt file, a case file, a runner, and result files that track what worked and what didn't.

    Now use it. Add your few-shot examples and strict output contract as summarize.v2.md. Run the full test set. Diff the two result files by case id. The diff shows you exactly which cases moved, which stayed the same, and which got worse. That is how you know if the change was worth the extra tokens.

    Then split your prompt into two calls: extract facts first in one call, then judge them in a second. Name this extract.v1.md and judge.v1.md. Run both paths end to end. Compare the accuracy against v2. Did the split fix the failures? Or did it just add latency for no gain?

    Then test reasoning on your original single prompt. Run the same twenty cases with step-by-step reasoning turned on and off. Record accuracy and token counts side by side. Does reasoning actually help, or does it just burn tokens? The answer might surprise you.

    Every change is now a row in a table you can read. No arguments. No feelings. Just numbers. The case that got worse is not a mystery anymore—you can see it and fix it.

    So: measure everything, then commit the prompts, the cases, and the result files. The results are the evidence. Future you will read the diff and know why that change was made.

    diff
    a side-by-side comparison showing what changed between two versions
    accuracy
    the fraction of test cases that produce the correct output
    evidence
    measurement, not opinion, committed alongside the code

    Close the page. Answer these from memory.

    1. What does diffing two result files show you that reading three outputs does not?
    2. Why commit the result files alongside the prompts?

    Your goal: three result files showing v1 vs v2 (with examples), single call vs split, and reasoning on vs off. A table showing accuracy and token cost for each strategy. A commit with all evidence.

    Mix it in. Look at your test results. Which case came out wrong the most? Is it from the edges (where your examples came from) or the middle? Should you change your examples?

    • Few-shot examples that are subtly wrong. The model copies the mistake and you blame the model.

    • What does diffing two result files show that reading three outputs does not?

      Which cases moved and in which direction. Twenty cases catch the fix that breaks two other things.

    • You test reasoning: same 20 cases, reasoning on and off. Accuracy is the same but tokens are higher with reasoning on. What should you do?

      Turn reasoning off. If accuracy is equal, reasoning is a tax. You are paying extra for no benefit.

    Teach it back

    Explain this day to a smart friend who writes prompts but has never measured them. What changed, and why does it matter? Start from the moment you realized that three test cases are not enough. Use four to six sentences.

    Watch for the words “basically”, “something happens here” and “you just”. Each one marks a gap. Go back to that spot in the page, fill the gap, and explain again.

    Where are you on the ladder?

    From tweaking to engineering.

    1. I have heard of few-shot, contracts, and decomposition.
    2. I can say what a contract does, when to split a prompt, and why reasoning burns tokens on obvious answers.
    3. Given a prompt that fails on two cases, I can split it or add examples and measure whether the split worked.
    4. I can run twenty test cases, measure three strategies, diff the results, and decide which strategy wins on accuracy and cost.

    Today the model stops being a chat toy and becomes a component. You build an extractor that turns messy text into clean typed objects. Nail this one and everything in the next 27 days gets easier.

    Why a model makes broken JSON

    Generation is one token at a time, sampled from probabilities. In a plain call, nothing in that loop knows what JSON is. The model has seen enormous amounts of JSON and imitates it beautifully. That is exactly the problem: the failures are rare enough to slip past your testing and land in production.

    Think of a musician improvising. They have heard thousands of songs, but they are making it up note by note as they go. Most of the time they nail it. Sometimes they hit a clinker.

    The shapes repeat. A fenced code block. A friendly "Here is the JSON:" wrapped around the object. A trailing comma. An unescaped quote inside a string. A number written as "about 40". A field you never asked for. A value outside your list of allowed options. And the most common one by far: the object stops mid-way because output hit max_tokens.

    That last one is not really a model failure — it is a configuration failure. From the outside it looks the same, but the fix is different. Every time you get broken JSON, check the stop reason first.

    So: models are good at imitating JSON but not flawless, and the stop reason tells you whether they were even trying.

    stop reason
    a field that says why the answer ended, like end_turn or max_tokens

    Schema enforcement: making invalid syntax unreachable

    Providers offer a mode where you hand over a JSON Schema and the output is forced to match it. No pleading required. This is constrained decoding.

    Here is the mechanism, and it is worth knowing because it tells you what the guarantee covers. At each generation step the provider works out which tokens could still lead to a document valid under your schema. Then it sets the probability of every other token to zero.

    Think of building a bridge. You could ask the workers politely not to drop anything. Or you could hand out harnesses. The second one does not rely on politeness.

    Invalid syntax becomes unreachable, not merely unlikely. That is the difference between asking a river not to flood and building the bank higher.

    There are two ways to ask for it. A response_format parameter carrying your schema, or a tool definition whose input schema is your object, with strict validation switched on. Both end in the same place — the model is forced to output valid syntax.

    Now the honest limit. Enforcement does not buy you correct values. A schema-valid object can still say the invoice total is 4,000 when it is 40.00. The model will not fabricate a syntax error, but it can fabricate data. That is where validation comes in, which is Round 3.

    So: enforcement makes the syntax valid, and validation checks whether the values make sense.

    constrained decoding
    forcing the output to match a JSON Schema by making invalid tokens unreachable
    response_format
    a parameter that tells the API to enforce your schema

    Close the page. Answer out loud, then write one sentence for each.

    1. Name three shapes of broken JSON. Which one is actually a configuration problem?
    2. What is the difference between asking the model not to make syntax errors and schema enforcement?

    Start tiny. Pick your document type and pick three to five fields that matter. Write a JSON Schema by hand that says what those fields are. Make one call with response_format (or a strict tool) and give it one real example to parse.

    Your schema should have 3–5 fields. String, number, or array. Make one simple field required and one optional. Turn on schema enforcement in the API call. Print the response. Is it valid JSON?

    • Blaming the model when the JSON is broken. Check the stop reason first. If it says max_tokens, you cut it off, not the model.
    • Writing a schema with no way to express "not present", so the model invents a plausible value rather than emitting null.

    • What does schema enforcement do?

      It makes invalid syntax unreachable. At each token, only the tokens that could lead to a valid document are allowed.

    • You get broken JSON from a call. You check the stop reason and it says max_tokens. Is this a model failure or a configuration problem?

      Configuration. You set the limit too low. The model was trying to output valid JSON but you cut it off.

    • Can schema enforcement give you correct values?

      No. It makes the syntax valid, but the values can still be wrong. Validation checks the values.

    One Pydantic class does three jobs

    Instead of writing a JSON Schema by hand, write it once as a Pydantic class. That single definition then fans out to three different places. See the Pydantic docs for the full reference.

    First, it generates the JSON Schema you send to the API. Second, it validates and coerces whatever comes back. Third, it gives your editor real types to autocomplete against. If you mess up the schema, all three stay in sync.

    Think of a recipe card. You write it once. The chef follows it, the grocery list comes from it, and it lives on the fridge. One card, three uses.

    How to design it. Make it flat, not deeply nested, because every level of nesting is more structure the model has to hold straight while generating. Use enums instead of free text wherever the values are known. A field called status with allowed values paid, pending, or overdue is better than a string that could say anything.

    Make optional fields explicitly nullable. If a field might not be in the document, make it None by default. Write a one-sentence field description as an instruction. The model reads it. Those descriptions are not documentation — they are instructions on a short leash.

    One more rule, and it heads off a whole category of quiet bugs: always give the model a legal way to say it does not know. A null, an "unknown" enum value, a confidence field. Without one, the only way to produce a valid object is to invent something — and it will. You do not want your extractor making up data.

    So: one class, three jobs, a flat design, enums where possible, and an escape hatch for uncertainty.

    Pydantic
    a Python library that defines data schemas as classes and validates data against them
    BaseModel
    the parent class you inherit from to make a Pydantic model
    enum
    a field with a fixed list of allowed values
    nullable
    a field that is allowed to be None, meaning absent or unknown

    2. Why should a field be explicitly nullable instead of having a made-up default value?

    Call the model with model.model_json_schema() to see the schema it generates. Pass that schema to the API call. Parse the response with YourModel.model_validate_json(response_text). You now have a typed object in your editor.

    • Deeply nested models. The model has to hold five levels of structure in its head while generating. Flat is faster and more reliable.
    • Free text fields where an enum would fit. If there are only three possible values, list them.

      One: generates the JSON Schema sent to the API. Two: validates the response. Three: provides types for your editor.

    • You define a Pydantic field as required, but the document sometimes doesn't have that field. What should you do?

      Make it optional with a default of None, or another sensible default. Never make the model invent a value.

    • Should a Pydantic model for the API be deeply nested or flat?

      Flat. Each level of nesting is more structure the model has to hold while generating.

    Catch, repair once, then stop

    The loop is short. Call the model, parse the output, validate it against your Pydantic model. On failure, send the bad output back to the model plus the exact error text from the validator. Ask for a corrected object. That is one repair attempt.

    The error string is unusually good context. "due_date: input should be a valid date" fixes far more often than "that was wrong" because it names the field and the expectation in the same breath. The model reads it and understands the problem.

    Now bound it, hard. Two attempts, then record the failure and move on. An unbounded loop sounds safe but it is not. On one bad input it can spend five times a normal record and still fail. If your extractor is running inside a web request, your user is watching a spinner the whole time.

    Keep a log of every field that failed, every time. After 50 inputs you have a ranked list of your schema's weak spots. The fix is usually a better field description or a split field, not a bigger model.

    Track first-attempt and second-attempt success separately. After 50 inputs, you should see something like: 90% valid on the first try, 95% after the repair. That pair of numbers is how you know you have hit the day's target.

    So: repair once with the exact error text, cap it at two attempts, log every failure, and let the numbers tell you whether your schema is working.

    validation
    checking that parsed output matches your Pydantic model
    repair
    resending invalid output with the error message to ask for a corrected version
    bounded loop
    a process that stops after a fixed number of attempts, no matter what

    Close the page. Without looking.

    1. Why is "due_date: input should be a valid date" better context than "that was wrong"?
    2. What do you do after a repair attempt fails twice?

    Your goal: add a repair loop to your extractor. Validate against your Pydantic model. On failure, resend the bad output plus the error text. Cap at two total attempts. Log every failure (which field, the error, whether repair fixed it).

    Hint 1 — a nudge

    Wrap the validation in a try-except block. Catch ValidationError from Pydantic. On the first failure, build a message that includes the bad JSON and the error text. Send it back as a repair attempt. If it fails again, give up and log it.

    Hint 2 — the shape of the answer

    Attempt counter starts at 1. Call the model, parse, validate. On ValidationError, increment counter. If counter is 1, resend with the error. If counter is 2, log the failure and move on. Log the field name, error message, and whether it succeeded on retry.

    Still stuck after 10 minutes? The step by step
    1. Catch ValidationError from pydantic.ValidationError in your parse step.
    2. Extract the error message: it usually has a field name and an expectation.
    3. On the first failure, make a repair prompt: "Here is the invalid output: [raw JSON]. The error was: [error message]. Please fix it and return only valid JSON."
    4. Resend to the model with schema enforcement again. Parse and validate once more.
    5. If it fails again, log: input_id, field, error_message, first_attempt_success, second_attempt_success. Then move on.
    6. After 50 inputs, print summary: X% succeeded first try, Y% succeeded after repair, Z% failed.

    Mix it in. Look at your last round's model. Does it have an escape hatch for "unknown"? If your model has an optional field with a sensible default, does your repair prompt mention it? Strengthen your field descriptions based on the repairs you are seeing.

    • Repair loops with no cap. They quietly triple cost on the handful of inputs that were never going to parse.
    • Not logging the field that failed. After 50 inputs you have no data about which fields are weak.

    • Why should you resend the error message, not just "try again"?

      The error message names the field and the expectation. "due_date: input should be a valid date" tells the model exactly what went wrong.

    • You run your extractor on 50 inputs. Forty-five succeed on the first try, four succeed after repair, one fails twice. Did you hit the day's target?

      Yes. Ninety percent first try, 98% after repair, 2% failed. That is above 95%, the target.

    • You run a repair loop with no cap. One bad input costs five times a normal record but still fails. Why is that bad?

      It wastes money and time. If it is running inside a web request, your user is watching a spinner. Two attempts and log it is the rule.

    Building the extractor that stays built

    Now you put it all together. Collect 50 real examples of your document type. Run your extractor on all of them. Track which fields fail and how often. Then strengthen your schema or field descriptions and re-run.

    After each failure, read the document yourself. The extractor is not guessing — it is trying to follow your instructions. If it misread "Bank of America" as a person's name or put the invoice total in the wrong field, your schema probably told it to. The field descriptions matter more than you think. A one-sentence instruction like "the person or company that sent this" is clearer than "sender".

    After your first 50-input run, sort the failures by field. The top three failing fields are your weak spots. Rewrite their Pydantic descriptions in plainer words. Then run all 50 again. Watch the failure count drop.

    Deliberately break it to find the edge cases. Truncate an input mid-sentence. Feed a document in the wrong language. Feed an empty file. Feed a typo in a date field. Each one should produce a logged failure, not a crash. You want to know where the extractor breaks, not discover it in production.

    The goal is at least 95% of 50 inputs parsing into valid objects on the first or second attempt. That is high enough to ship. Not perfect — perfect is a trap — but high enough to be useful. Ninety-five percent means at most two or three documents per hundred need human review.

    Commit the model, the runner, the 50 inputs, and the results table when you are done. Everything lives together in git so you can track what changed and why.

    So: 50 real inputs, iterate on schema, test edge cases, measure success rate, commit when you hit 95%.

    iterate
    to run the process, measure the result, change one thing, and run again

    Close the page. From memory.

    1. What percentage success rate is the goal for this day?
    2. When an extractor misreads a field, whose instructions was it following?

    Your goal: run your extractor on 50 real inputs. Log the results: first-attempt valid, second-attempt valid, failed, plus the failing field for every failure. Iterate on your schema and descriptions until you hit at least 95% success rate. Test three edge cases. Commit.

    Hint 1 — a nudge

    Make a CSV or a results table. One row per input: input_id, field, error_message, first_attempt, second_attempt. Grep the failures by field name. The top three fields are your weak spots. Rewrite their descriptions and re-run.

    Hint 2 — the shape of the answer

    For each of your 50 inputs, call the extractor, log success or failure. Total it at the end: first-attempt successes / 50, second-attempt successes / 50, failed / 50. Target: ≥95% total. Deliberately test: truncate mid-sentence, wrong language, empty file.

    Still stuck after 10 minutes? The step by step
    1. Collect or download 50 real examples of your document type. Save them with IDs (e.g., invoice_001.txt through invoice_050.txt).
    2. Write a runner that loops over all 50. Call your extractor on each. Log: input_id, first_attempt_valid, second_attempt_valid, failure_field, error_message.
    3. Print a summary: "45/50 first try (90%), 48/50 total (96%), 2/50 failed (4%)."
    4. Find the top three failing fields. Rewrite their Pydantic descriptions in plainer words. Re-run all 50.
    5. Test three edge cases: truncate one input mid-sentence, feed one in a different language, feed an empty file. Each should log a failure, not crash.
    6. When you hit ≥95% total success, commit the model, runner, all 50 inputs, and the final results table.

    Mix it in. Look at your failures. The top failing field: is the problem the schema (you asked for the wrong thing), or the description (you did not explain it clearly enough)? Which did you fix?

    • Running on 10 inputs and calling it done. Ten is too few to see the pattern. Fifty shows you the real weak spots.
    • Not reading the failures. The numbers tell you which field fails; reading the inputs tells you why.

    • What is the success-rate target for this day?

      At least 95% of 50 real inputs should parse into valid objects on the first or second attempt.

    • Your extractor fails on the same field in 12 out of 50 inputs. You rewrite the field description. Should you also change the Pydantic type?

      Maybe. First read the 12 failures. If the problem is unclear wording, a better description fixes it. If the problem is structural, change the type or split the field.

    • You feed your extractor an empty file. It crashes instead of logging a failure. What did you forget to test?

      Edge cases. You need to handle empty input, truncated input, wrong language, and other things your 50 examples might not cover.

    Teach it back

    Explain this day to a smart friend who has never built an extractor. What is the problem, how does the solution work, and what is the difference between a schema that is valid syntax and a schema that gives you correct values? Use four to six sentences. Say it out loud, or write it down.

    Watch for the words "basically", "something happens here" and "you just". Each one marks a gap. Go back to that spot in the page, fill the gap, and explain again.

    Where are you on the ladder?

    Being able to say "I have seen this" is only the first rung. Climb all four.

    1. I have seen schema enforcement, Pydantic models, and repair loops before.
    2. I can say what constrained decoding does, why Pydantic models do three jobs, and why repair loops need a cap, without looking.
    3. Given a new document type, I can write a Pydantic model and run it on 10 examples and see which fields fail.
    4. I can design an extractor for a messy document type that hits 95% success on 50 real inputs, and defend each choice in the schema.

    Models now read hundreds of pages in one call, and that quietly changes what you should build. For many problems, you do not need a retrieval pipeline. Instead, put documents straight into the prompt, budget the space carefully, and make the cached repeats nearly free. By tonight you should be able to say: “I can put a 50-page PDF in a prompt, extract facts with citations, check the citations are real, and know what it cost.”

    Images and PDFs cost tokens

    An image does not escape the token meter. It gets cut into a grid of small square patches. Each patch becomes a vector. Each vector occupies token slots.

    A bigger image means more patches and more tokens, until you cross a limit and the provider shrinks it. A full page scan costs about one to two thousand tokens. Which means photographing a table is not cheaper than typing it.

    PDFs travel two different paths, and you should choose deliberately. Extract the text layer—fast, exact, cheap, and it throws the layout away. Or render each page as an image—expensive, but now the model sees the table structure, the checked box, the signature.

    Many providers do both automatically, and bill you for both.

    Here is the trap. A scanned PDF has no text layer. A text extractor returns empty strings. Your pipeline confidently summarizes nothing at all.

    So: print the extracted character count per page before you call anything. One line of code that catches this whole failure.

    text extraction
    pulling the text layer out of a PDF; fast and cheap but ignores layout
    image rendering
    turning each PDF page into an image so the model sees structure like tables and checkboxes
    scanned PDF
    a PDF made from photographs, with no text layer, so extraction returns empty strings

    Print character counts as a sanity check

    The trap is silent. A scanned PDF returns empty strings. Your pipeline summarizes nothing confidently.

    Before you send anything to the model, print the extracted character count per page. One line of code. If any page shows zero characters, stop and ask: is this a scanned PDF or a corrupted text layer?

    This catches an entire category of failure before you spend tokens.

    So: a sanity check that takes one line saves hours of debugging.

    sanity check
    a simple test that catches obvious failures before they waste tokens or time

    2. Why does a scanned PDF silently produce an empty summary?

    2. Extract text per page. Print page number and character count.
    3. For any page with fewer than 100 characters, note it.

    • Rendering a clean text PDF page as an image anyway, and paying 1,500 tokens for what the text path gave you in 300.

    • Why does rendering a PDF page as an image cost more tokens than extracting text?

      An image is divided into patches. Each patch is a vector. Each vector is tokens. A page rendering costs 1,000 to 2,000 tokens.

    • You extract a PDF page and get zero characters. What are two possible reasons, and what should you try?

      It is a scanned page with no text layer, or the text layer is corrupted. Render the page as an image and try extracting from that.

    Budget the context window

    The context window is one shared space. Everything competes for it: your system prompt, documents, conversation history, reasoning tokens, and the answer itself.

    So if the window is 200,000 tokens and your document is 190,000, there is no room left to write with. Decide the reserve for output first. Then fill what is left with the document.

    Quality also degrades well before you reach the hard limit. Facts buried in the middle of a very long input are recalled less reliably than facts near the beginning or the end. That is the "lost in the middle" effect.

    Two practical consequences fall straight out of it. Put your instructions and question after the document, where they sit closest to where generation begins. And put the document you care most about first.

    So: reserve the answer's room before you spend the input's, and keep what matters at the edges.

    context window
    the total capacity for tokens, shared among input and output
    lost in the middle
    the effect where facts in the middle of a long input are recalled less reliably than those at the edges

    Order matters when caching

    Reading your input is real computation. The model builds internal state as it goes. Prompt caching stores that state for a prefix of your request.

    If the next request starts with byte-identical content, the provider resumes from the stored state instead of recomputing. The savings are large. Cached input bills at roughly a tenth of the normal rate. Writing to the cache costs slightly more than normal input.

    The word doing all the work here is prefix. Caching matches from the start forward, and stops at the first byte that differs.

    Your whole structure follows from that one fact. Stable content first—tool definitions, system prompt, the document. Volatile content last—the user's question, the timestamp, the request id.

    Watch how easy this is to break. Put datetime.now() at the top and you disable caching for your entire application while everything still looks like it works.

    Two more limits worth holding: caches expire after minutes, and very short prefixes are not cached at all.

    So verify instead of assuming. The response reports cache-read and cache-write tokens, and a cache-read of zero across repeated calls means something in your prefix is changing. See the caching docs.

    So: put what never changes at the front, and trust the cache-read number rather than your memory of where you put things.

    prompt caching
    storing the model's internal state for a prefix of the request so repeated requests don't recompute
    cache-read tokens
    tokens read from the cache instead of recomputed, billed at roughly a tenth of the normal rate
    prefix
    the leading part of the request that must be byte-identical for a cache hit

    Summaries with citations

    When the corpus is a handful of documents (or one per request), put the whole thing in the prompt. Sixty pages is roughly 45,000 tokens. At $3 per million, that is about 13 cents a call, and about 1.3 cents on a cache hit.

    Set that against a retrieval pipeline: a week of your work, plus its own failure modes—bad chunking, missed matches, stale indexes—every one of which you have to evaluate.

    It flips when the corpus is hundreds of documents, when different users see different subsets, or when your latency budget cannot absorb 45,000 tokens per request. That is Week 2, built knowing exactly what it bought you.

    Now add citations. A summary with page numbers looks trustworthy. That is the hazard—looking trustworthy and being checkable are different properties, and only one of them is yours.

    Put the citation in the schema: a quoted span plus a page number for every claim. Then verify in code that the quoted string actually appears on that page.

    So: the cheapest retrieval system is the one the numbers told you not to build yet, and an unverified citation makes a wrong answer look more convincing, not less.

    whole-document prompt
    putting an entire document in the prompt instead of retrieving pieces; cheap and simple when the corpus is small
    citation
    a reference to the source of a claim, including a page number and a quoted span
    verified citation
    a citation where the quoted text has been checked against the actual document

    • A scanned PDF that extracts to empty strings, producing a confident summary of nothing at all.

    • When does putting the whole document in the prompt beat building a retrieval pipeline?

      When the corpus is a handful of documents, or one per request. When sixty pages of tokens costs thirteen cents, and a retrieval system costs you a week of work.

    • Your model returns a finding with a page number but the quote does not appear on that page. What do you do?

      Flag it or drop it. The citation is wrong. Without verification, the page number is just decoration that makes the wrong answer look more convincing.

    Measuring the whole system

    You now have three decisions to measure: text extraction vs. image rendering for scanned pages. Caching on vs. off. Citation verification pass rate.

    For a scanned page, render it as an image and send it to the model. Compare the extracted facts against the text path. Which one is more accurate? Which one is cheaper? One page is not enough—try five scanned pages and see the pattern.

    For caching, run the same document with three different questions and record cache-read tokens, cost, and time to first token for each. Does the cache hit bring down latency? Does it save money? On a large document, the savings can be dramatic. On a short document, caching might not matter.

    For citations, run your 20-case test set through the verifier. What is the pass rate? Are mismatches real errors or minor rewording? A 95 percent pass rate is good. Eighty-five percent means the model is hallucinating citations, and that is a problem you need to solve before shipping.

    Every measurement is a row in a table you can read. No arguments. No feelings. Just numbers. The case that broke is no longer a mystery—you can see it, measure it, and fix it.

    So: measure everything. Commit the numbers. The results are the evidence for which decisions to make in Week 2. You will know which documents fit in a prompt, which ones need retrieval, and whether your citations are real or invented.

    pass rate
    the fraction of citations where the quote was found on the claimed page
    cache efficiency
    the cost and speed improvements from repeated requests sharing the same prefix
    latency
    time to first token and total time, which respond differently to input size and output size

    Streaming means words arrive as they're written

    Think of a restaurant. The food comes out one plate at a time instead of waiting for all twelve dishes before the first one leaves the kitchen. You see your appetizer immediately, even though dessert is still cooking.

    With an API call, the model sends each chunk as it finishes generating it, instead of holding everything until the last word is done. The protocol is called server-sent events, or SSE. Your FastAPI endpoint returns a StreamingResponse with text/event-stream as the content type. Each chunk is a line of the form data: .... The browser reads these lines using EventSource or a reader on the response body. The FastAPI response docs show the exact shape. The provider streams to you, and you stream to your client.

    Here is the hard part: every hop has to refuse to wait. Your handler yields each chunk instead of building up a string. Compression is off for that route. Any proxy in the chain is told not to buffer. One middleman that collects everything before forwarding and your streaming endpoint looks exactly like a normal slow one — but only from your phone, not from your laptop.

    Streaming does not make anything faster. The total time is the same. What it does is make the first word arrive early. That is what people feel as speed.

    So: every hop passes the chunk on right away, or streaming becomes just a slow regular call.

    server-sent events (SSE)
    a way to send one message at a time over HTTP, used for streaming
    StreamingResponse
    FastAPI's type for an endpoint that sends chunks as they arrive
    buffer
    to hold something in memory before sending it

    Close the page. Say or write the answer.

    1. Streaming makes time to first token fast. What does it not change?
    2. Why does a streaming endpoint work on localhost but buffer on a deployed server?

    Your goal: a streaming endpoint that sends the summary in chunks, where each chunk is one event. A client reads the stream and prints each chunk as it arrives, recording the wall-clock time of the first and last chunk.

    The endpoint yields lines of data: {chunk} and ends with data: [DONE]. The client reads the stream line by line and notes the time of the first and last line. Both times are printed with the output.

    3. Write a client that makes a request to the stream endpoint and reads the response line by line.
    4. Start a monotonic timer just before the request. Note the timer when the first line arrives and when the last one does. Print both times along with the output.
    5. Test locally, then test from a different network (tether to your phone). If times are the same or better deployed, the stream works. If deployed is much slower, a proxy is buffering.

    Mix it in. Look back at Round 4 of Day 1. You measured two clocks: time to first token and total time. Does your streaming client measure the same two clocks correctly now?

    A response cache saves whole answers

    Imagine your friend always asks the same three questions. You write down your answers. Next time, you just read your notebook instead of thinking again. That is a response cache.

    The key is a hash of everything that decides the answer: the prompt version, the model, the parameters like temperature, and the normalized input. The value is the whole response. A hit costs zero model tokens and about one millisecond.

    It only works when the same key genuinely means the same answer. So keep temperature near 0, do not put personal data into a shared cache key, and set a time to live so stale answers eventually expire.

    So: a response cache answers repeated questions from memory.

    response cache
    a store of whole answers, keyed on prompt + model + parameters, so identical questions get answered instantly
    cache hit
    when a request finds its answer already stored
    cache miss
    when a request has to run the model because the answer is not stored

    A prompt cache saves the reading

    Your response cache works when the question is identical. The prompt cache is the provider's trick, and it works when the first part of the input is identical. So when you send the same document and ask different questions about it, the provider remembers reading the document and charges less for it the second time.

    They compose. Your response cache catches exact repeats — same document, same question, zero tokens. Below that, the prompt cache catches shared prefixes — same document, different question, and only the question gets charged at full price.

    Measure the hit rate: hits divided by total requests. A 30 percent response cache hit rate takes about 30 percent off the bill and drags latency down toward zero, because a third of your requests never touch a model.

    So: one cache remembers whole answers, the other remembers the reading you already paid for.

    prompt cache
    the provider's cache of cached tokens, charged at a discount for input the provider has already processed recently
    cached tokens
    input tokens that the provider has in cache, charged at a lower rate than new input

    Close the page. Say or write the answer.

    2. A 30 percent response cache hit rate — how much does that cut off the bill?

    Send to the small model first. Escalate on evidence

    Think of a library. A question goes to a student volunteer first. They try to answer it. If they are not sure or get it wrong, it escalates to the librarian. The librarian only ever sees what the volunteer couldn't handle. Cost stays low because the student handles most of it.

    A router is the same idea. Send the request to a small model first. Accept the answer if it passes a check. Escalate to the big model only when it does not.

    The check has to be something a machine can decide, not a matter of taste. Did the JSON validate against the schema? Does the required field have a value? Did the citation quote match the document? Do the numbers add up? Check the answer, not the model's confidence. Confidence scores in model responses are generated text, not a measurement of anything.

    Why does this save money? The small model handles most of what arrives. The big model only sees what failed. A small model at $0.25 per million and a large one at $3, with 20 percent escalating, gives you an average close to the small model's price and quality close to the large model's.

    Watch the escalation rate. If it goes above a third, the small model is doing too little — either improve its prompt or just use the big model. You are paying for both paths and adding latency on top.

    So: escalate on something you can check, and only for the requests that actually failed the check.

    router
    logic that sends easy requests to a cheap model and hard ones to an expensive model
    escalate
    to send a request to a more powerful model after a cheaper one fails
    check
    a mechanical test — schema valid, field non-null — that decides whether to escalate

    Close the page. Say or write the answer.

    P95 is the unluckiest user

    An average is a lie. Nine requests at 400 milliseconds and one at 9 seconds average to 1.2 seconds — but one user in ten waited 9 seconds. That one user in ten will report the service as broken.

    Collect the latency of every request in a list and sort it shortest to longest. The value at the halfway point is the P50, or median. The value 95 percent of the way up is the P95 — the slowest one in twenty. That one is your bottleneck.

    P95 is the number that blows through timeouts. It is the experience of your unluckiest users. It is the number that shows up in a support ticket. Put this number in your README, not the average.

    Measure the categories separately. A cached request and an uncached one live in two different worlds. A request that hit the small model and one that escalated are different. A request on a cold start and one on a warm server are not comparable. Count them apart, or the fast ones will hide the slow ones. Then compute P95 for each category separately.

    Fifty runs gives you a rough P95. A few hundred makes it stable. Once you have two hundred requests, the P95 of the next hundred will look similar to the P95 of the first hundred, and you know the number is real.

    So: report the slowest one in twenty, per category, and never report an average.

    P50
    the median latency, where half of requests are faster
    P95
    the latency where 95 percent of requests are faster and 5 percent are slower
    percentile
    a rank in a sorted list, so P95 means the 95th percentile

    Six kinds of failure, two actions

    A call fails in one of six ways. The first three are not really errors — they are successful responses that are wrong in different ways.

    Hallucination. The model writes something confident and plausible that is not true. Retrying just gives you a different plausible wrong answer. The fix is grounding — making the model point to a source — or verification that checks the answer against the world.

    Truncation. The output hit max_tokens or a stop sequence before the model finished. The stop_reason field tells you this, and it is still the failure people misdiagnose most often. Read that field on every call.

    Refusal. A safety layer or the model itself declines to answer. It arrives as a successful response with a refusal in the stop reason, or an apologetic paragraph in the text. Retrying the identical input produces the same refusal.

    The last three are real network failures.

    Rate limits. A 429 response, usually with a retry-after header, from a per-minute budget. This one is retryable — wait and try again.

    Timeouts. Your client gave up before the answer came back. Dangerous because the work may have completed on the server, so a naive retry might run the work twice. The idempotency key fixes this.

    Outages. A 5xx response from a struggling server. Retryable, but the server is already in trouble, so retrying too fast makes it worse.

    The taxonomy is the deliverable. Retry 429, 5xx, and connection errors. Never retry 400 or 401 — they stay malformed and unauthorized no matter how many times you send them.

    So: name the failure before you respond to it, because retrying the wrong one just costs money for the same answer.

    hallucination
    a model's confident, false claim
    truncation
    when max_tokens cuts off the answer mid-word
    refusal
    when the model or a safety filter declines to answer
    idempotency
    when an operation produces the same result every time, no matter how many times you run it

    Close the page. Say or write the answer.

    2. You get a 400 bad request. Should you retry?
