    Exponential backoff and jitter

    A provider is struggling. You retry immediately. So do a thousand other clients. The provider gets a wall of requests exactly when it is trying to recover. That makes it worse.

    Exponential backoff spreads out the retries. Wait 1 second. Then 2. Then 4, then 8. Each wait is double the last. This gives a struggling service room to breathe instead of a steady drumbeat of new load.

    But jitter is what saves the provider. A thousand clients all fail in the same second, and without jitter, they all retry in the same second. With jitter, a random fraction is added to each wait. So retries spread across time, and the provider can answer them one by one instead of facing a thundering herd.

    If the response carries a retry-after header, that number beats your formula. The server is telling you what it can currently handle.

    Cap the whole retry loop against your latency budget, not against an attempt count. Five retries of 30 seconds each means a user waited 150 seconds to be told it failed.

    And check what your SDK already does. Most SDKs retry a couple of times on their own. Your retry loop wrapped around their retries is six attempts you didn't plan.

    So: double, jitter, obey retry-after, and stop when the clock says stop.

    exponential backoff
    waiting times that double with each retry: 1, 2, 4, 8 seconds…
    jitter
    random variation added to backoff times so that retries don't all happen at once
    retry-after
    a response header telling the client how long to wait before retrying

    Close the page. Say or write the answer.

    1. Why does exponential backoff help a struggling provider?
    2. One thousand clients all fail in the same second. Without jitter, when do they all retry?

    Your goal: wrap your API call in a retry function. Double the wait between attempts. Add jitter — a random fraction of each wait. Stop when the total time reaches your latency budget. Log the attempt number and the wait time before each retry.

    Hint 1 — a nudge

    Start simple: 1, 2, 4, 8 second waits. After each failure, compute wait * (1 + random() * 0.1) to add 10 percent jitter. Check the total time before each retry.

    Hint 2 — the shape of the answer

    One function: call_with_retries(). Inside, track elapsed time. On a retryable failure, double the wait, add random jitter, and sleep. Check if total time exceeds budget before the sleep. If yes, give up. Log each attempt and each wait.

    Still stuck after 10 minutes? The step by step
    1. Wrap the API call in a try/except. On a retryable failure, initialize wait to 1 second and attempt to 1.
    2. Calculate wait_with_jitter = wait * (1 + random() * 0.1). Add it to elapsed time.
    3. If elapsed time now exceeds your budget (say 30 seconds), give up and return the error. Otherwise, sleep and retry.
    4. Double the wait and increment attempts. Go back to step 2.
    5. Test it: call the endpoint with a fake provider that always returns 429. Confirm it retries three times over about 7 seconds, then gives up.

    Mix it in. Look at the retry logic you just wrote. If your SDK already retries twice, how many total attempts will your code make on a 429?

    • Retries stacked on top of the SDK's own retries, silently making six attempts when you only wanted three.
    • A timeout so generous it exceeds your caller's own timeout, so your retry logic is still running after the user hung up.

    • What does jitter do?

      It spreads retries across time so that a thousand clients don't all retry in the same second and overwhelm the recovering server.

    • You retry with waits of 1, 2, 4, 8 seconds. Add 10 percent jitter to the last wait. About how long was it?

      8 * 1.1 = 8.8 seconds, or anywhere from 8 to 8.8 depending on the random number.

    By tomorrow you can reproduce: how to add exponential backoff and jitter, and why you stop at a time budget instead of an attempt count.

    A key ensures one timeout doesn't run the job twice

    A timeout does not mean nothing happened. It means you stopped listening.

    The work may have completed on the server. Your retry is then a second delivery of work that already ran. For a read operation that is harmless — you pay twice and move on. For anything that writes data, sends a message, or charges money, it is a duplicate with real consequences.

    The fix is an idempotency key. Generate a unique id for each logical operation. Store it with the result when the work completes. On the next request with the same key, return the stored result instead of running the work again.

    Accept an idempotency key from your own callers too. This lets them be as careful with you as you are being with your provider.

    So: a key turns “did that go through?” from a guess into a lookup.

    idempotency key
    a unique id for each logical operation, so a retry with the same key returns the cached result instead of running again
    idempotent
    an operation that produces the same result every time, no matter how many times you run it

    A circuit breaker fails fast

    When a provider is genuinely down, retries stop helping and start hurting. Every request burns your whole backoff budget before it fails. Users wait 40 seconds to receive an error, and your traffic piles onto a service that is already in trouble.

    A circuit breaker is a counter and three states. Closed: calls pass through and you count failures in a rolling window. Cross the threshold — say 5 failures in 30 seconds — and it flips to open, where every call fails instantly without a request leaving your process. After a cooldown it moves to half-open and lets exactly one call through. Success closes the circuit. Failure opens it again for another cooldown.

    Failing in one millisecond is a much better product than failing in forty seconds, and it is what lets your fallback path stay fast.

    So: one counter is the difference between an outage that costs you a second and one that costs you every user's patience.

    circuit breaker
    logic that stops trying to reach a failing service and fails fast instead
    half-open
    a state where the circuit breaker lets one test call through to see if the service recovered

    Close the page. Say or write the answer.

    1. A timeout happens and you retry. The work already completed on the server. What stops a duplicate?
    2. Why should you accept an idempotency key from your own callers?

    Your goal: your endpoint accepts an idempotency key in the request. It checks if the key exists. If yes, return the stored result. If no, run the work, store the result with the key, and return it. Test it by sending the same key twice and confirming the result is identical.

    Hint 1 — a nudge

    Add a table or cache that maps keys to results. Before the work, check if the key is there. If yes, return it. If no, do the work and store it.

    Hint 2 — the shape of the answer

    Add a parameter idempotency_key to your endpoint. At the start, query your cache: if the key exists, return its result. Otherwise, run your logic, store the result with the key, and return it.

    Still stuck after 10 minutes? The step by step
    1. Add a table or dict that maps idempotency keys to results.
    2. At the start of the endpoint, check if the request carries an idempotency_key parameter.
    3. If it does and the key is in the cache, return the cached result immediately.
    4. If not, run the work as usual. When done, store the result with the key in the cache.
    5. Test: send a request with a key. Then send the same key again. Confirm both get the exact same result.

    Mix it in. Look at your idempotency implementation. How long do you keep a cached result? What happens if you keep them forever?

    • A key scheme that includes a timestamp or unsorted data, so every request gets a unique key and you get zero cache hits.
    • Keeping cached results forever, so your memory grows without bound.

    • What does an idempotency key do?

      It prevents duplicate work. The same key returns the stored result, not a new job, so a retry after a timeout doesn't run the work twice.

    • You send a request with key abc, and it times out. You retry with key abc. What should happen?

      The server should recognize the key and return the cached result from the first request, not run the work again.

    By tomorrow you can reproduce: how to store an idempotency key with its result, and why a key lookup is safer than a retry.

    The ladder of degradation

    Between a perfect answer and a stack trace is a ladder. Every rung is a few lines of code, not a rewrite.

    At the top: a full answer, fresh from the model. One rung down: a stale answer from the response cache, clearly labeled as stale. Next: a smaller model or a secondary provider — this is why you keep a backup. Next: a partial result with missing fields marked null. At the bottom: a plain message with a request id and one sentence about what to do next.

    Decide in advance which rung each endpoint lands on. Do not decide in an incident. A search endpoint might fall to a stale answer. A payment endpoint might fall to a partial result, but never to a guess. A message endpoint might fail completely, but only after returning an acknowledgment to the user.

    Treat error text as part of the product. Never leak an API key. Never dump a raw provider message — sometimes they include parts of the prompt. Never send a traceback to the user. Log those with the request id; show the user the id.

    So: the goal was never to stop failing, it is to fail one rung at a time.

    degradation
    providing a reduced or partial service instead of failing completely
    circuit breaker
    a counter and three states that fails fast when a service is struggling, instead of trying and timing out

    Close the page. Say or write the answer.

    2. Why should you decide which rung each endpoint lands on before an incident?

    3. On cache miss, try the small model. On success, return with degraded_to: "small_model".
    4. On failure, return the response shape with all fields as null, plus a request id. Return with degraded_to: "partial".
    5. Test each path: call with normal input (gets fresh), break the provider and check cache (gets cached), break the cache and check small model, break the small model and check partial.

    • Error messages that leak the provider response or the traceback. Log those with the request id. Show the user only the id.

    • What is the degradation ladder?

      From fresh answer to stale cached answer to smaller model to partial result to an error message with a request id. Each rung is one level worse than the last.

    • A search endpoint can use a stale answer. A payment endpoint cannot. Why not?

      Search is about giving the user something useful right away. Staleness is acceptable. Payment is about money, so accuracy matters more than speed. A stale answer means the wrong price or wrong quantity.

    Where are you on the ladder?

    Four rungs: from seeing it to building it.

    1. I have heard of hallucination, truncation, refusal, rate limits, timeouts, and outages.
    2. I can say which ones should be retried and which should not, and why idempotency keys stop duplicates.
    3. Given a failure mode, I can predict whether exponential backoff or idempotency keys would help, and which rung of the ladder to use.
    4. I can build a service that classifies failures, retries smart with backoff, stays idempotent, and degrades gracefully through five rungs.

    Today you put the service on the public internet and write a README that makes it legible to a stranger in 90 seconds. By tonight you should be able to say: “A stranger can use this from a link, and they can read what one run costs.” Then you take half a day off.

    What changes when the URL is public

    On your laptop, your code runs in a safe box. You have the API key in a file. Nobody else can call it. The network is yours. When you put it on the internet, four things flip.

    First, the secret. You cannot put a key in a file anymore, because anyone who can read the server's disk can steal it. Your host has a secret store, a locked cabinet where keys live instead. Your code reads from there, not a file. It is the only place a key should ever be on a deployed machine.

    Second, the spend ceiling. An open endpoint with no rate limit is an invoice waiting to happen. One visitor with a script can run your code all night. So before you go live, set a rate limit — a rule that says “this address can make five calls per minute, or one hundred per hour.” And set a spend ceiling on your provider account: “stop taking requests if today's bill hits fifty dollars.” That takes five minutes and saves five thousand.

    Third, cold starts. If your code sits unused for a while, the hosting platform puts it to sleep to save power. The next request wakes it up, and that startup takes extra time. On your laptop this never happens. On the internet, you have to measure it. A code that feels slow might be a cold start, not a slow model.

    Fourth, buffering. Your Week 1 tool streams the answer so the user sees words appear. On your laptop, the words flow straight through. On some hosting platforms, a proxy — a middleman between the user and your code — collects all the words before sending them. From your phone, it looks like your code got slow. It did not. From your laptop, you never see it.

    So: deployed is different. Your key lives in a secret store. Spending is capped. Cold starts cost time. And a proxy may hide the stream, but only if you test from outside your own network.

    secret store
    a locked cabinet on the host where API keys and secrets live, instead of files
    rate limit
    a rule that limits how many requests one address can make in a time window
    spend ceiling
    a hard stop: the provider refuses requests if spending hits this number today
    proxy
    a middleman that receives data from your code, then sends it to the user

    The README is the deliverable

    The tool works. The next question is: can you explain what you built? A README is not a manual. It is not a tutorial. It is six short sections, written in an hour, that tell a stranger what happened. Imagine a hiring manager reads it for 90 seconds. What do they want to see?

    They do not want to hear “uses AI.” They want numbers. “$0.004 per request. P95 latency is 2.4 seconds. We got a 31 percent cache hit rate. Here is why I chose the small model first.” That is evidence that you reason about trade-offs.

    Write six sections: one paragraph about what it does, in words a non-expert understands. An architecture diagram — a simple block diagram is fine. Cost per request, with the arithmetic shown. The P50 and P95 latency, and how you measured them. Known failure modes, and what you'd fix with another week. And a live link.

    The numbers you collected all week are not hidden in a notebook. They are the whole point. Put them in a table. Show that you can measure your own work and reason about it. A hiring manager reads for 90 seconds and moves on. If the numbers are there, they notice.

    So: the README is where the numbers live, and the numbers are proof you understand what you built.

    README
    a short document that explains what a project does, what it costs, and how fast it is
    P50 latency
    the time where half your requests were faster and half slower
    P95 latency
    the time where 95 percent of requests were faster and only 5 percent slower

    The map for this week

    Week 1 taught the model to do what you say. This week it answers from documents it has never seen: your notes, your code, your policies. No retraining needed. The mechanism is simple. Find the paragraphs that answer the question. Paste them into the prompt. Ask again. The whole idea lives in one word: find.

    You build the finder twice. First from scratch with numpy, so no library hides the math from you. Then properly: a real store, two search methods that fail differently, and a second model that reorders results. This is where demos become systems. On Day 11 you hand-label a test set and measure. By Sunday you can say something like: "Hybrid search plus reranking moved recall from 0.62 to 0.84 on a 40-question test set." That sentence is the whole week.

    embedding
    a number that represents meaning, so documents that mean the same thing have numbers close to each other
    chunking
    breaking long documents into pieces small enough for a prompt
    retrieval
    finding the documents that match a question, before you send them to the model
    recall
    what fraction of the right answers you found (did you miss any?)
    reranking
    using a second model to sort the results, usually more accurate than the first score
    RAG
    retrieval-augmented generation: search first, then ask the model to answer from those results

    Before Day 8 (25 minutes): read this map once. Then close it and draw the week on paper from memory: the big ideas, the words, and arrows for how they connect. Open it again and fix what you missed. Do not try to learn anything yet.

    Today you build a complete retrieval system with no database, no framework, and no import you can’t explain. By tonight you should be able to say: “I wrote semantic search with numpy. I know exactly what a vector database does.”

    An embedding is a list of numbers with a location

    Start with what the machine actually does. An embedding model is a language model with its last layer swapped out. A normal model reads text and predicts the next token. This one reads a whole piece of text and emits a fixed-length list of numbers instead — 384 of them, or 768, or 1536, depending on the model.

    Hold on to the words fixed length. Five words in, 1536 numbers out. Five hundred words in, still 1536 numbers out. Same text, same numbers, every time.

    Now treat those numbers as coordinates, the way latitude and longitude are coordinates. Every piece of text you own becomes a point in a very large space, and the model was trained so that texts about the same thing land near each other.

    Don't go hunting for meaning inside any single coordinate. There is no "cat" axis and no slot that holds "money". Meaning lives in the arrangement — in where a point sits relative to all the other points.

    So why does this matter? Because it buys you a kind of search that keyword matching cannot do. A page that says "we return your money within 30 days" never contains the word refund. Look for refund anyway, and there it is, sitting right beside you.

    Now the trap, and it is a quiet, total one: query and documents must be embedded by the same model. Two models build two unrelated coordinate systems. Compare across them and you get numbers that look perfectly reasonable and mean nothing at all. Some models also want a prefix on the input, like query: versus passage:. Read the model card before you embed 50,000 chunks the wrong way.

    So: an embedding is a fixed-length address in meaning-space, and every address in your system has to be issued by the same model.

    embedding
    a fixed-length list of numbers that represents the meaning of a piece of text
    fixed length
    the list is always the same size, no matter how long the input text is
    coordinate
    a number that marks a position, like latitude on a map

    Cosine similarity: measure the angle, ignore the length

    You have two lists of numbers. How do you tell whether they point the same way? Multiply them element by element, add the products up, then divide by both lengths. That is cosine similarity, and it is the entire comparison.

    Do it by hand once and it stops being magic. Take a = [0.6, 0.8] and b = [0.8, 0.6]. The products are 0.48 and 0.48, so the sum is 0.96, and both vectors already have length 1 — similarity 0.96, nearly the same direction. Now take c = [-0.8, 0.6]: the products are -0.48 and 0.48, summing to exactly 0. Unrelated. A right angle, written as a number.

    Why the angle and not plain straight-line distance? Because a vector's length tracks things you don't care about, like how long the text was. Direction carries the topic. So normalize every vector once at ingestion — divide it by its own length — and from then on cosine similarity is the dot product. One multiply and one add per dimension, and nothing else.

    Now, the scores themselves. In theory they run from -1 to 1. In practice unrelated pairs sit around 0.0 to 0.3 and related pairs around 0.6 to 0.85, and those bands shift from model to model. So "0.7 means relevant", copied off a blog post, is worthless to you. Score ten pairs whose answers you already know, and read your own model's scale off them.

    Here's the trap that catches everyone. Top-k always returns k results. Ask your corpus a question it has no answer to and you get back the five least-irrelevant chunks, with total confidence. A similarity score is not a claim that the answer is in there.

    So: cosine is one dot product between normalized vectors, and the number it gives you only means something on the scale you measured yourself.

    cosine similarity
    a number from -1 to 1 that measures how much two vectors point the same way
    dot product
    multiply element by element and add the results
    normalize
    divide a vector by its own length so it points the same direction but has length 1

    Load your array from yesterday. Normalize each row. Create a 3x3 table by taking M @ M.T (matrix times its transpose). The diagonal is all 1.0, because each vector is perfectly similar to itself.

    3. Compute all pairwise scores: scores = M @ M.T.
    4. Print the score matrix. It should be symmetric, with 1.0 on the diagonal.
    5. Look at the three off-diagonal scores. Which pairs are close in meaning? Which are far?

      The two texts point mostly the same way. On your model's scale, this might be similar or might not; you have to calibrate by looking at pairs you already know.

    • You normalize two vectors and compute their dot product. What have you just computed?

      Cosine similarity. The dot product of normalized vectors is cosine similarity.

    Dimensions cost money, and you can spend fewer

    Do this arithmetic once and no storage bill will ever surprise you. One vector of 1536 dimensions, at 4 bytes per number (that's float32), is about 6 KB.

    Ten thousand chunks is 61 MB. That is a numpy array that sits in memory without complaint, on the laptop you already own.

    Ten million chunks is 61 GB. That is not a bigger version of the same problem. That is a different engineering problem, with sharding and disk-backed indexes in it.

    What do the extra dimensions buy you? Finer distinctions — more room to keep two similar ideas apart. And they cost you in exact proportion: more memory per row, and more multiply-adds on every single search.

    Some models let you truncate the vector. Keep the first 256 numbers of 1536, lose a little accuracy, and save three quarters of the storage. Both dimension count and truncation are real dials you can turn.

    Neither one gets turned today, though, because you have nothing to measure the result with until Day 11.

    So: a vector is a fixed number of bytes, and multiplying that by your chunk count tells you which kind of system you are building before you build it.

    truncate
    cut off part of a vector: keep the first N numbers and throw away the rest
    dimension
    one number in the embedding vector
    float32
    a number stored in 4 bytes, with decimal places

    Close the page. Calculate without a calculator.

    2. If you truncate from 1536 dimensions to 512, what fraction of the space do you save?

    Truncate by slicing: M_truncated = M[:, :256]. Normalize the truncated vectors and compute dot products just like you did before.

    Hint 2 — the shape of the answer

    Start with your normalized 3x1536 array. Slice to 3x256, normalize again, compute similarity. Then slice to 3x64 and repeat. Print the three score matrices.

    2. Slice to 256 dimensions: M_256 = M[:, :256]. Normalize and compute similarity. Print one off-diagonal score.
    3. Slice to 64 dimensions. Repeat.

    Mix it in. Look at your three similarity tables. Compare the 256-d and 64-d scores. How much did the score go down? Does that surprise you?

    • Computing similarity without normalizing the truncated vectors. You get wrong numbers.

    • One embedding costs 6 KB. How much space do 100,000 embeddings take?

      100,000 times 6 KB is 600,000 KB, or 600 MB.

    • You truncate an embedding from 1536 dimensions to 384. What fraction of the storage do you save?

      You keep 384/1536 = 1/4, so you save 3/4 of the storage.

    Exact search, approximate search, and what a vector database does

    Exact search is the obvious thing: compare the query against every vector you have. In numpy that is one matrix multiply — scores = M @ q — and for 10,000 chunks at 1536 dimensions it is about 15 million multiply-adds, which takes a few milliseconds. Exact also means guaranteed. The true top 5 is the top 5, with no asterisk.

    Approximate nearest neighbor search gives up that guarantee in order to skip most of the work. Watch how it does it.

    The usual structure is a graph. Every vector is a node, linked to its nearest neighbors, plus a few long-range links thrown across the space. Search enters at one node and hops greedily to whichever neighbor is closer to the query, then repeats, and stops when no neighbor is closer.

    Think of it as asking for directions in a city instead of visiting every house. You touch maybe a thousand nodes out of ten million — and in exchange, you sometimes miss a true top-5 item. Index recall is typically 0.95 to 0.99, and it is a knob you set, not an accident.

    So at this week's scale, exact search is not the beginner's option. It is the correct one. Ten thousand rows and a matrix multiply is genuinely the right engineering.

    Which raises the fair question: what is a vector database actually for? Four things. Durable storage that survives a restart. An approximate index that stays fast as rows grow. Metadata filters applied during the search. Safe concurrent updates. Not intelligence — those four.

    So: exact search is a guarantee you can afford today, and a vector database is the machinery you buy when you can no longer afford it.

    exact search
    compare the query to every vector you have; guaranteed correct, but gets slow with millions of vectors
    approximate search
    skip most vectors by using a graph index; trades some accuracy for speed
    vector database
    software that stores vectors with approximate search, durability, filtering, and concurrent updates

    Close the page. Answer from memory.

    1. Why does exact search get slow as your corpus grows, and what does approximate search do about it?
    2. What are two things a vector database does besides finding nearest neighbors?

    Your goal: build a complete RAG system in about 200 lines. Start with a small corpus of 100–300 paragraphs you know well. Embed them all. Normalize. Search for a query using exact search. Retrieve the top 5 chunks. Paste them into a prompt and call the chat model. Log the cost and the tokens.

    Hint 1 — a nudge

    The seven steps are: collect and list paragraphs, embed in batches, normalize, search with M @ q, rank and return top 5, paste into a prompt, call chat model.

    Still stuck after 10 minutes? The step by step

    2. Embed them in batches of 64. Stack the results into a numpy array of shape (N, D).
    3. Normalize every row. Check that all rows have length 1.0.
    4. Embed a query. Normalize. Compute scores = M @ q. Take np.argsort(-scores)[:5].

    • Comparing scores across models, or a normalized vector against an unnormalized one. Both give you plausible numbers that mean nothing.

    • What is exact search?

      Compare the query to every vector you have and return the top results. Slow for millions of vectors, but guaranteed correct.

    • You have a corpus of 10,000 documents and you are building your first version. Should you use exact search or approximate search?

      Exact search. 10,000 rows and a matrix multiply takes a few milliseconds. You can afford it, and it is simpler and guaranteed correct.

    Explain this to a smart friend who has never heard of embeddings. What is an embedding, and how does it let you search without keywords? Start from one piece of text turning into numbers and use four to six sentences.

    Watch for the words “basically”, “something happens here” and “you just”. Each one marks a gap. Go back to that spot in the page, fill the gap, and explain again.

    Where are you on the ladder?

    From seeing embeddings to building retrieval from scratch.

    1. I have heard the words embedding, cosine similarity, and vector database.
    2. I can say what an embedding is, why cosine is the right similarity, and what four things a vector database does.
    3. Given a small corpus, I can build a complete RAG system with exact search and explain why it is the right choice for 10,000 rows.
    4. I can design an ingestion pipeline that scales from 100,000 to millions of vectors and explain where to switch to approximate search.

    Yesterday's demo ran on text you had already cleaned by hand. Real corpora are not like that: two-column PDFs, web pages wrapped in navigation, Markdown holding 300-line code blocks. Today you turn that into chunks worth embedding. Most of the difficulty turns out not to be AI at all.

    Parsing is the actual job

    Here is the thing nobody tells you about PDFs. A PDF does not store paragraphs. It stores instructions: draw this glyph, at this coordinate, on this page. There is no sentence in there. There is no paragraph in there.

    Your parser has to reconstruct reading order from positions, and it guesses. In a two-column layout the guesses interleave the columns, so the sentence you retrieve is half of the left column and half of the right one. Tables collapse into a row of words with no relationship left between them. Page headers and footers get pulled into every chunk on the way past.

    HTML has the opposite problem. It has plenty of structure — most of it is just not content. Strip navigation, sidebars, footers and cookie banners first.

    Skip that and watch what happens. A third of every chunk becomes the same boilerplate. Every chunk starts to look a little like every other chunk. And the keyword search you add tomorrow is poisoned before you even write it.

    Markdown and code are the easy cases, because the structure is written down: headings, fenced blocks, function definitions. Split code on function and class boundaries, never on line count — a chunk that starts halfway through a function teaches the model nothing.

    Now the discipline that saves you a week. Dump the parser's output for 20 random documents and read it before you embed anything. Most retrieval bugs that look like model failures are parser failures nobody ever looked at.

    So: your parser decides what the model can possibly know, which makes twenty minutes of reading its output the highest-value work of the day.

    parser
    code that reads a file format and extracts the text
    interleave
    mix two things together in the wrong order
    glyphs
    individual letters or symbols drawn on a page

    Why chunking exists, and what a bad chunk does

    Two forces push you to split documents up, and they are worth separating.

    The first is yesterday's fixed-length rule. An embedding is the same size no matter how much text you feed it. Embed a 40-page manual as one vector and you get the average of forty topics: mildly near everything, strongly near nothing.

    The second is money. Whatever you retrieve gets pasted into a prompt, and you pay per token, every single query.

    So chunks can be wrong in two directions, and the failures look nothing alike. Too big is dilution again, plus you pay for 2,000 tokens to deliver one useful sentence. Too small is worse in a sneaky way: the chunk reads "It expires after 90 days" and "it" was named in the chunk before. Retrieval succeeded. The answer is still not available. The model fills the gap with a guess.

    Where do you start? 400 to 800 tokens per chunk, with 10 to 15 percent overlap — 50 to 100 repeated tokens at each seam.

    Overlap exists for exactly one reason, so don't overthink it: a sentence cut in half by a boundary survives whole in one of the two copies.

    Then tune these numbers against Day 11's measurements, not against how the chunks feel when you scroll past them.

    So: chunk size trades dilution against orphaned context, and you pick the default now and let the golden set argue with it later.

    chunk
    one piece of text that will be embedded and retrieved
    dilution
    mixing many different topics into one chunk so it is similar to everything and specific to nothing
    overlap
    repeated text at the boundary between two chunks, so a sentence split by the boundary survives whole

    3. Create overlap by copying the last 50 tokens from chunk N to the start of chunk N+1.
    4. Print the token count distribution. If there is a long tail past 1200, your splitter is missing a case.

      Overlap is repeated text at the boundary between chunks. It keeps a sentence whole if the boundary cuts it in half.

    Structural chunking, and keeping the heading attached

    There are two ways to decide where a chunk ends, and one of them is almost always right.

    Structural chunking splits on the document's own boundaries: headings, sections, list items, function definitions. It is cheap, it is deterministic, and it usually wins — because the author already decided where the ideas end, and you are just believing them.

    Semantic chunking embeds sentence by sentence and cuts where consecutive sentences stop being similar. It costs an embedding call per sentence, and it occasionally helps on flowing prose that has no headings at all. Try it second, if ever.

    Now here's the trick, and it is the highest-return line of code you will write today. It is one string concatenation: prepend the breadcrumb.

    Start the chunk's text with Employee Handbook > Leave > Parental leave, then the section body. That's it. The chunk now describes itself.

    Watch what that fixes. A question about parental leave matches heading words the body never bothered to repeat, because the author assumed you could see the heading. And when the chunk lands in a prompt, the model knows what it is reading instead of inferring it. For code, use the file path and the class name the same way.

    So: cut on the structure the author already gave you, and staple the heading path to the front of every chunk so it can stand alone.

    structural chunking
    split documents on their own boundaries: headings, sections, list items, function definitions
    semantic chunking
    embed sentence by sentence and cut where consecutive sentences stop being similar
    breadcrumb
    the heading path prepended to a chunk, like "Handbook > Leave > Parental leave"

    Close the page. Say or write the answer.

    3. Create a stable ID from (source_path, heading_path, chunk_index).
    4. Store each chunk as a dict with: text, source, heading_path, chunk_index, stable_id.
    5. Save to JSON.

    Mix it in. Look at three random chunks. For each one, check: does it make sense without the heading? Does the breadcrumb give it the words its author assumed were obvious?

    • What is structural chunking?

      Split on the document's own boundaries: headings, sections, list items, function definitions. The author already decided where ideas end.

    • You are chunking code and you split every 20 lines. Is that structural chunking?

      No. Structural would split on function and class boundaries. Line-based chunks are arbitrary and teach the model nothing about structure.

    Stable ids, dedupe, and re-indexing only what changed

    Every chunk needs an identifier you can regenerate from the source. Compose it from three things you already have: the source path, the section path, and the chunk's index within that section.

    Test it the obvious way. Run ingestion twice over an unchanged document. The identifiers must come out identical. If they don't, the second run duplicates your corpus, and soon every search returns the same chunk five times.

    Then dedupe on content: hash the chunk text after lowercasing it and collapsing the spacing, and keep one copy. Real corpora are full of repeated footers and copy-pasted sections, and every duplicate steals a slot in your top 5.

    For incremental re-indexing, store one hash per source document and compare on each run. Unchanged: skip it, pay nothing. Changed: delete every chunk carrying that document's prefix, then re-insert. Gone from the source: delete.

    Always delete-then-insert rather than update in place. Here's why: when the text changes, the chunk boundaries move, so the old identifiers no longer line up with the new chunks. Updating in place quietly leaves orphans behind.

    The cost math is what actually decides whether your index stays fresh. A full rebuild of 50,000 chunks costs a few dollars and 40 minutes. An incremental run over 12 changed documents costs cents and finishes in seconds. Only one of those is something you will run several times a day.

    So: stable identifiers plus one hash comparison turn re-indexing from an event into a background job.

    stable identifier
    an ID that you can regenerate the same way every time from the source
    dedupe
    find and delete exact duplicate chunks
    incremental re-indexing
    re-embed only the documents that changed since the last run

    Close the page. Answer from memory.

    1. What makes an identifier "stable"? Why does it matter?
    2. Why should you delete-then-insert instead of updating a chunk in place?

    Your goal: add stable IDs to your chunks. Hash each chunk's normalized text and drop exact duplicates. Store one hash per source document. Re-run ingestion on your unchanged corpus and confirm zero embedding calls. Change one file and confirm only its chunks move.

    Hint 1 — a nudge

    Stable ID = hash(source_path + heading_path + chunk_index). Content hash = hash of normalized chunk text (lowercase, collapsed spaces). Store a document hash alongside each chunk.

    Hint 2 — the shape of the answer

    Create stable IDs from (source_path, heading_path, chunk_index). Hash chunk text and drop duplicates. Store document hashes in a JSON file. On the next run, compare hashes and skip unchanged documents.

    Still stuck after 10 minutes? The step by step
    1. Add a stable ID to each chunk: id = hashlib.md5(f"{source}|{heading}|{index}".encode()).hexdigest().
    2. Hash the normalized chunk text. Drop chunks with duplicate content hashes.
    3. Compute one hash per source document (the hash of all its content). Store in a JSON file.
    4. On the next run, load the document hashes. Skip any document whose hash hasn't changed.
    5. Change one file, re-run, and confirm only its chunks were re-embedded.

    Mix it in. How many duplicate chunks did you find? Count them. The number usually surprises people.

    • Unstable identifiers built from a timestamp, a list position, or a random value. Every re-run duplicates the corpus instead of updating it.
    • Deleting a source document and forgetting its chunks. The index keeps answering from documents that no longer exist.

    • What is a stable identifier?

      An ID you can regenerate the same way every run from the source. Usually made from source path, heading path, and chunk index.

    • You change one file in your corpus and re-run ingestion. With stable IDs and document hashes, how many embedding calls will you make?

      Only the calls for chunks from that one file. Unchanged files are skipped.

    What a vector store adds

    Yesterday your embeddings lived in a numpy array inside one Python process. Today they move into a real database — PostgreSQL with pgvector, Qdrant, Chroma, or Weaviate. Pick one in ten minutes and move on. Comparing them is not a day's work, and any of the three will do.

    Think of your array as a toolbox on your workbench. Fast to use while you are there. But the moment you close the shop, the tools vanish. A vector store is a locked cabinet at the warehouse. Slower to reach, but the tools survive the night.

    Underneath is the boring part, which is good news. One row per chunk holds an identifier, the vector, the text, and a JSON column of metadata. Search becomes ORDER BY embedding <=> $1 LIMIT 20, which is the cosine distance you already coded by hand — just running inside the database instead of in your Python process.

    What do you actually gain? Four concrete things. The index survives a restart, so your data does not live inside one Python process. An approximate index keeps search fast as your corpus grows, which your matrix multiply eventually cannot do. Metadata filters run inside the search instead of after it, which turns out to matter enormously. And upsert-by-identifier makes yesterday's re-indexing a single call instead of a delete-and-rebuild dance.

    So: a vector store is the same arithmetic you already wrote, wrapped in durability, speed, filtering, and safe updates.

    vector store
    a database that holds embeddings, text, and metadata, and can search by similarity
    upsert
    update if exists, insert if not, all in one call
    approximate index
    a speed trick that finds nearly-closest vectors without checking every one

    Why dense search misses error codes, surnames, and rare tokens

    An embedding is lossy compression. It squashes meaning into a fixed number of slots. The very first thing it throws away is exact character sequences.

    Three failures follow directly. Error code ERR-4021 and ERR-4012 are nearly identical to an embedding model — both are error codes of roughly this shape. Their vectors sit nearly on top of each other, and ranking one above the other is a coin flip.

    Rare surnames the model barely saw during training land somewhere generic, with no learned position. And short queries with one rare token carry almost no signal to embed in the first place.

    Now meet BM25, which works the opposite way. It scores a document using three countable quantities — no machine learning. First, how often the query's words appear in the document, with diminishing returns: the tenth occurrence adds almost nothing over the ninth. Second, how rare each word is across the whole corpus, so "the" contributes near zero while ERR-4021 contributes enormously. Third, the document's length, so long documents do not win just by containing more words.

    Put plainly: it is exact-token matching that weighs rare terms heavily. Precisely the inverse of dense search's weakness.

    So run both. Hybrid search is not hedging your bets. The two methods fail on different inputs, and combining them helps because that is the only reason.

    So: dense search knows what you meant, keyword search knows what you typed, and you need both because your users do both.

    embedding
    lossy compression of text into a fixed-length vector of numbers
    BM25
    a keyword ranking algorithm that weighs rare words heavily and ignores common ones
    hybrid search
    running both dense and keyword retrieval, then combining the results

    Combining two ranked lists

    You have two lists of results. You need one. The obvious move is to add the scores together, and it is wrong.

    Cosine similarity ranges roughly from 0 to 1. BM25 is unbounded — its range depends on your corpus. Adding them does not combine two opinions; it silently lets whichever scale happens to be bigger decide everything.

    Reciprocal rank fusion throws scores away and uses only positions. For each document, add up 1 / (60 + rank) across the lanes it appears in.

    Watch the numbers. Rank 1 scores 1/61 = 0.0164. Rank 5 scores 1/65 = 0.0154. Nearly identical.

    That flattening is the entire point. When first place and fifth place are worth nearly the same, appearing in both lists matters more than topping one. Which is exactly the behavior you want when the two lanes disagree about a document.

    So: fuse on rank, not on score, because ranks from two lanes are comparable and their raw scores never were.

    reciprocal rank fusion
    a way to combine two ranked lists by treating their positions as comparable
    rank
    the position in a sorted list: rank 1 is best, rank 20 is twentieth-best

    Reranking, and seeing both texts at once

    Everything so far used a bi-encoder. Query and chunk are embedded separately, never read together, and compared with one dot product.

    That separation is fast — you embed the corpus once, months before anyone asks a question. It is also blunt. The chunk's vector was computed with no idea what you would eventually ask.

    A cross-encoder reads the query and one chunk together, in one pass, and outputs one score. Because it reads both at once, it can tell that the "it" in the chunk refers to the thing you asked about.

    It is far more accurate, and structurally unable to scale. One forward pass per query-chunk pair means fifty thousand passes per question over a fifty-thousand-chunk corpus. That is not a tuning problem, it is arithmetic.

    So it goes second. Retrieve fifty candidates cheaply, rerank those fifty, keep five. The cost is typically one hundred to four hundred milliseconds and a small fee, once per query. That is the trade: a fixed slice of latency, spent entirely on fixing the ordering.

    So: cheap retrieval decides what is possible, and the reranker decides what the model actually reads.

    bi-encoder
    embeds query and chunk separately, comparing the vectors with one dot product
    cross-encoder
    reads query and chunk together in one pass, outputting one relevance score
    reranker
    a model that re-orders a small set of candidates using cross-encoding

    Close the page. From memory, answer these.

    1. Why can you not add a cosine score and a BM25 score together?
    2. Why can a cross-encoder see things a bi-encoder cannot?

    Your goal: fused search that takes the top fifty results from each lane and combines them with reciprocal rank fusion, keeping the best fifty. Then a reranker reorders those fifty and you keep five. You measure the time the reranker takes.

    1. Write one fusion function: take the top twenty from each lane, assign each result a reciprocal-rank score, sort by fused score, keep top fifty.
    2. Plug in a reranker: Cohere, Jina, or another hosted service. Call it on the fifty and keep the top five.
    3. Time the reranker call from request to response. Write the number down.
    4. Compare the top five before and after reranking. Does the order change? Should it?

    Mix it in. Look at your queries from Round 2. Does the reranker put keyword-lane winners ahead of dense-lane winners? Or does it see through both and pick differently?

    • Adding raw scores from dense and keyword search. Different scales, so the bigger one always wins.
    • Reranking too few candidates. A reranker can only reorder what it sees; if recall at fifty is bad, a perfect reranker changes nothing.

    • Why can you not add a cosine score and a BM25 score together?

      Cosine ranges from 0 to 1. BM25 is unbounded and depends on the corpus. Adding them lets the bigger scale decide everything.

    • You fused dense and keyword results and got a reranker to reorder them. The reranker put a keyword-lane winner first. What did it see that the lanes missed?

      The reranker read the query and chunk together. It could tell the chunk's meaning matched even if both lanes ranked it differently.

    By tomorrow you can reproduce: why you fuse by rank not score, and what a reranker buys you for a hundred milliseconds.

    Putting it together

    You have four pieces: a vector store, dense search, keyword search, and a reranker. Today you wire them into one pipeline and measure it.

    The shape is simple. Given a query, search both lanes in parallel to save time. Fuse the results by reciprocal rank, keeping the top fifty. Rerank those fifty to sort them by cross-encoder accuracy, and keep the top five. Return their source documents, their scores, and their ranks.

    That is the retrieval path that works. It catches what dense search misses because keyword search runs too. It sorts by what matters because the reranker reads both query and chunk together. From here, Day 12 puts a generator on top that reads what you found and has to cite it.

    Where you put metadata filters matters. The filter belongs inside the search, before ranking. If you ask for twenty results and the filter removes eighteen after ranking, the user sees two. But if you filter during the search, you get twenty filtered results instead — which is what you promised.

    One more detail before you ship. Keep the Day 8 reference search as a comparison. When the hybrid results look wrong, run both and decide which one is right. Bad retrieval hides until you measure it side by side.

    So: one pipeline, wired with care, measured and compared against a known good.

    pipeline
    a series of steps that process data in order, each feeding the next
    parallel
    running two or more steps at the same time instead of one after another
    recall
    the percentage of relevant results that your search actually returned

    The golden set: questions with known answers

    A golden set is a pile of truth. It holds 30 to 50 rows. Each row has a question and the identifiers of the chunks that actually answer it. That is the whole thing.

    Think of a courtroom. The jury needs evidence. The evidence is real, labeled documents. Your golden set is the evidence. Your retrieval code is the witness. The metric is the verdict.

    It will outlast your code. You can rewrite the retriever in an hour. But you spent a day labeling. Those labels stay true no matter what you change underneath.

    Build it in this order. First, real questions from somewhere real: customer support tickets, chat logs, your search history. Then questions you write yourself while reading the corpus. Model-generated questions last, and only after you rewrite them in someone else's words.

    Here is the discipline that makes it work: label chunk identifiers, not the answer text itself. Label the ID, like hb-leave-3 or policy-2. This lets you score retrieval with no model in the loop. It is milliseconds, free, and exactly repeatable. A set comparison is all you need.

    Three traps hide here. First: a model writing a question from a chunk borrows the chunk's vocabulary. Dense retrieval solves it too easily. Your recall reads 0.95 but real users sit at 0.5. Fix it by rewriting generated questions in the words of someone who never read the document. Second: an all-easy set teaches you nothing. Include error codes, questions that need two documents, and questions your corpus cannot answer. Third: tuning on all 40 forever. Hold back 10 rows you do not look at, just for ship decisions.

    So: a golden set is hand-labeled truth. It is the only reason any later number means anything.

    golden set
    30–50 hand-labeled questions, where each row holds the ids of chunks that answer it
    identifier
    a short name for a chunk, like hb-leave-3 or policy-2
    set comparison
    checking whether the labeled ids and returned ids have any overlap

    recall@k: did the answer reach the model?

    One question at a time, ask one yes-or-no thing: did at least one labeled chunk appear in the top k results? Yes scores 1. No scores 0. Average across all your questions. That is recall@k.

    Worked example: 40 questions, 5 chunks each; in 25 a labeled chunk is somewhere in those five. recall@5 = 25/40 = 0.625.

    Why recall and not precision? Because of what each failure costs. The generator can ignore an irrelevant chunk you handed it. It cannot use a chunk that was never retrieved. That chunk is gone.

    This makes the number a ceiling on everything downstream. At recall@5 of 0.62, no amount of prompt work gets you past 62 percent correct answers. Zero. The information is not in the room.

    Measure at the k you actually feed the model. Then measure the whole curve, at k of 1, 3, 5, 10 and 20. The curve's shape tells you what is broken. If recall climbs as k increases — recall@5 is 0.62 but recall@20 is 0.95 — then the right chunk is there but ranked badly. A reranker would help. If recall@20 is also flat at 0.65, the problem is not ranking. Your chunker or parser is losing the answer before the retriever even sees it. No reranker will save you.

    So: recall@k is the percentage of questions whose answer reached the prompt at all. It caps every number that comes after it.

    recall@k
    the percentage of questions where at least one labeled chunk is in the top k results
    curve
    the shape of recall at k=1, 5, 10, 20; the shape tells you what is broken

    2. If recall@20 is 0.95 but recall@5 is 0.62, what is the problem: ranking or chunking?

    MRR: where the answer sits on the list

    recall@5 has a blind spot. It treats rank 1 and rank 5 as equally good, and they are not. Position decides what the generator reads tomorrow, once you order the prompt.

    Add a second number: reciprocal rank. Take the position of the first correct chunk, divide 1 by it. Rank 1 gives 1.0. Rank 2 gives 0.5. Rank 3 gives 0.33. Not found gives 0. MRR is the mean of that across all questions.

    Worked example: four questions with the first correct chunk at ranks 1, 3, 2, and nowhere: (1 + 0.33 + 0.5 + 0) / 4 = 0.46.

    Read that as: "the first right answer sits around position two."

    Notice how steep the drop from 1.0 to 0.5 is. That steepness is on purpose. Slipping from first to second is a bigger deal than slipping from fourth to fifth, because the model reads the top of the pack with more care.

    So: report both recall@5 and MRR. Recall says the information reached the prompt. MRR says it arrived at the top.

    MRR
    mean reciprocal rank: 1 divided by the position of the first correct chunk, averaged across questions
    reciprocal rank
    1 divided by the position where the correct answer was found

    Faithfulness and answer relevance

    Retrieval metrics stop at one question: did the right text reach the prompt? Two more questions remain, and both need a judge — a model with a rubric, or a human.

    Faithfulness, also called groundedness, splits the answer into claims and asks: per claim, is it supported by the retrieved chunks? Three of four supported scores 0.75.

    This is the one that protects trust. It catches the failure that destroys a product: a fluent, confident answer with one invented number in the middle.

    Answer relevance asks something different. Did it answer your question, or a neighboring one? It is judged against the question, not against the sources.

    With all four numbers in hand you can locate any failure exactly. No labeled chunk retrieved: chunking or retrieval. Chunk retrieved but unsupported: generation problem. Supported but off-target: prompt problem.

    So: two retrieval numbers tell you what reached the model. Two judged numbers tell you what it did with that.

    faithfulness
    whether the answer is supported, claim by claim, by the retrieved chunks
    answer relevance
    whether the answer addresses the actual question asked
    groundedness
    another word for faithfulness

    Close the page. Answer without looking.

    2. No chunk is retrieved. The answer is made up. Which box does that go in?

    The harness: small code, big discipline

    The tool is smaller than it sounds. A dataset file, a runner that executes one named configuration, a scorer, and a printed table. About 150 lines total. Ragas gives you tested implementations, but hand-rolling recall@k and MRR takes 20 minutes and teaches you more.

    Two rules make the numbers mean something. Both are about discipline, not code.

    Rule one: change one thing per run. Chunk size, or fusion, or the reranker. Never two together. Record every run with its configuration, date, metrics, and question count. A number without its configuration is a rumor.

    Rule two: respect your sample size. On 40 questions, a move from 0.62 to 0.65 is one question flipping. That is noise. Nine questions flipped (0.62 to 0.84) is real. Count the questions, not the decimal places.

    Read each table row as a sentence you can defend. Not "it improved." Say: "hybrid plus rerank moved recall@5 from 0.62 to 0.84 on a 40-question golden set." Every word is defensible.

    So: the harness is small. The discipline is the hard part. The output is a sentence you can stand behind in an interview.

    harness
    a small testing tool that loads a golden set and scores a retriever
    configuration
    one specific set of choices for the retriever (chunker, embedding model, reranker)

    Grounding is a contract you enforce in code

    Number the chunks. Give each one a short tag like S1 or S2, a header line carrying its source and date, then the text. Instruct the model to answer only from these chunks, and to put the relevant tag after each sentence it writes.

    The model will comply most of the time. And "most of the time" is not a system.

    So you check it in code. The check is three lines of logic. Parse the tags out of the answer. Confirm every tag matches a chunk you actually sent. Confirm at least one tag is present.

    When the check fails, retry once with the failure named in the prompt — models usually fix a mistake they can see. If it fails a second time, return a safe fallback instead of the answer. Do not ship the third attempt.

    One upgrade worth the extra work: keep character offsets when you chunk. Then a tag resolves to a document plus a highlighted span, not just a filename. That is the difference between “source: handbook.pdf”, which nobody can check, and a link that scrolls the reader to the exact sentence.

    The trap is shipping citations you never verify. Users learn to trust them within a day. An unverified citation sitting next to an invented claim is worse than no citation at all — you lent your credibility to a guess.

    So: a citation is a claim your code checks, not a formatting instruction you hope the model followed.

    grounding
    constraining a model's answer to use only information from a specific set of documents
    citation
    a reference back to a source, verified by code before being shown to users
    tag
    a short label attached to each chunk, which the model includes in its answer

    Two defenses against inventing

    Ask a model a question its context cannot answer and it will usually answer anyway. That is not a bug in the model. Predicting plausible next tokens is the entire mechanism. There is no separate part that knows it is out of material.

    So you need two defenses, and you need both of them.

    The first sits before generation: gate on retrieval. If the top reranked score is below a threshold you calibrated on your golden set, do not call the generator at all. You just saved the money and the wrong answer.

    The second sits inside the prompt: make refusal an allowed output with an exact shape. One specified sentence, plus the closest topics you did find so the person can re-ask usefully.

    Why does that work better than a rule? Because models refuse far more reliably when refusal is a format they can produce than when it is a prohibition they must respect. Give it something to say, and it will say that instead of inventing.

    And notice what you now have: those five unanswerable questions in your golden set finally have a right answer to score against.

    So: refuse in two places — before the call, on a score you calibrated, and inside the call, as an output shape the model can actually produce.

    gate
    a yes-or-no check before an expensive operation: if the gate fails, skip the operation
    threshold
    a number that divides go from no-go
    fallback
    a safe answer shown when the main system cannot proceed

    When sources disagree or are out of date

    Retrieval does not check dates. It hands over the 2023 policy and the 2025 policy with identical enthusiasm, because they are about the same topic and that is the only thing it measures.

    Then the model does what models do: it blends them into one fluent answer that matches neither document. Nobody involved has lied. The answer is still wrong.

    Fix number one: put the metadata where the model can see it. Each chunk's header line carries source, section, and last-modified date — the same header you already built for citations.

    Fix number two: state the tie-break rule explicitly. Prefer the most recent. And when two current sources disagree, say so and cite both. A visible disagreement is a genuinely useful answer. A silent average is not.

    But prefer index hygiene to prompt gymnastics wherever you can. The cheapest way to stop the model citing a superseded document is to not retrieve it in the first place. Mark superseded documents in metadata, filter them out by default, and keep archives in a separate collection.

    So: the model can only weigh dates you gave it, and it should never have to weigh a document you could have filtered out.

    tie-break rule
    an explicit instruction for what to do when two sources disagree
    superseded
    no longer current; replaced by a newer version
    metadata filter
    a rule applied during retrieval to exclude documents you do not want

    Close the page. Say or write the answers.

    1. Without dates in the headers, why does a model blend two policies instead of picking one?
    2. What is cheaper than prompting: preventing superseded documents from being retrieved?

    Your goal: your chunk headers now carry source, section, and date. A clear tie-break rule is in the generator prompt: prefer the most recent, and when two current sources disagree, cite both. You have tested on two questions where your corpus has conflicting information at different dates.

    • Letting the model see superseded documents. Filter in retrieval, not in prompting.

      It has no information about which is newer. It sees two answers to the same question and produces a fluent combination.

    Lost in the middle, and why fewer chunks work better

    Models do not attend evenly across a long context. Put a fact near the start or the end and they use it reliably. Put the same fact in the middle of twenty chunks and accuracy drops measurably — same model, same question, same document, different position.

    Sit with that for a second, because it is strange. The information is present. The model has read it. And it still gets used less.

    Three consequences you can act on today. Order deliberately: the reranker's best chunk goes first, not last. Repeat the question after the context as well as before it, so the instruction sits in a strong end position.

    And stop padding. Twenty chunks at recall@20 of 0.95 can produce worse answers than five chunks at recall@5 of 0.84, because the right chunk got buried in the middle. More context is not more information. It is more places to lose the point — and it costs more tokens and more seconds while it does that.

    Do not take the claim on faith. Test it on your own stack. Take questions your system answers correctly with five chunks and re-run them with the same five in reverse order. If the answers change, ordering is a lever you own.

    So: position is a variable you control, and the best chunk goes where the model actually looks.

    context window
    the maximum length of text a model can read in one call
    lost in the middle
    the phenomenon where facts in the middle of a long context are used less reliably
    recall
    the percentage of relevant results that your search actually found

    Close the page. Answer from memory.

    1. Why does a fact in the middle of twenty chunks get used less than one at the start?
    2. When does repeating the question at the end matter more?

    Your goal: your chunk pack is ordered by reranker score, best first. The question is repeated after the context. You have tested on five questions: once with that ordering, once in reverse order. The answers changed on at least three questions.

    Hint 1 — a nudge

    Sort chunks by reranker score, descending. Put the question again at the end. Run five questions twice: once normal, once reversed. Log which answers changed.

    Order: reranker score DESC. Repeat question at end. Test on five questions. Reverse the chunk order for each. Count changes. Commit with the count.

    4. Run each once in normal order, once in reverse order (lowest-scored chunk first).
    5. Log: question, normal answer, reversed answer, changed?
    6. Count how many changed. Commit with a message: "Verified ordering effect on X of 5 questions."

    Mix it in. Look at your test queries. On the questions where ordering changed the answer, was it always a worse answer in reverse order? Or did reversing sometimes help?

    • Padding with extra chunks when five chunks with recall@5 of 0.84 beat twenty chunks with recall@20 of 0.95. Less is more.
    • Not repeating the question. When the question is only at the start, it is in the middle by the time the model reads the end.

    • Why does a fact in the middle of twenty chunks get used less than one at the start?

      Models attend less reliably to the middle of long contexts. Attention peaks at the start and end.

    • You have five chunks ordered by relevance score, highest first. Should you repeat the question at the end, or is once enough?

      Repeat it. The question at the start ends up in the middle by the time the model finishes the chunks. Repeating it puts the instruction back in a high-attention spot.

    Access control lives in the search, not in the prompt

    One rule: the query must be incapable of returning a document the user cannot read. Never retrieve broadly and then ask the model to hide things. Once text is in the context, one follow-up question can expose it. The model cannot be a security boundary.

    Think of a library catalog. If you show someone a list of secret books and ask them not to read them, they might agree. But a determined person can still read the list. The safe way is a different catalog for each person, or a turnstile that only shows books they can read.

    There are two approaches. You build separate collections per tenant — clean isolation, but lots of moving parts. Or you use one shared index with a mandatory filter. The second is simpler, but one forgotten filter is a data breach. The safest design makes unfiltered queries impossible.

    Every chunk carries access facts as metadata: who owns it, what group reads it, if it is public. Every query has a filter from the authenticated session, never from the request body. A tenant ID from the client is not a permission. It is a suggestion anybody can change.

    The safe design makes unfiltered queries impossible. One function, one required argument, no raw queries elsewhere.

    So: access control is a property of the search call, and the safest design is one where a query without a filter is impossible to build.

    access metadata
    facts on a chunk saying who can read it: tenant, group, or visibility level
    pre-filter
    restrict the search candidates before ranking, so all results are readable
    post-filter
    rank everything, then remove restricted results; leaves thin result sets

    Close the page. Say or write the answer to each.

    1. Why is filtering the results after retrieval not a real security boundary?
    2. What happens to the user experience when you filter after ranking instead of before?

    Your goal: your query endpoint derives the user’s permissions from the session, never from the request. Two users with different access ask the same question and get different answers.

    Hint 1 — a nudge

    Add a login endpoint or mock one. Store the session somewhere, and derive the tenant and group identifiers from it. Pass those to the search function as a required filter argument.

    Hint 2 — the shape of the answer

    One query function that requires the access filter as an argument. Wrap your store behind this function. Do not call the store directly anywhere else. Then create two users with different tenants or groups and ask the same question as both.

    Still stuck after 10 minutes? The step by step
    1. Add a simple mock session store. Store a user ID, tenant ID, and list of groups.
    2. Add an /auth endpoint that returns a fake session. Keep it in memory for the test.
    3. Modify your query endpoint to read the session and extract tenant and group.
    4. Wrap your search behind one function that requires the access filter. Delete every other call path to the store.
    5. Add access metadata to the chunks you indexed: mark some as tenant A, some as tenant B, some as public.
    6. Call the query endpoint as user A, then user B, with the same question. Record the answers and citations.

    Mix it in. What happens if you try to pass a different tenant in the request body? Show that the endpoint ignores it and uses the session instead.

    • Reading the tenant from the request body instead of the session. Any user can change it, and your index will obey.
    • Filtering after retrieval and calling it access control. It looks fine until a clever person changes the request and reads what they should not.

    • Why is filtering results after retrieval not a real security boundary?

      Once text is in the context, it is one follow-up question away from the user’s screen. Discretion at the model stage is not a security boundary.

    • A visitor sends a request with "tenant": "competitor" in the JSON body. Your code reads that tenant from the request instead of the session. What can they read?

      Whatever documents are accessible to the competitor’s tenant. Any user can forge the request.

    Say the staleness budget out loud, then build to it

    You have one sentence to write down: “An edited document is searchable within X.” Fill in the X. Fifteen minutes? One hour? One day? That one sentence picks your whole architecture.

    Fifteen minutes means event-driven. The source emits a change, a job re-indexes that one document, and nothing else moves. One day means a scheduled crawl. Run it every morning. Most documents are unchanged, so check hashes and skip them. Hours means something in between. The number is not a guess. Write it down, say it out loud, and build to it.

    Think of a newspaper. If the paper comes out once a day, you crawl the newsroom every morning for changes. Whole stack is fresh every 24 hours. But a live website that changes every minute needs something watching all the time. That is event-driven. Choose which one fits your data.

    People forget deletion. A removed document stays searchable forever unless something deletes its chunks. Answering from deleted text is a legal problem. Build a reconciliation job: list source documents, list indexed documents, delete the difference. Run it on a schedule, every week or every day. This job is separate from your main indexing pipeline and catches deletions no matter what.

    So: say the staleness number first. Let it choose your architecture. Then build the deletion job because data only ever moves in one direction at the source.

    staleness budget
    the time it is allowed to take before an edited document is searchable
    event-driven
    a job runs immediately when the source changes a document
    reconciliation
    comparing source documents to indexed documents and deleting the difference

    Close the page. Answer out loud without looking.

    1. What does your staleness budget decide about how you build the system?
    2. Why do deleted documents stay in the index forever unless something removes them?

    Your goal: a reconciliation job that lists source documents, lists indexed documents, and deletes the difference. You delete a document on purpose and prove the job removed it from the index.

    Hint 1 — a nudge

    Write a function that lists all IDs in your source (your corpus folder, a database, whatever). Write another that lists all chunk IDs in your index. Compute the difference and delete those chunks.

    Hint 2 — the shape of the answer

    Three lines of code: source IDs minus indexed IDs equals chunks to delete. Loop over the difference and call your store’s delete function. Test it on a document you removed on purpose, and confirm it is gone from search.

    Still stuck after 10 minutes? The step by step
    1. Add a function that returns all source document IDs.
    2. Add a function that returns all indexed chunk IDs (or the document IDs they came from).
    3. Write a reconciliation function that computes the difference and deletes those chunks.
    4. Remove a document from your source on purpose.
    5. Run the reconciliation and confirm the chunks are gone.
    6. Search for something that would have matched that document. Confirm it does not show up.

    Mix it in. Look at Round 1. Does your reconciliation job respect the access filter? If a document belonged to tenant A and tenant A was deleted, should the chunks stay or go? What does your code do?

    • Forgetting that deletion is not a cascade. The document is gone at the source but lives forever in the index unless you explicitly delete it.
    • Building only the event-driven pipeline and skipping the scheduled reconciliation. A bug somewhere will eventually lose a deletion, and you will not notice until months later.

    • What does your staleness budget decide about the system?

      Minutes means event-driven ingestion. Hours or a day means a scheduled crawl. Either way, deletion needs its own job.

    • A document is deleted at the source. Nobody runs the reconciliation job. A user queries for something that document mentioned. What happens?

      The search returns that document. The model answers from text that no longer exists. The answer sounds fine but is outdated and misleading.

    Name indexes for their configuration, keep the old one, and flip an alias

    Three things together define an index: your parser, your chunking strategy, and your embedding model. Change any one and every vector has to be rebuilt. Vectors from two different models cannot be compared. So “let’s try the new embedding model” is never small. It is a full rebuild, which is why you plan it.

    Name the index for what it contains: docs-v4-800tok means version 4 with 800-token chunks. Build the new one alongside the old one, not on top. Test both against your golden set of questions. If the new one is better, flip an alias — a pointer that says which index is live. Keep the old index there. If something breaks, flip the alias back in seconds.

    Rollback means flip a pointer. Not rebuild at 2am while people wait. Also keep a log for each version: configuration, build date, document count, recall score, build cost. One minute per version, and it answers the question every reviewer asks: why is it configured this way?

    Keep a log for each version: configuration, build date, document count, recall score, build cost. One minute per version and it answers the question reviewers ask: why this configuration?

    So: name indexes for their configuration, build the new one alongside the old, test with your golden set, and let an alias be the only thing that changes when you go live.

    alias
    a pointer that says which index version the app reads
    golden set
    a fixed set of test questions you use to compare index versions
    rollback
    reversing a change by pointing at an older version that was kept alive

    Close the page. Say or write the answer.

    1. Why does changing the embedding model mean you have to rebuild the entire index?
    2. What does keeping the old index alive enable you to do?

    Your goal: build a new index with a different configuration, test both with your golden set, and flip the alias to point at the winner. Then flip it back as a rollback test.

    Hint 1 — a nudge

    Change one thing: maybe chunk size, maybe the embedding model, maybe the retrieval strategy. Build the new index with a new name. Test both against the same golden set. Calculate recall@5 for each.

    Hint 2 — the shape of the answer

    Build docs-v2 with a different parameter. Set up an alias that points to docs-v1. Run your golden set against both. If docs-v2 wins, flip the alias. Record the recall for both in a table. Then flip back and time it.

    Still stuck after 10 minutes? The step by step
    1. Build your current index, name it docs-v1. Run your golden set against it. Record the recall@5.
    2. Change one configuration parameter (chunk size, embedding model, or retrieval strategy).
    3. Build a new index and name it docs-v2.
    4. Run the same golden set against docs-v2. Record the recall@5.
    5. Create an alias that points to docs-v1.
    6. If docs-v2 is better, flip the alias to point at it. If not, leave it on v1.
    7. Start a timer and flip the alias back. Record how long the rollback took.

    Mix it in. Look at your two recall scores. Which configuration is better? Why might you choose the worse one anyway?

    • Rebuilding the index in place and throwing away the old one. When something goes wrong, you have no rollback.
    • Changing the embedding model without rebuilding the index. Nothing crashes. Retrieval just becomes quietly random and you do not notice for weeks.

    • Why does changing the embedding model require rebuilding the index?

      Vectors from two different models cannot be compared. The similarity scores become meaningless.

    • You tested two index versions. Version 2 has slightly better recall but costs twice as much to build. What should you choose and why?

      That depends on your latency and cost budget. Better recall is worthless if it costs more than the system can afford per query.
