    The budget: measure each stage, then find the real bottleneck

    Write down the path: embed, search, rerank, generate. Measure each stage separately. Guessing costs a week optimizing search and saving 30 milliseconds, then finding the model took three seconds all along.

    Typical numbers: 20 to 40 milliseconds to embed, 10 to 50 to search, 100 to 400 to rerank 50 candidates, 1 to 4 seconds to generate. Look at the shape. Generation dominates. Retrieval is a rounding error. The user feels time to first token. Stream the answer and 300 milliseconds of retrieval becomes invisible.

    Cost is the same exercise with different units. Embedding is a fraction of a cent. Reranker charges per request. Generation charges for input tokens — five chunks at 600 tokens each is 3,000 tokens before the question is even added — plus output. Compute once and say “one query costs this” from memory. That is what separates builders from API users.

    Your levers, in order: cache embeddings for the same query; send fewer chunks to the generator, which is cheaper and often more accurate; rerank fewer candidates; route to a larger model only when confidence is low.

    So: measure once, and you will find that streaming, not search optimization, is what makes the system feel fast.

    latency budget
    the time you promise for each stage of the pipeline
    cost budget
    the dollars per query you can afford
    time to first token
    the latency the user actually feels, because generation dominates

    Close the page. Answer from memory.

    1. Which stage of the retrieval pipeline takes the most time, and why?
    2. If generation takes 2.5 seconds and retrieval takes 0.3, what is the biggest latency win you can get?

    Your goal: measure the time of each stage and the cost of each stage. Then run at least 20 real queries and calculate P50 and P95 latency and total cost per query.

    Hint 1 — a nudge

    Wrap each stage in a timer. Log the time and cost right after each one. After 20 queries, sort the latencies and find the 50th and 95th percentile.

    Hint 2 — the shape of the answer

    Four timers: one for embedding, one for search, one for reranking, one for generation. Log all four after each query. Log cost from the API responses. After 20+ queries, create a table with p50/p95 latency and average cost.

    Still stuck after 10 minutes? The step by step
    1. Add a timer before each stage and log its duration. Query embedding, vector search, reranking, generation.
    2. Log the cost from the API response after generation.
    3. Run at least 20 queries with different questions.
    4. Sort the latencies. Find the value at position count * 0.50 (P50) and count * 0.95 (P95).
    5. Calculate the average cost per query.
    6. Create a table: P50 latency, P95 latency, average cost. Include the breakdown of time by stage.

    Mix it in. Look at your numbers. Is generation the biggest chunk of latency? If search or reranking is slow, think about why. If generation is slow, what happens if you stream it?

    • Measuring the whole program instead of each stage. Imports and setup pollute the numbers and you optimize the wrong thing.
    • Measuring on localhost and ignoring network time. Production latency is higher than you think.

    • Which stage of the pipeline takes the most time?

      Generation. Retrieval is a rounding error next to it.

    • Your system takes 2.5 seconds total. Generation is 2.2 seconds. What will make the biggest latency win?

      Streaming the answer. The retrieval stages are invisible. Make the first token appear quickly and the wait feels much shorter.

    Lead with the eval table, not the feature list

    Most retrieval repos open with features. Yours opens with Day 11’s eval table: each configuration, the recall score, the mean reciprocal rank, the size of the golden set, the date. Then architecture. Then cost per query and P95 latency. Then known failure modes. Then a link.

    This order is deliberate. Nobody can tell from your code whether your retrieval works. That impossibility is the entire reason evaluation exists. What a reader can tell instantly is whether you know that. The table proves you measured. The failure-modes section proves you looked at the failures instead of hiding them.

    Write it in this order: what it does (one paragraph, plain words). The eval table from Day 11, with numbers. Architecture in one diagram. Cost per query with the arithmetic shown. P50 and P95 latency measured on the deployed service. Known failure modes and what you would fix with another week. A link to the live demo. An install-and-run command for someone else to index their own corpus.

    Everything else is packaging. The table is the portfolio piece because it proves you did not guess. A hiring manager reads for 90 seconds. If they see numbers, they notice.

    So: the README is the deliverable, and the eval table is proof you did the work.

    The index is not application code

    Split the work in two. Build the index offline once, in a managed store, separate from the deployed service. The deployed service holds only the query path: embed the question, search, rerank, generate, cite. Nothing else. This split gives you three wins.

    First, the container stays small. A 5 GB index file plus a 2 GB embedding model inside Docker means slower deploys and cold starts. A service that only runs the query path is 100 MB. Deploy in seconds. Second, cold starts stay fast. A fresh instance does not waste time loading an index. Third, re-indexing stops being a deploy. You build a new index offline, test it, flip an alias. The service never restarts.

    Ship with keys read from environment variables, not files. Never hardcode secrets. Log one line per request with tokens, cost, and timings for each stage. This log becomes your source of truth for performance tuning. Provide a public demo corpus that works on the first click, no sign-up needed. Document the ingestion command so someone can point it at their own documents in five minutes and have a working system. Also update LOG.md with your deployment notes and metrics, so the next time you ship you remember what worked.

    So: keep the index out of the service. Ship a small, fast container that only runs the query path.

    managed index
    an index stored outside your application, not bundled with the code
    query path
    the steps that run on every request: embed, search, rerank, generate
    cold start
    the time it takes for a freshly booted instance to answer the first request

      The service stays small. Cold starts stay fast. Re-indexing stops being a deploy.

    • You rebuild the index offline and flip an alias to point at it. How many services need to restart?

      Zero. The service reads from the managed index at query time, so no restart is needed.

    By tomorrow you can reproduce: the split between offline indexing and the query service, and why it keeps deploys small and fast.

    Teach it back

    Explain this day to someone who is about to ship their first retrieval system. What should the README have, and what should the code do? Start from the moment you have a working system and use four to six sentences.

    Watch for the words “basically”, “something happens here” and “you just”. Each one marks a gap. Go back and explain again.

    Where are you on the ladder?

    From shipping code to shipping work.

    1. I have seen a README with an eval table and a deployed service with a managed index.
    2. I can explain why the eval table goes in the second section and why the index should not be bundled with the service.
    3. Given a retrieval system, I can write a README that a hiring manager would spend 90 seconds reading.
    4. I can ship a retrieval system with a strong README and a small, fast service that reads from a managed index.

    The map for this week

    Until now your system answered questions. This week it acts: it runs a query, writes a file, searches the web. A model still only emits text, so the shift is smaller than it sounds. But text from the web now steers what your code does, which makes it more dangerous than it sounds.

    You start with tool calling: the model requests a tool, you run it, you hand the result back. Then you wrap it in an agent loop with guardrails. Days 18 and 19 are the hardest: you hand-label fifty failures and build a judge to grade yourself. Then you wire a regression gate into your CI so a worse prompt blocks your merge. Day 20 you attack your own agent on purpose, trying to trick it. By Sunday you can say what your system does, how often it works, and what happens when someone tries to break it.

    tool
    a function the model can request to run, like searching the web or writing a file
    agent
    a loop: ask the model, run the tool it requests, send the result back, repeat
    MCP
    model context protocol: a standard way to hand tools and data to the model
    eval
    a test that grades the output, so you can measure whether your system got better
    regression
    when a change made things worse, not better
    adversarial
    testing by trying to trick the system, looking for ways it fails

    Before Day 15 (25 minutes): read this map once. Then close it and draw the week on paper from memory: the big ideas, the words, and arrows for how they connect. Open it again and fix what you missed. Do not try to learn anything yet.

    Today your model stops being a text box. It can look something up, do arithmetic, query your database, and write a file. The mechanism underneath is much smaller than the hype: the model asks, and your code decides whether to say yes.

    What the model actually sees

    When you give a model a tool, you are not giving it code. You are adding a small block of text to your request. Nothing more than that.

    That block has three parts. A name, such as sql_query. A description in plain English of what it does and when to use it. And a JSON Schema listing the arguments and their types. That is everything the model ever sees. It has no reach into your function, your database, or your machine.

    Think of a restaurant menu. The model can read the menu and point at a dish. It never walks into the kitchen, and it never learns what the kitchen looks like. Your code is the kitchen. The menu is all it knows.

    Here is why the description matters so much. A careful description is a prompt. It is the entire prompt for one decision — should I call this tool, and with what arguments? A vague description gets ignored. A clear one gets called correctly.

    Bad description: "Queries the DB." Good description: "Runs a read-only SQL query against the orders database. Use it for counts, sums, or specific order records. Tables: orders, customers, refunds."

    So: a tool is text the model reads, and the description is everything.

    tool definition
    a name, description, and schema that tell the model what a tool does
    JSON Schema
    a format that describes what arguments a tool needs and what types they are
    tool choice
    the model's decision about which tool to call, if any

    The cost and the trap

    Tool definitions travel with every single request. You pay input tokens for them on every call. Four careful tools might cost 400 tokens each time. Forty tools is a prompt of its own, and the model gets worse at choosing as the list grows.

    This is the trap that catches everyone once. They define one tool per possible action, until they have thirty tools, and then wonder why the model is confused. Start with four. Pick the ones that matter, describe them carefully, and add more only when you run out of arguments for one tool.

    So: tool definitions cost tokens on every call, and careful descriptions are cheaper than many vague ones.

    input tokens
    the tokens you send; tool definitions add to this cost
    tool list growth
    the problem of defining too many tools at once

    Close the page. Without looking, say or write the answers.

    1. What three things make up a tool definition?
    2. Why is a detailed description better than four vague descriptions?

    Your goal: write four tool definitions by hand. Name, description, and JSON Schema for each. They should be web_search, calculator, sql_query, and file_write.

    Hint 1 — a nudge

    The description is the hard part. For each one, write when to use it and what fields it needs. One or two sentences. Then the schema is just a list of those fields and their types.

    Hint 2 — the shape of the answer

    Each tool is a Python dict with keys "name", "description", and "input_schema". The input_schema has "type": "object", "properties" (a dict of field names to types), and "required" (a list of field names that must be provided).

    Still stuck after 10 minutes? The step by step

    2. For calculator: takes an expression string. When to use: arithmetic that needs precision.
    3. For sql_query: takes sql, limit (1 to 100, default 20). When to use: retrieve data from the database.
    4. For file_write: takes filename, content. When to use: create or update a file.

    • A vague description, then blaming the model for not calling the tool. Rewrite the description first.
    • Too many tools. Start with four, describe each one clearly.

    • What three things make up a tool definition the model reads?

      Name, description, and JSON Schema. The description says when to use it and what arguments it needs.

    • You define 30 tools because your app has 30 actions. What will probably happen?

      The model will be confused and choose tools randomly. Tool definitions cost tokens on every call, and too many hurt more than they help.

    By tomorrow you can reproduce: four tool definitions, each with a name, a one-sentence description, and a JSON Schema, written by hand.

    Four steps between you and the model

    Here is the entire mechanism. Learn it once and you have learned every agent framework you will ever see, because all of them are wrappers around these four steps.

    Step 1: You send the conversation plus the tool definitions.

    Step 2: The model replies with a stop reason meaning "I want a tool", and a block holding the tool name, the arguments as JSON, and an identifier for this call. Nothing has run yet. The model emitted a description of a call it would like made. It is a request, not an action.

    Step 3: Your code parses those arguments, checks them, runs the real Python function, and gets a result. This is the step where you are in charge, and it is the only step where anything actually happens.

    Step 4: You append two things to the message list. The model's request exactly as it came back. And a tool-result message carrying the output plus that same call identifier. Then you send the whole conversation again.

    Why the whole conversation? Because the API is stateless. It remembers nothing between requests. Your growing message list is the memory of the interaction; there is no session on the other end holding your place. From there the model either answers in plain text or asks for another tool.

    So: the model requests, your code runs it, and both halves of that exchange go back into the list before you send it again.

    tool request
    the model's message asking to call a tool, with arguments as JSON
    tool result
    your message sending back what the tool did
    stateless
    the API remembers nothing; your message list is the memory

    One common break

    The break is small and maddening: you append the result but forget to append the model's request first. The pair no longer matches, and you get either an API error or a model that asks for the same thing again.

    Think of a waltz. The leader goes first, then the follower mirrors the step. If the follower steps without the leader, they crash into each other. Your message list is the same: the request leads, the result follows.

    Trace through the four steps once when you build it. Print the message list before you send it on Step 1, print what the model asked for on Step 2, print what you computed on Step 3, and print the new message list on Step 4. You will see the pair mismatch instantly.

    So: always append the request before the result, and the pair will stay aligned.

    message pair
    the model's request and your result, which must stay matched by call ID

    1. Why do you send the whole conversation again on Step 4?
    2. What is the common break that happens on Step 4?

    Your goal: a simple loop that does the four steps once. Send a conversation with one tool definition. Get the model to ask for a tool. Run a dummy function. Send the result back. Get the model's final answer. Print the message list before and after the result.

    Start with your four tools from Round 1, but only send one of them in the first call. That makes it simpler to test.

    Hint 2 — the shape of the answer

    The loop is two calls: one that asks the model to use a tool, one after you send the result. The first call has the messages plus tool definitions. The second call is the same messages plus the tool request plus the tool result.

    2. Parse the tool request. Print it with the call ID.
    3. Run a dummy function that returns "4".
    4. Append the tool request to messages. Append the tool result. Print the message list.
    5. Send the messages again (no tool definitions this time, just the conversation).
    6. Print the model's final text answer.

    • Forgetting to append the model's request before the result. The pair breaks and the model gets confused.

    • Why do you send the whole conversation again after the tool result?

      The API is stateless. Every request is independent. The message list is your memory, and you have to send all of it each time.

    • You send a tool request and a result, but they don't have matching call IDs. What will the model probably do?

      Get confused and ask for the same tool again, or refuse to answer because the result doesn't match a request.

    By tomorrow you can reproduce: the four-step loop by hand, and which step is where your code actually runs something.

    Tool choice and calling several at once

    You control how eager the model is with one setting per request. Auto lets it decide, and is the default. None forbids tools for that turn. Required forces it to pick something. Naming one exact tool forces that call.

    That last one deserves a second look, because it is the trick behind reliable structured output. Define a tool whose schema is your output shape, then require it. Now the model has to fill in your fields.

    Here is the other thing one reply can do: ask for several tools at once. That happens when the calls do not depend on each other. Search the web and check the calculator at the same time, where neither needs the other's answer first.

    Run those concurrently, then return all the results in one message. Split them across separate messages and the pairing breaks; the model quietly stops batching, and every later turn costs you an extra round trip.

    So: decide how much freedom the model gets, and when it asks for three things at once, answer all three together.

    tool choice
    a setting that controls whether the model can call tools, must call them, or must call a specific one
    parallel calls
    multiple tools called in the same turn because they don't depend on each other

    When to batch and when not to

    Batching is free only if both calls finish before you send the results. If one finishes early and you send partial results, the model will think both finished and move on.

    Think of waiting for two friends at a restaurant. You can send the appetizers as one arrives, or you can wait for both. Send one early and the other person thinks the meal is done before they even arrive.

    In practice, this means: do not return one result and wait. Collect all results (or all errors) and send them in one batch. If a tool is hanging, time it out after a reasonable period and return a timeout error along with the other results.

    The gain is one fewer round trip. At scale that adds up. Early on, it makes no difference to your cost, but the discipline saves you later when one result takes longer than you expected.

    So: batch results only when you can return all of them, or timeout waiting and return an error.

    timeout
    a time limit on how long your code waits for a tool to finish

    Close the page. From memory.

    1. When is it safe to call two tools at the same time?
    2. Why return all results in one message instead of sending them as they finish?

    Your goal: a task that genuinely needs two tools that don't depend on each other. Ask the model to use both. Catch both in your code. Run them at the same time. Return both results in one message. Print the total time and confirm it is faster than running them one after the other.

    Pick a question like "What is the capital of France and what is 2 to the power of 8?" Two tools, no dependency.

    Hint 2 — the shape of the answer

    Collect both tool calls from the model's reply. Use asyncio.gather() or threading to run them at the same time. Collect both results and append them to messages in a single call.

    2. Send it with both tool definitions and tool_choice="auto".
    3. Parse the response. You should get two tool calls.
    4. Run both at the same time using async or threads.

    Mix it in. Look at your round trip: are you appending the tool requests before the tool results? Check with a print statement, just like Round 2.

    • Returning results as they finish instead of batching them. The model thinks the first one finished and the second is a whole new turn.

    • When is it safe to ask the model to call two tools at the same time?

      When the two calls don't depend on each other. The model asks for them both in one turn, and your code runs them in parallel.

    • Your web_search takes 0.5 seconds and your calculator takes 0.1 seconds. You run them one after the other, then in parallel. What is the time difference?

      One after the other is 0.6 seconds. In parallel is 0.5 seconds (wait for the slower one). Saving is 0.1 seconds, one fewer round trip.

    By tomorrow you can reproduce: how to detect that the model asked for two tools, run them concurrently, and return both results in one message.

    Errors are results, not crashes

    Your SQL tool will receive a malformed query. Not maybe — it will. Your file_write tool will get a path that tries to escape the sandbox. Your tools will hang or timeout. That is not a bug. That is the normal case.

    The instinct is to let the exception propagate. That kills the loop, and the person waiting gets nothing at all. Do this instead. Catch it, and send the error text back as the tool result, flagged as an error.

    Models are good at fixing a query when you show them the message. For example, relation "order" does not exist; tables are orders, customers, refunds. Then the model rewrites the query and tries again. That one behavior converts a large share of your failures into self-repair.

    Two limits keep self-repair from becoming a treadmill. Cap retries of the same tool at two, then stop and report honestly. And truncate results. A fetched web page can be 200,000 tokens. Once it is in the conversation you pay for it on every remaining step. Return the first 2,000 tokens plus a note that it was cut.

    So: an error is just one more thing the model can read, but an untrimmed result is a bill you keep paying.

    error result
    an error message from your tool, sent back to the model as a tool result
    self-repair
    the model fixing its own tool call after reading an error message
    truncate
    cut a long result at a character or token limit

    Validating before you run

    The model produced those arguments from text. Treat them as untrusted input. Validate before you execute.

    Think of a security checkpoint. The guard checks your ID before you pass. A tool is the same: check the arguments before they reach the database or the disk.

    For SQL, use a Pydantic model to parse the arguments. For file paths, take a bare filename, join it to one output directory, and reject any name containing a path separator or a parent reference. Make your tools safe by construction: a read-only database connection, a forced row limit, a guard on what files can be written.

    This is not paranoia. This is engineering. The model is not trying to break your tool. It is just guessing at arguments, and sometimes those guesses look like a path escape.

    So: validate the arguments before the tool ever runs, then run it in a limited environment.

    validation
    checking that the model's arguments are the right type and don't break the safety rules
    Pydantic
    a Python library for parsing and validating structured data

    Close the page. Answer from memory.

    1. Instead of crashing, what do you do with an error from a tool?
    2. Why truncate a 200,000-token result to 2,000 tokens?

    Your goal: a SQL tool that is safe by construction. It takes a query and a limit. It validates the query (reject anything that is not a SELECT, use Pydantic). It connects read-only. It enforces the limit and truncates the result. When the query is bad, it catches the error, sends the error text back, and lets the model try again.

    Use a Pydantic model for the arguments. Use re.match() to check that the query starts with SELECT. Use a try-except to catch SQL errors and return them as a tool result.

    2. Write a function that validates: check the query starts with SELECT, reject anything else.

    • Trusting the arguments. Never concatenate them into SQL, a shell command, or a file path without validation.

    • Letting an exception kill the loop. Return it as a tool result instead, and the model usually fixes itself.

    • What do you do when your SQL tool gets a malformed query?

      Catch the error, format it as a message, and send it back as a tool result. The model reads the error and usually fixes the query.

      You send all 500,000 tokens again, doubling your bill. Truncate large results when you return them.

    Teach it back

    Explain this to a smart friend who has never used a tool API. What is a tool definition, and what happens when the model asks to use one? Start from the moment you send your request and use four to six sentences. Say it out loud, or write it down.

    Watch for the words "basically", "something happens here" and "you just". Each one marks a gap. Go back to that spot in the page, fill the gap, and explain again.

    Where are you on the ladder?

    Being able to say "I've seen this" is only the first rung. Climb all four.

    1. I have seen tool definitions and the four-step round trip.
    2. I can say what a tool definition is, why descriptions matter, and what your code does in step 3, without looking.
    3. Given a broken tool call, I can write validation code and error handling to make it self-repair.
    4. I can design four tools, build the round-trip loop, handle errors, and defend each choice.

    One tool call is a function call. Many calls, chosen by the model, where each result changes what it does next — that is an agent. Today you build one, put a fence around it, and learn when not to build one at all.

    An agent is a while loop

    People describe agents as "plan, act, observe, repeat". That is a fair description of what the model does inside its own text. It is not what your code does.

    Your code is a while loop. Send the messages. Look at the stop reason. Branch. If the model asked for tools, run them, append the results, and go around again. If it did not, you have your answer and the loop ends. That is the whole program.

    There is no hidden state anywhere. Everything the agent "knows" is the message list you keep resending: the original task, every tool request, every result. When someone says an agent "remembers" what it did three steps ago, they mean a list in your process got longer.

    So: an agent is a while loop over a list you own, and nothing else.

    agent
    a loop that sends messages, gets tool requests, runs the tools, and loops until the model answers
    stop reason
    a field saying whether the model is done, asked for a tool, or hit a limit

    Why the loop is worth writing yourself

    That is worth sitting with, because every framework you might adopt later is this loop plus opinions — about retries, about logging, about how the list gets trimmed. Build the thing once and you will read those opinions as choices rather than magic.

    The first time, the loop is small. Write it yourself. Later, when you have run a hundred agents, a framework saves you time. At that point you already know what you are buying.

    So: build your own loop first, and you will understand every framework later.

    framework
    a library that wraps your loop with extra features like retries and logging

    2. Why does the model think it "remembers" what happened three steps ago?

    An unbounded loop is a bill

    Do the arithmetic once and it stops being abstract. Suppose each step carries 30,000 tokens of history and the agent takes 40 steps. That is 1.2 million input tokens for a task you expected to cost pennies.

    Worse, a stuck agent does not look stuck. It looks busy. It is calling tools, printing lines, making progress-shaped noise while it goes nowhere.

    So give the loop four independent ceilings, and check all four every single iteration. A step limit — start at 12. A token or dollar budget you add up as you go. A wall-clock limit. And a no-progress rule: the same tool called with the same arguments twice in a row means stop.

    Then make every exit useful. Each one should return what it achieved, what it was trying to do, and why it stopped. "Hit the step limit while retrying the SQL tool" is a debuggable answer. A stack trace is not.

    So: decide in advance how the loop ends, in four different ways, and make each ending say something out loud.

    step limit
    a maximum number of iterations before the loop stops
    budget
    a total spending cap in tokens or dollars
    wall-clock limit
    a time limit in seconds before the loop stops
    no-progress rule
    stop if the same tool is called twice with the same arguments

    Tracking cost across the loop

    Every API call returns usage information. Add up the usage from each call as you go. At the end of each iteration, print the cumulative cost. That number tells you whether you are headed for the budget limit.

    So: sum usage on each iteration and check the total against your limits.

    cumulative cost
    the total spending across all iterations so far

    Your goal: the loop from Round 1, now with all four ceilings in place. The loop checks: steps (limit 12), cumulative cost (limit 50 cents), wall-clock time (limit 90 seconds), and repeated tool calls. It returns a structured result saying which limit was hit and when.

    Keep four variables: step counter, cumulative cost (sum on each iteration), a timer (started before the loop), and the last tool call. On each iteration, check all four and break if any is exceeded.

    Before the loop: counter = 0, cost = 0, start_time = now(), last_tool = None. In the loop: check counter < 12, cost < 0.50, time < 90s, tool != last_tool. At the end: return {achieved, goal, reason, steps, cost, elapsed}.

    1. Add four variables before the loop: step_count, cumulative_cost, start_time, last_tool_call.
    2. On each iteration: increment step_count, add usage to cumulative_cost, check elapsed time.
    3. Before running a tool, check if it matches last_tool_call. If so, break with reason "repeated tool".
    4. After each iteration, check if any ceiling is hit. If so, break and return the reason.
    5. Return a dict with the final state: why it stopped, how many steps, what the cost was, how long it took.

    • No step limit during development. One overnight loop can outspend a week of careful work.
    • Ignoring the cost curve: the same agent that costs 2 cents at step 2 costs 10 cents at step 10 because the history keeps riding along.

    • What are the four ceilings that stop an agent loop?

      Step limit (12), budget limit (50 cents), wall-clock limit (90 seconds), and no-progress rule (same tool twice).

    • The agent is on step 11. It needs one more tool call to finish, which will cost 2 cents. The budget is 50 cents and you have spent 49 cents. What should happen?

      The call will put you over budget. The loop should stop before running the tool and say why.

    By tomorrow you can reproduce: how to track cost on each iteration and stop the loop on any of four limits.

    Short-term memory gets expensive

    Short-term memory is the message list. It grows every step, and you resend all of it every step, so the cost per step climbs even when the work does not. By step 10 you may be paying five times what step 2 cost.

    Think of a growing notebook. Every time you read your own notes, you have to read the whole thing. It gets thicker, and reading takes longer.

    So: short-term memory is your message list, and it costs money on every step.

    short-term memory
    the message list that grows with each iteration

    Long-term memory is written on purpose

    Compaction is the fix. Once the history passes a threshold, replace the oldest steps with a short summary the model writes itself — "searched three sources, found the invoice total is 4,180, still need the tax rate" — and keep the last two steps verbatim.

    Where do the discarded details go? To disk. Write full tool outputs to files and leave the path in the summary, so the agent can re-read anything it actually needs instead of carrying everything just in case.

    Long-term memory is a different kind of thing entirely. It is a store you write to deliberately, keyed by user or topic, that outlives the run: a table, a file, a small index.

    The trap is treating an ever-growing transcript as memory. A transcript is a cost curve. Memory is something you chose to save and can look up later.

    So: trim what you resend, and save on purpose the few things you want to keep.

    compaction
    replacing old steps with a summary to reduce the message list size
    long-term memory
    a store that outlives one run, keyed by user or topic

    2. What is the difference between a transcript and memory?

Save full tool outputs to files and include the file paths in the summary.

    Hint 1 — a nudge

    When message count hits your threshold, send the model a message like "Please summarize steps 1-5 in two sentences, mentioning key facts and any files we saved." Then truncate the list to [summary, step-1, step-2] and continue.

    Hint 2 — the shape of the answer

    After each iteration: check if len(messages) > threshold. If so, call the model with a summary prompt, get the text back, write any full results to files, rebuild the list with the summary plus the last two steps, and continue.

    Still stuck after 10 minutes? The step by step
    1. On each iteration after running tools, check if the message list is getting long.
    2. If it passes your threshold, send a "summarize this history" prompt to the model.
    3. Write any full tool outputs to files (e.g., step_1_output.txt).
    4. Replace the old steps with the summary plus file paths.
    5. Keep only the summary and the last two steps in memory.
    6. Continue the loop with the compacted list.

    Mix it in. Look at your compacted list after the summary. Can the agent still reason about what happened, or did you lose important details? Test it.

    • Ignoring the cost curve: the same agent that costs 2 cents at step 2 costs 10 cents at step 10 because the history keeps riding along.
    • Treating a transcript as memory. A transcript is a cost curve that never ends; memory is something you chose to save.

    • Why does each step cost more than the last?

      The message list grows and you resend all of it. At step 2 you send 2 messages. At step 10 you send 10 messages. The input tokens keep climbing.

    • The message list is at 15 messages and cost is 20 cents. The next step will add 5 more messages. Will it cost the same 2 cents?

      No, it will cost more because you are resending 15 messages now, not 10. The cost per step climbs.

    By tomorrow you can reproduce: how to compact the message list when it gets long, and why writing to disk beats keeping everything in memory.

    The test: can you draw the flowchart?

    Here is the test, and it fits on one line: if you can draw the flowchart, write the flowchart.

    Suppose the job is always "classify the request, retrieve the right documents, draft an answer, check the format". You already know the steps and their order. Three or four ordinary model calls in a fixed sequence beat an agent on every axis that matters.

    Cheaper, because you never resend a growing history. Faster, because no round trips get spent deciding something that was already obvious to you. And testable, because each step has its own input, its own output, and its own eval.

    So: a pipeline is a sequence of model calls in a fixed order. Use it when you know the steps.

    pipeline
    a sequence of model calls in a fixed order, where each one's output feeds the next

    When an agent earns its cost

    An agent earns its cost in one situation: when the number and order of steps genuinely depend on what gets discovered along the way. A debugging task. An open-ended research question. A repair loop that runs until a test passes.

    Even then, the strongest systems are mostly pipeline with one small agentic segment in the middle, not one agent doing everything.

    The trap is reaching for an orchestration library before feeling the pain it solves. Adopt one when your own loop hurts, not before.

    So: reach for the loop only where the path is genuinely unknown, and write plain steps everywhere else.

    hybrid
    a system that combines fixed pipeline steps with a small agentic loop in the middle

    Close the page. Answer from memory.

    1. When is a fixed pipeline cheaper than an agent?
    2. What is the weakest reason to build an agent instead of a pipeline?

    Your goal: write the same task as both an agent loop and a fixed three-call pipeline. Time both, price both, and record the numbers. The task: "find the three most-refunded products last quarter, look up each one's return policy in the docs, and write a summary file".

    Hint 1 — a nudge

    The agent discovers which products to look up on the fly. The pipeline assumes you already know the products and just needs to fetch policies and draft the summary.

    Hint 2 — the shape of the answer

    Agent: loop until it finds three products and their policies. Pipeline: call 1 (find products), call 2 (fetch policies), call 3 (draft summary). Run both on the same input and record time and cost for each.

    Still stuck after 10 minutes? The step by step
    1. Write an agent loop that can call sql_query and lookup_policy (a dummy) until it has three products' policies.
    2. Write a pipeline: one call to get the products, one to fetch policies, one to draft the summary.
    3. Run both on the same data set. Time each and record the cost.
    4. Write the results in LOG.md as a comparison table: time, cost, calls, result quality.
    5. Which one would you ship? Why?

    Mix it in. Look at your pipeline cost and your agent cost. If the agent costs three times as much but finds the right answer half the time, was it worth it?

    • Reaching for an orchestration library before feeling the pain it solves. Adopt one when your own loop hurts, not before.
    • Judging the agent by watching it work. "It usually gets there" is not a measurement.

    • When is a pipeline better than an agent?

      When you know the steps and their order in advance. A pipeline is cheaper, faster, and testable.

    • The agent costs $0.10 and takes 5 calls. The pipeline costs $0.02 and takes 3 calls. The agent finds the right answer 90 percent of the time, the pipeline 70 percent. Which do you ship?

      It depends on the failure cost. If wrong answers are cheap to catch, ship the pipeline and add human review. If they are expensive, the agent might be worth the cost.

    By tomorrow you can reproduce: a pipeline and an agent for the same task, with time and cost numbers, and a decision about which one to ship.

    Teach it back

    Explain this to a smart friend who has never built an agent. What is the loop, what keeps it from running forever, and when would you use a pipeline instead? Start from the moment you send messages and use four to six sentences. Say it out loud, or write it down.

    Watch for the words "basically", "something happens here" and "you just". Each one marks a gap. Go back to that spot in the page, fill the gap, and explain again.

    Where are you on the ladder?

    Four rungs: from seeing it to building it.

    1. I have seen an agent loop and the four termination rules.
    2. I can say what a while loop does, what the four limits are, and why memory costs climb, without looking.
    3. Given a business problem, I can decide whether an agent or a pipeline would work better.
    4. I can build a bounded agent with all four termination rules, compaction, and a pipeline alternative, and defend each choice.

    Yesterday's tools were wired into one program: yours. Today you make one of them speak a standard protocol, so a desktop app, a coding agent, or somebody else's product can call it with no glue written on either side. By tonight your Week-2 corpus is something you can query from inside the editor you already use.

    Wiring is explosive

    Imagine you have built a good tool. A calendar search, a database lookup, a retrieval system. You want it to work inside three different applications: a desktop editor, a coding agent, a chat window. That is six separate pieces of custom code to write: three on the tool side, three on the application side.

    Now the math gets worse. If there are 5 different applications you use and 20 different tools worth having, that is 100 separate integrations. And each one gets written twice — once by the person who built the tool, once by the person who built the application.

    Nobody builds that. Most of those 100 connections never exist, which is why your database is not in your chat app and your chat app does not know about your calendar.

    So: the explosion is unavoidable, and it is why tools stay in silos.

    integration
    custom code that connects two programs so one can use the other
    protocol
    a fixed message format that two programs agree to speak

    A standard turns multiplication into addition

    The Model Context Protocol is a single message format. Every tool author writes one MCP server — a program that speaks this format. Every application author writes one MCP client. That is it.

    Now the math is 5 plus 20 instead of 5 times 20. Any client can reach any server without rewriting anything. It is the same trick as a printer driver or USB. The value is not cleverness. The value is that everybody agreed on the shape of the plug.

    So: MCP exists to turn a multiplication into an addition, and that is the whole reason to care about it.

    MCP
    Model Context Protocol: a standard message format for tools and applications
    server
    a program that exposes tools through the MCP protocol
    client
    a program that uses MCP servers and offers them to a model

    Close the page. Without looking, say or write the answers.

    1. Why does connecting 5 applications to 20 tools without a standard create so much work?
    2. How does MCP change the math from multiplication to addition?

    Your goal: explain, to someone who has not heard of MCP, why a standard message format matters. Give a concrete example of two applications and two tools, and show the wiring difference.

    Hint 1 — a nudge

    Draw the wires. On one side, draw what happens if every application connects directly to every tool. On the other, draw what happens if they all use a standard.

    Hint 2 — the shape of the answer

    Two applications, two tools. Direct wiring: four lines. With MCP: each app connects once, each tool connects once. Show the numbers.

    Still stuck after 10 minutes? The step by step
    1. Draw four boxes: two for applications (chat, editor), two for tools (calendar, search).
    2. Draw all four direct wires without MCP. Count them.
    3. Add an MCP box in the middle. Erase the four wires and draw new ones: each app to MCP, each tool to MCP.
    4. Write the number of wires before and after.
    • Thinking MCP is a specific tool or language. It is a message format. Any language can implement it.
    • Assuming every tool needs to change. A tool implements MCP once. It then works with any MCP client.

    • Why does connecting N applications to M tools without a standard require N times M separate integrations?

      Each application needs custom code to understand each tool. Each one is a separate wiring job.

    • You have built a search tool and want it to work in a chat app, an editor, and a coding agent. How many integrations do you have to write if there is no standard? How many with MCP?

      Without MCP: three integrations (one per application). With MCP: one server, and three client developers implement the client side once each.

    By tomorrow you can reproduce: the arithmetic of the integration problem, with a concrete example.

    Three kinds of thing

    An MCP server is not mysterious. It exposes three kinds of thing, and they are easy to mix up.

    Tools are actions. They have the same name-description-schema shape you wrote on Day 15. The model calls them. Nothing new to learn here.

    Resources are readable data at a URI — a file path, a document ID, a database record. The application can pull them without asking the model. The model does not call them.

    Prompts are named templates a person picks from a menu. They are for the human using the application, not for the model.

    So: a server exposes tools for the model, resources for the application, and prompts for the person.

    tool
    an action the model can call, with a name, description, and schema
    resource
    readable data at a URI that the application can fetch
    prompt
    a named template that a person selects from a menu

    Transport: how the bytes move

    A server can reach a client in two ways, and transport is only about which one fits your situation.

    Standard input and output means the client launches your server as a subprocess on the same machine. The two exchange JSON over the pipes, no network, no ports, no passwords. This is the simplest place to start.

    HTTP is for a server running somewhere else. The client makes web requests to it, which means you need authentication and a network path.

    Now here is the part that surprises people: underneath all of it, nothing about the model changed. The client asks your server what tools it has, hands those to the model as ordinary tool definitions, and when the model calls one, the client forwards the call to your server and puts the result back in the conversation. MCP standardizes discovery and transport. The round trip from Day 15 is untouched. The specification is at modelcontextprotocol.io.

    So: a server publishes tools, resources, and prompts over pipes or HTTP, and the model never knows the difference.

    stdio transport
    the client launches a server as a subprocess and exchanges JSON over pipes
    HTTP transport
    the server runs elsewhere and the client makes web requests to it

    Close the page. Answer without looking.

    1. Name the three kinds of thing a server exposes. Which one does the model call?
    2. What is the difference between stdio and HTTP transport?

    Your goal: design a server for your Week-2 corpus. Decide what tools, resources, and prompts it will expose. Write the names and one-line descriptions for each.

    Hint 1 — a nudge

    Hint 2 — the shape of the answer

    At least one tool (search) and at least one resource (a list of documents). Optionally one prompt template for a person.

    Still stuck after 10 minutes? The step by step
    1. Write one tool: search_docs(query, k). What should it return?
    2. Write one resource: a URI and name for a list of indexed documents with their dates.
    3. Optionally write one prompt template a person could pick from a menu.

    Mix it in. On Day 15 you defined a tool by hand. Look at that tool definition. How is MCP different? What stayed the same?

    • Mixing tools and resources. Tools are for the model. Resources are for the application.
    • Thinking a stdio server runs in some magical sandbox. It runs as your user, with your files and your keys.

    • What is the difference between a tool and a resource in MCP?

      Tools are actions the model calls. Resources are readable data the application fetches at a URI.

    • You want your corpus to appear in a chat app, and you want the chat app's user to be able to browse the full document list without asking the model. Should that list be a tool or a resource?

      A resource. The application can fetch it directly without calling the model.

    By tomorrow you can reproduce: the three kinds of MCP exports, and which transport you would pick for an application on the same machine.

    An installed server runs as you

    Installing a server from a link is not like installing a browser extension in a sandbox. A local stdio server is a program running as you. Your files. Your environment variables. Your network.

    It also gets two direct hooks into your model call. Its tool descriptions land in your prompt. Its output lands directly in your context.

    That is two attack surfaces at once. First: a hostile server can do whatever your account can do. It can read your files, change things, make network calls. Second: even an honest server that reads from the internet can carry instructions written by a stranger straight into a model holding your keys. If a server fetches a web page and hands it to your model, and that page contains instructions like "ignore your safety guidelines," the model sees it in context alongside your own queries.

    Why does this matter? Think about it like inviting someone into your house. You would not let a stranger from the internet run arbitrary commands on your computer. But that is exactly what happens when you install a server — you are granting it all your permissions. The difference from a browser extension is that the browser extension runs in a sandbox. An MCP server runs as you.

    The defenses are boring and they work. Read the source code of what you install, line by line if it is short. Keep secrets out of any server you did not write — do not put API keys inside server code. Prefer read-only servers that only fetch and search, never write or delete. Do not install a server from someone you do not trust. A later day turns this into a proper threat model with specific questions to ask.

    So: treat a server the way you would treat a shell script from a stranger, because that is exactly what it is.

    attack surface
    a way a hostile program can harm you or steal your data
    read-only
    a server that can only fetch data, not change anything

    Close the page. Answer without looking.

    1. A server runs as a subprocess on your machine. What does that mean it can access?
    2. What is the risk of installing a server that fetches from the internet?

    Your goal: audit your planned server for security. Decide: what files does it read? Does it write anything? Does it fetch from the network? Does it have access to your keys? Write your answers.

    Go back to Round 2. You decided what your server exposes. Now trace each one backwards: where does it get its data?

    2. For each one, write down what files or data it reads.
    3. Does it need access to any API keys or secrets?
    4. Does it make network calls?
    5. Does it change anything (write, delete)?
    • Assuming a server is sandboxed. It runs as you, with your privileges. It is not a browser extension.
    • Storing API keys inside the server code. A server you install is code anyone can read.

    • What does it mean that a stdio server runs as a subprocess on your machine?

      It runs with your permissions, can read your files, and has access to your environment variables and network.

    • You find a good MCP server on GitHub. It fetches web pages and passes them to your model. What is the security risk?

      The server reads from the internet and passes it into your context. A hostile web page could contain instructions for the model that misuse your keys.

    By tomorrow you can reproduce: the two attack surfaces of an installed server, and what kind of server is safer to install.

    Building a real server

    An MCP server is just code. You install the official SDK for your language, follow the smallest example in the docs, and build from there. The SDK handles all the protocol details — the message framing, the discovery protocol, the client setup. You write only the logic. Start with "hello world" and confirm it runs before you add anything real. This matters because the SDK abstracts away complexity, but it takes work to understand it by reading.

    Expose one tool, search_docs(query, k), that calls your Week-2 hybrid retrieval and returns the top chunks with document title, source path, and score. Write the tool description as carefully as a prompt: what corpus it covers, what a good query looks like, when the client should reach for it. The client's model chooses whether to use your tool based entirely on that text. Be thorough.

    Why cap every result? At most 5 chunks and roughly 1,500 tokens. When more results matched, add a note saying so. Never return a whole document. The client pays for every token you send back, on every step of its own loop. If you dump 10,000 tokens of raw text into every query, the client's costs balloon and its latency gets worse.

    Add one resource: a list of indexed documents with their last-updated dates, so a client can browse the corpus without the model calling your tool. This is data the application reads directly — not something the model decides to call.

    So: build it step by step using the official SDK, then register it in a real client.

    SDK
    a toolkit that handles the MCP protocol details for you

    Close the page. Answer without looking.

    1. What does the MCP SDK do for you?
    2. Why cap the search results at 5 chunks and 1,500 tokens?

    Your goal: a working MCP server that exposes your Week-2 search as a tool, a document list as a resource, and a request log on disk. Register it in a real client and ask a question only your corpus can answer.

    Hint 1 — a nudge

    Start with the SDK's smallest working example. Run it before you change anything. Then add your search tool one line at a time.

    Hint 2 — the shape of the answer

    Three parts: (1) start the SDK example and confirm it works. (2) Add the search tool calling your Week-2 retrieval, capped at 5 chunks. (3) Add a resource listing your documents. (4) Register it in a real client and test it.

    Still stuck after 10 minutes? The step by step
    1. Install the official MCP SDK for your language.
    2. Copy the smallest server example from the docs. Run it and confirm it starts.
    3. Add one tool, search_docs, that calls your hybrid retrieval and returns top 5 chunks with title, path, score.
    4. Write a detailed tool description: what corpus it covers, how to query it, when to use it.
    5. Add one resource listing the indexed documents and their last-updated dates.
    6. Add stderr logging for every call: query text, number of results, latency in milliseconds.
    7. Register the server in a real client (Claude desktop, a coding agent, or another MCP client).
    8. Ask the client a question that only your corpus can answer. Check that it finds the right document and cites it correctly.

    Mix it in. Look at the tool description you wrote. Compare it to the system prompts you wrote for Day 15. What is the same? What changed?

    • Printing to standard output for logging. On a stdio transport that is the protocol channel itself, and a stray print corrupts every message. Log to standard error or a file.
    • Missing environment: the client launches your server as a subprocess that may not inherit your shell variables, so paths or API keys come back empty. Pass them in the client config explicitly.
    • A terse tool description, then puzzlement that the client never uses it. The client's model chooses on that text alone. Be thorough.
    • Returning whole documents. The client pays for every token you send, on every step of its own loop. Cap it.

    • Why should you log every call to your server on the server side instead of in the application?

      The server is the only place that sees every call. You get the first look at how applications actually phrase queries and use your tools.

    • Your server is running in a client as a subprocess, but a query returns with missing paths. What likely happened?

      The client did not pass your environment variables to the subprocess. Pass them explicitly in the client config instead.
