    Shrinking the file without breaking it

    Start with the memory arithmetic, because it decides everything else. Each number in the weights file is normally stored in 16 bits — two bytes. Eight billion weights therefore take about 16 GB of memory just to sit there, before you send it a single input. Most laptops do not have that much.

    Quantization makes each number smaller. Here is the trick. Split all the weights into blocks. For each block, keep one scale factor plus a smaller number for every weight. To use a weight, multiply its small number by the block's scale factor. That is the whole mechanism.

    Now watch the memory fall. At 8 bits you halve the memory. At 4 bits you quarter it. Eight billion weights shrink to about 4.5 GB — small enough to fit on most laptops, and the runner moves memory faster because there is less of it.

    What do you pay? Accuracy. Rounding every weight adds noise everywhere. On easy jobs you will not see it at all. It shows up on hard work: long reasoning chains, strict output formats, rare words, languages other than English, or when the model needs to remember details deep in a long context.

    The danger is that failures do not yell. Nothing breaks loudly, so people quantize hard and never know what broke. So measure it. Run your golden set through the 4-bit build, the 8-bit build, and your hosted model. Compare the scores. The usual result: 8-bit is nearly free, 4-bit is a real drop that you can live with, and below 4 bits things get strange.

    So: quantization is a choice about memory, and the accuracy cost depends on your work, not on the technique.

    quantization
    storing each weight in fewer bits by using a scale factor and a smaller number
    4-bit, 8-bit
    how many bits each weight uses; smaller means less memory and less speed, with more noise

    Why servers scale and laptops do not

    A hosted API stays fast for a thousand users at once. Your laptop struggles with two. Same arithmetic in both cases. Wildly different results. Two mechanisms explain the gap.

    The first is the KV cache. To produce token 501, the model looks back at all 500 earlier tokens. It needs a key vector and a value vector for each one, in every layer. If the model recomputed all of that at every step, answering a long question would become quadratically expensive — each new token would cost more than the one before.

    So servers compute those vectors once and save them. Each new token then costs one fresh step plus a read from storage. The price you pay is memory: the cache grows with (tokens times layers times conversations at once). Usually the cache fills the GPU before the weights do. That is the fundamental reason a laptop struggles with concurrency.

    The second is batching. A GPU running one request is mostly idle, waiting for memory. Run 32 requests together, and each step handles 32 tokens for close to the price of one. Throughput multiplies; each individual request gets a bit slower. vLLM's trick is continuous batching: new requests join and old ones leave between steps instead of waiting for the group.

    Now combine those two. Self-hosting is a utilization problem. A GPU costs two dollars an hour whether you send it one request or five hundred. Providers are cheap because everyone's traffic keeps their batches full. Your traffic will not.

    So: speed at scale comes from storing work so you do not repeat it, and from never letting the GPU idle. Only one of those is something you can buy on your laptop.

    So: a cache and batching are what servers have that laptops do not, and that is why they scale.

    KV cache
    storing key and value vectors from earlier tokens so they do not need to be recomputed
    batching
    running many requests together so the GPU does more work per step
    continuous batching
    letting requests join and leave between steps instead of waiting for the whole batch to finish

    • Forgetting that context needs memory too. A model that fits in 6 GB with a short input may not fit once you send it 32,000 tokens of context, because the KV cache grows with each token.

    • What is quantization and what does it trade off?

      Fewer bits per weight: less memory and faster movement, but more noise from rounding.

    • You run a local model at 4-bit and it scores lower on your golden set than the hosted model. Should you use 8-bit instead?

      Maybe. Check the score at 8-bit and see if the improvement matters for your task. Some tasks notice the drop, others do not.

    • Why does a hosted API stay fast for many users while a laptop struggles?

      The KV cache and batching. Servers cache tokens so they do not recompute them, and batch many users together to fill the GPU. Laptops do neither.

    Three reasons to self-host, and why they are rare

    Privacy and compliance. The data cannot legally or contractually leave your network. This is the most common honest reason, and no cost calculation overrides it. The arithmetic does not get a vote.

    Extreme, steady volume. Do the math, do not go on feeling. A GPU instance costs two dollars an hour, or about $1,450 a month. If it serves two million requests of your size per month, that works out to $0.0007 each. Now compare that number against what your provider charges for the same tokens.

    The key word is steady. The GPU bills you all month long whether traffic shows up or not. Below the break-even point, you are renting idle silicon and calling it savings.

    Latency floors. No network round trip. No shared queue. Nobody ahead of you. A small model on your own hardware answers a routing call in tens of milliseconds, which matters a lot when that call sits in front of everything else.

    Against all three reasons, put the ownership cost: uptime, capacity planning, upgrades, and the awkward fact that the frontier moves every few months while your deployment sits exactly where you left it.

    So: say these two sentences cold. "I self-host when the data cannot leave, or when volume is huge and steady. Otherwise I pay per token and spend the time on the product."

    So: self-hosting is a utilization problem, and only three situations justify buying.

    break-even
    the point where self-hosting costs and pay-per-token costs are equal
    utilization
    how full the GPU is; the lower the utilization, the more you pay per request

    Close the page. Say or write your answers.

    1. Name one situation where self-hosting makes sense even though it is harder than using an API.
    2. A GPU costs $1,450 a month. Your requests cost $0.004 each. How many requests do you need per month to break even?

    Your goal: you have worked out your own break-even point. In LOG.md, you have four sentences: one on what your local model was good at, one on where it fell over, one on what serving actually costs, and one on when you would choose it.

    Take your cost per request and your token counts. Divide $1,450 by your cost per request. That is your break-even monthly requests. Then write one sentence on whether you would ever hit that number for your actual use case.

    2. Compute your cost per request from your provider's pricing.
    3. Divide $1,450 by that cost. That is your break-even requests per month.
    4. For your actual use case, estimate realistic monthly requests. Would you hit break-even?
    5. Write four sentences in LOG.md. (1) What your local model did well. (2) Where it fell over. (3) Cost structure for each approach. (4) When you would choose self-hosting.

    • The rabbit hole itself. Quantization formats, sampler settings and GPU shopping can eat a week and teach you nothing about building products. Hence the timer at the start.
    • Treating "my model is slower" as proof that open models are useless. Measure on your task, with your evals. For routing, classification and extraction, small models are often fine.

    Teach it back

    Explain today to a smart friend who has never used an AI model. What can you run on your laptop? What does it cost to run something that many people use? When would you do each one? Start from the idea of downloading a file and run through to the decision. Use four to six sentences.

    Watch for the words "basically", "something happens here" and "you just". Each one marks a gap. Go back to that spot in the page, fill the gap, and explain again.

    Where are you on the ladder?

    From seeing it to using it to deciding when to use it.

    1. I have heard of quantization, the KV cache, and open-weights models.
    2. I can say what each one does and why a local model is slower than an API.
    3. Given the size and cost numbers, I can work out when self-hosting beats paying per token.
    4. I can run a local model, benchmark it, and decide whether to use it instead of an API for a real task.

    Three days, one product using everything you have learned. You build a retrieval system with tools, evals that gate CI, tracing wired from the start, auth for your own use, and a public URL. The hard part is not the code — it is deciding what not to build.

    The scope rule is the design

    You want to build something ambitious. The constraint is ruthless: pick something you would personally use every week. That is not motivation. That is an engineering rule.

    It solves three problems at once. First, you know the domain. You can spot a good answer from a plausible one in half a second, without borrowing an expert. Second, you have real inputs. Your test cases come from things people actually ask, not from your imagination. Third, you keep using it after the deadline, so it keeps failing, and failures are your only honest supply of improvements.

    The corollary is ruthless: one user, and that user is you. One job. One week of use. If you cannot describe the whole idea in a single sentence with a real verb — “turns my week of meeting notes into tracked action items I can search later” — it is too vague to finish in three days.

    The trap is building a platform. Every capstone wants to grow into a general assistant, because general feels ambitious. But general has no golden set (you cannot write cases for “anything”), no clear failure (nothing was promised), and nothing to measure. Untestable means unprovable. Narrow is what gets shipped, and narrow is what gets you hired.

    So: narrow is your design constraint, and the constraint decides what the product is.

    scope
    the boundary of what the product does, narrow enough to finish in three days and test honestly
    golden set
    a collection of real cases with known correct answers, used to measure the system

    Close the page. Without looking, answer each one in a sentence.

    1. Why does using the tool yourself for a week matter?
    2. What happens if you build a general assistant instead of one-sentence product?

    Your goal: a one-sentence description of the product, a domain you know, and a list of three things you are explicitly not building.

    One of each, all small

    Your capstone has six parts: retrieval over your documents, a model call, one tool that changes something real, evals with a golden set, tracing on every call, and auth with per-user scoping. Not a beautiful version of each — an honest version of each. You are proving you can wire a whole system together, not that any single part is remarkable.

    Retrieval: your corpus chunked with structure preserved, hybrid search plus a reranker, answers that cite their sources. One tool: writes a file, opens an issue, drafts a message, updates a row. This single tool is the entire difference between a chatbot and a product. Evals: twenty to thirty golden cases from your own real use, a runner, a judge, and a gate in CI. Tracing: wired before your first model call, not bolted on after. Auth: a login and per-user document scoping even with one user, because it forces you to answer whose data is whose. Deploy: a public URL.

    One honest version of each also keeps three days survivable. A beautiful retriever with no evals proves nothing you can say in a sentence. Six pieces wired together and measured prove the one thing the work is actually about. You are teaching yourself how to build a complete system, step by step.

    So: six small pieces, end to end, where the wiring is the skill you are demonstrating.

    pipeline
    a fixed sequence of steps that the data passes through
    traced
    every step logged so you can see what happened and how much it cost

    Close the page. Answer each one in one sentence.

    1. Why does adding just one tool make it a product instead of a chatbot?
    2. Why would you wire tracing before building the retriever?

    3. Say why you chose a pipeline (fixed steps) over an agent loop (decision-based steps), if that matters for your idea.
    4. Write the “not doing” list from Round 1, but this time with reasons.

    • What are the six pieces of a capstone?

      Retrieval, model call, one tool, evals with a golden set, tracing on every call, and auth with per-user scoping.

      A chatbot. The tool is what turns it into a product, because it changes something real in the world.

    Decide on paper, once

    You have a choice: a pipeline or an agent loop. The difference matters, and you should decide before you code. If you can draw the flowchart, write the flowchart.

    A pipeline is a fixed sequence. You retrieve, pass to the model, call the tool. Three steps, every time. It is cheap, fast, testable one step at a time, and structurally incapable of looping forever. You know what every call will cost and how long it will take because the path is fixed.

    An agent loop is a cycle. The model decides what to do, you do it, and feed the result back to the model. Decide, act, read, repeat. It earns its cost in exactly one situation: when the next step genuinely depends on what the last step found. Unknown number of searches. A repair loop. A branch only the data can choose. If you can name the steps in advance, you do not have that situation.

    Most good capstones are a pipeline with one small, bounded agent living inside one step. That is usually right. Write it down in your README on Day 25, when you remember why. Reconstructing it later is far harder. A decision made under deadline pressure is often rushed. A decision made on paper before you code has a better chance of being right.

    So: if the honest answer is always “retrieve, then answer, then check”, build a pipeline. Do not add a loop because it sounds more ambitious.

    pipeline
    a sequence of steps that run in the same order every time
    agent loop
    a cycle where the model decides what to do, the tool does it, and the result feeds back to the model

    Close the page. Answer each one.

    1. If you can name all the steps in advance, what should you build?
    2. When does an agent loop earn its cost?

    Your goal: update your README with a paragraph that says pipeline or agent loop, the steps in order, and why this shape serves your scope.

    Hint 1 — a nudge

    2. Mark every decision point. Do all of them have a fixed answer, or do they depend on what happened before?
    3. If all fixed, write pipeline. If not, write agent loop with a step cap (e.g., max 5 tool calls).
    4. Add the paragraph to your README: shape, steps, and why.

    Mix it in. Your architecture from Round 2 has retrieval, a model, and a tool. Draw that as a pipeline or a loop. Label whether the model decides what to do next or whether it is always the same.

    • Building an agent loop because it sounds more sophisticated. If your honest flowchart is a pipeline, that is the right choice for a three-day deadline.

    • What is the difference between a pipeline and an agent loop?

      A pipeline runs fixed steps every time. An agent loop has the model decide what to do, and repeats based on the result.

    • Your product always retrieves, always sends to the model, always calls one tool. Should it be a pipeline or an agent loop?

      A pipeline. The steps are fixed, so there is no reason to pay the cost of a loop.

    Deploy early, not on deadline day

    The rule is unforgiving: deploy on Day 25, not Day 27. Why so early? Because deployment is where the surprises live. Environment variables, cold starts, request timeouts, memory limits, and the vector store that only existed on your laptop. You will meet all of them. The only question is whether you meet them with two days of slack or two hours before your deadline.

    On Day 25, you deploy the ugliest end-to-end path that works. Twenty documents, hard-coded. No styling. One question in, one cited answer out. Deployed and traced. That one afternoon saves you a day of firefighting on Day 27.

    Three days, three clear modes. Day 25 — skeleton. Ugly, deployed, traced. Day 26 — quality. Use it for real, ten times. Every failure becomes a golden-set case. Fix by cluster. Feature freeze at sundown. Day 27 — ship. Auth, failure paths, README with metrics, deploy again.

    The deadline itself is a design tool. It decides what the product is, faster than you can. Before Day 25 morning, write a “not doing” list: no multi-user, no billing, no second data source, no mobile layout. You will fall behind on Day 27 — everyone does — and the list decides what gives way. You cut features. You do not cut evals, tracing, or the README. The feature is the demo. Evals and tracing are the proof, and the deadline forces you to choose.

    So: deploy early to own the surprises, not to let them own you.

    deployment
    putting your code on a public server with a URL other people can reach
    environment variable
    a setting your code reads at start time, like a database password or API key

    Close the page. Answer each one in one sentence.

    1. Why deploy on Day 25 instead of Day 27?
    2. What goes in the “not doing” list, and why?

    3. Ingest about twenty documents and chunk them with structure preserved (titles, headings, metadata).
    4. Write a retriever: hybrid search (keyword + vector), rerank the results, and pass the top chunks to the model.

      Deployment has surprises: environment variables, cold starts, timeouts, memory limits, the vector store that only existed locally. Better to meet them early than on the deadline.

    Retrieve with hybrid search and rerank

    Retrieval is the bridge between your documents and the model. A bad retriever gives the model the wrong context, and the model cannot fix wrong context. You cannot inspect what the model thinks — you can only see what you gave it. The quality of your answer is bounded by the quality of your retrieval.

    A hybrid search uses two kinds of search at once: keyword search (fast, exact, good for names and dates) and vector search (slow, approximate, good for meaning). Search twice, merge the results, and keep the top chunk. You then rerank those chunks using a second model trained to rank by relevance. Cheap, fast, and honest about what the model will actually see. It feels like more work upfront. It pays back immediately when your answers get better.

    You build the pipeline like this: ingest your documents and chunk them at structure boundaries (end of sections, not mid-sentence). Attach metadata (source, date, section title). Search with both kinds at once. Rerank. Pass the top chunk with its metadata to your main model call. The model sees the source and can cite it. This is the entire difference between an answer and a cited answer.

    So: retrieve twice, rerank once, and always pass the source chunks to the model so it can cite them.

    hybrid search
    searching by both keyword (exact) and vector (meaning) at once
    rerank
    a second model that scores chunks by how relevant they are to the question
    metadata
    information about a chunk, like its source document, date, or section title

    Close the page. Answer each one in one sentence.

    1. Why use hybrid search instead of vector search alone?
    2. Why does the model need to see the source chunk ID?

    Your goal: your skeleton now returns the top chunk with its metadata, the model cites the source in its answer, and you have tested it on ten questions you wrote by hand.

    Hint 1 — a nudge

    First, test your retriever in isolation. Ask it ten questions you wrote from your documents. Does it return the right chunk? If not, tune the search or the reranker before you touch the model.

    Hint 2 — the shape of the answer

    Chunk your documents at section boundaries and attach metadata. Search with keyword and vector. Rerank. Pass the top result to the model. Ask the model to cite the source in its answer.

    Still stuck after 10 minutes? The step by step
    1. Ingest your documents and chunk at section boundaries, not by token count alone. Keep the section title and document name as metadata.
    2. Build a retriever that searches both by keyword (using re or an indexer) and by vector (using embeddings and a vector DB or similarity).
    3. Merge the two result sets. Rerank the merged set using a model API or a reranker library.
    4. Pass the top chunk and its metadata to your main model call.
    5. Add an instruction to the system prompt: “Always cite the source document and chunk ID for your answer.”
    6. Test on ten questions you wrote from your documents. Write the results in a table: question, retrieved chunk ID, model answer, did it cite correctly?

    Mix it in. In Round 4 you deployed a skeleton. Now add retrieval to it and deploy the update. Does your code still work on the deployed server? Does anything slow down?

    • Using vector search alone and wondering why questions about dates or names fail. Keyword search is cheap and catches what vectors miss.
    • Not passing the source to the model, so the model guesses at citations and gets them wrong.

    • What is hybrid search?

      Searching by both keyword (exact, fast) and vector (meaning, approximate). Both at once, merged, so you get the best of each.

    • Your vector search misses questions about dates. How would you fix it?

      Add keyword search. Keywords are exact, so a question like “What happened on June 15?” will find “June 15” in the text.

    One tool that changes something

    A chatbot answers. A product does. You add one tool that writes a file, opens a GitHub issue, drafts an email, or updates a database row. It must be a thing people actually ask for. The tool is the entire difference between a chatbot and a product that solves a real problem.

    The tool takes two forms: a dry-run mode that shows what would happen without doing it, and a confirmation step where the user approves before the action runs. This protects the user from mistakes and from your model making errors with real consequences. Give the user a chance to see what is about to happen and say no.

    The model sends a tool call with arguments. Your code validates the arguments, shows the user what is about to happen, waits for a yes, and runs it. If the user says no, nothing happens and you can refine and try again. This is what turns a prototype into something you would actually use with real data.

    Wire this before Day 27 because it is where most of the complexity lives. Ask the user, in a clear prompt on your tool, what they want to happen. Let the model see the tool definition. Test it by hand: type a command, see the dry-run output, approve, watch it happen.

    So: one honest tool, with a dry-run mode and a confirmation step.

    tool
    a function the model can call to do something in the real world: write, update, create, send
    dry-run
    showing what would happen without actually doing it
    confirmation step
    asking the user to approve before running an irreversible action

    Close the page. Answer each one.

    1. What is the difference between a chatbot and a product?
    2. Why show a dry-run before you run the tool?

    Your goal: your product has one tool that does something real. You have tested it on five commands: dry-run, approve, and watch it run.

    Hint 1 — a nudge

    Start with the tool in isolation. Write the logic to validate arguments and generate the dry-run output. Test it by hand before you wire it to the model.

    Hint 2 — the shape of the answer

    Define a tool with clear arguments. Give the model the tool definition. When the model calls it, validate the arguments, show the dry-run, ask the user yes or no, and run it if yes.

    Still stuck after 10 minutes? The step by step
    1. Define your tool: what does it do, what arguments does it take, what does it return? Write the tool description in plain words.
    2. Implement the tool as a function. Add a dry-run mode that shows what would happen without doing it.
    3. Wire it to your model call. When the model sends a tool call, validate, show the dry-run, ask the user to approve.
    4. Test it on five commands: dry-run output, approve, watch it run, deny (it should stop), and a bad argument (it should reject).
    5. Write the test results in your LOG.md: command, dry-run output, user decision, actual result.

    Mix it in. Your retriever from Round 5 returns chunks with sources. Your tool from this round creates a file or opens an issue. Can the model combine them? Can it retrieve the sources and ask the tool to create something based on them?

    • Letting the tool run without a confirmation step. You will deploy a bug to production before you know it.
    • Giving the model a tool that is too powerful or too vague. Keep it narrow and specific.

    • What is the difference between a chatbot and a product?

      A chatbot answers. A product does. The tool is what turns an answer into an action in the real world.

    • Your model calls a tool to write a file. The dry-run shows the wrong path. What should happen?

      The code should reject the call and ask the user to correct the path before running it.

    Twenty to thirty golden cases, a runner, and a judge

    An eval is a test that measures whether your system works. A golden set is a collection of inputs with their correct answers. You use it to catch regressions: when a change you made broke something that used to work. It is your insurance policy against breaking things while you improve them.

    On Day 26 morning, use your product ten times for real work. Write down the question, what you wanted, and what you got. If the answer was wrong, note what the right answer should have been. This is your golden set. Do not imagine cases. Use the product, fail, and learn. Real failures teach you more than imagined ones ever could. Every time you run it and get a wrong answer, you have learned something about your system.

    Then you run the harness: a script that sends every golden-set question to your product, captures the answer, and scores it using an automated judge (another model or a hand-written rule). Cluster the failures by cause. Fix the biggest clusters. Re-run. This is where you spend most of Day 26 — not writing new features, but understanding what is broken and fixing the root cause.

    On Day 27, wire make eval into your CI so the build fails if your score drops. Break a prompt on purpose and watch the build fail. That tells you the gate actually works and will catch real regressions.

    So: twenty to thirty real cases, a runner, a judge, and a gate that stops regressions.

    golden set
    a collection of test inputs with their correct answers
    harness
    a script that runs all golden-set cases and scores them
    judge
    a model or a rule that scores whether an answer is correct

    Close the page. Answer each one.

    1. Why use your real product instead of imagining test cases?
    2. What does the judge do?

    Your goal: a golden set of twenty to thirty real cases from your own use, a harness that runs them all, a judge that scores each one, and a report showing which clusters of failures are biggest.

    Hint 1 — a nudge

    Do not write evals. Use your product. Every time you use it, save the input and the expected output. That is your golden set.

    Hint 2 — the shape of the answer

    A golden-set file has twenty to thirty rows: question, correct answer, answer type (e.g., retrieved source). A harness script sends each question to your product, gets the answer, and scores it. Group the failures by cause.

    Still stuck after 10 minutes? The step by step
    1. Use your product for real work. Every run, save the question and what you wanted. If wrong, write the correct answer.
    2. Save the golden set as a JSON or CSV file: question, expected answer, category (e.g., retrieval, reasoning, tool call).
    3. Write a harness script that reads the golden set, sends each question to your product, and captures the answer.
    4. Write a judge: either a model that scores “correct” or “incorrect”, or a hand-written rule that checks key details.
    5. Run the harness and generate a report: pass/fail per case, grouped by category. Which categories have the most failures?
    6. Fix the biggest cluster, re-run, and show the improvement in your LOG.md.

    Mix it in. From Round 4, you deployed your skeleton with tracing. Now run your evals harness on those traces. Can you see why the cases that failed, failed? Can tracing data help you fix them?

    • Leaving the golden set until Day 28. Then every change you made on Day 26 was made blind, and you cannot say whether the system got better or only different.
    • Imagining test cases instead of using the product. Imagined cases miss the real failures.

    • What is a golden set?

      A collection of test inputs with their correct answers, built from real use of the product.

    • You ran your harness and your score is 70 percent. Should you fix the hardest case first or the most common failure cluster?

      The most common cluster. You get more improvement per fix, and there are only two days left.

    By tomorrow you can reproduce: how to build a golden set from real use, wire a harness, write a judge, and cluster failures by cause.

    On Day 27, auth and failure paths

    On Day 27 morning, you add auth. Even with one user, auth forces you to answer whose data is whose. Every document, every trace, every call belongs to a user account. This is not optional if you ever want to go from prototype to product. It is also the easiest part to add now, before your system has real data.

    Then you walk every failure path: provider is down (your API call fails), empty retrieval (no documents match the question), tool error (the tool fails or the user denies it), oversized input (the question is too long for the context window), and injected instruction (a document contains text designed to override your prompt). Each one must return something useful. A clear error message is better than a crash. When something goes wrong, tell the user what went wrong and what they can try next.

    Write the README with real numbers from your traces: cost per request, p95 latency, eval score. These numbers are your proof that the system works and is predictable. Commit at end of day. Finished or not, you ship. No extensions. No more features. The system is what it is. You have measured it. You have fixed the biggest problems. Now you deploy.

    Where are you on the ladder?

    Being able to say “I have seen this” is only the first rung. Climb all four.

    Your system works when people use it gently, one request at a time. Today you find out what happens when they do not. You turn every claim in your README into a real measurement.     What a load test measures

    A load tool — k6, Locust, or a twenty-line script — runs pretend users in a loop against your endpoint for a few minutes. Each request records its latency and success or failure. At the end you have numbers: p50, p95, p99 latency, error rate, and requests per second.

    You are hunting for one thing in all that data: the knee. The knee is the concurrency where p95 latency stops being flat and starts climbing steeply. Below the knee, you have headroom. Above it, requests are queuing and piling up.

    Think of a restaurant taking orders. With five customers, the kitchen keeps up. At fifteen, orders wait in the queue. The knee is where the wait times climb. That is where you learn what your actual capacity is.

    Ramp deliberately: 1 user, then 5, then 10, then 25, then 50. Run each for three minutes and record p95 at every level. That curve is a real engineering finding. It goes straight into your write-up.

    But a load test will lie to you in three ways. First, send the same input every time and your cache serves it perfectly — you have measured your cache, not your capacity. Use a pool of fifty varied real inputs instead. Second, you will often hit your provider's rate limit before you hit your own ceiling — that is a real finding to record, not a broken test. Third, tokens cost money. Ten minutes at ten concurrent users can cost several dollars. Do that multiplication before you press go, not after.

    So: a load test does not give you a capacity number, it gives you the point where the latency line turns upward, and that is the number worth having.

    So: a load test finds the knee. That is where you learn what your system actually does under stress.

    knee
    the concurrency at which latency stops being flat and starts climbing
    concurrent users
    how many requests your endpoint handles at the same time
    p95 latency
    the latency where 95 percent of requests were faster and 5 percent were slower

    Close the page. Answer out loud, then write it.

    Your goal: a load test ramp showing p50, p95, p99 and error rate at 1, 5, 10, 25 and 50 concurrent users. A graph or table showing where the knee is. And a note of what happened: did you hit your own ceiling, or your provider's rate limit first?

    Hint 1 — a nudge

    Hint 2 — the shape of the answer

    Still stuck after 10 minutes? The step by step
    1. Build an input pool of fifty varied real requests from your traces.
    2. Write a load script that loops those inputs at increasing concurrency: 1, 5, 10, 25, 50.
    3. Estimate the cost. Fifty inputs times 5 concurrency levels times 3 minutes each. That is how many requests and tokens?
    4. Run the load test for 1 user and record p50, p95, p99, error rate.
    5. Repeat for 5, 10, 25 and 50 concurrent users.
    6. Plot p95 against concurrency. Where does it start climbing? That is your knee.
    7. Note whether you hit your own ceiling or your provider's rate limit first.

    Mix it in. Look at your p95 latency at your knee point. Use your knowledge of the model's speed and your traces to estimate what fraction was waiting in queue and what fraction was the model working.

    • Load testing with the same API key your users depend on. You will rate-limit yourself and then call it an outage.
    • Testing with one repeated input. Your cache makes the graph beautiful and the graph means nothing.
    • Chasing p99 on a system with eleven samples. p99 of 100 requests is one request. Fix p95 first, and say how many samples you measured.

    • What is the knee in a load test?

      The concurrency where p95 latency stops being flat and starts climbing. Below it you have headroom. Above it, requests queue.

    • You run a load test with the same input fifty times in a loop. Your cache serves it every time. What does your graph tell you?

      Nothing useful. It tells you cache performance, not real capacity. Use fifty different real inputs instead.

    Cost per user, not per request

    Pull requests per session out of your traces. Count them. Now multiply cost per request times requests per session. That is cost per user, and it is the number that matters to anyone running the service.

    Why the unit matters: "$0.004 per request" means nothing to anybody. "About $0.15 per user per week, 80 percent of it in the generation call" is a business fact that someone can act on. You can make a bet about retention, churn and unit economics. The first number lets you make nothing.

    So: cost per user, not per request.

    cost per user
    the average spending on one person from their first request to their last in a period

    p95 latency end to end, broken down by span

    Measure p95 latency at the edge, including your own overhead. Not the model's time in isolation, which always flatters you. Then break it down by span: retrieval 180 ms, rerank 120 ms, generation 1.9 s, your own code 40 ms.

    Look at what that breakdown just did for you. Retrieval is 180 ms of a 2.24-second request. You could optimize it into nothing and the user would barely notice. Without the breakdown, that is exactly the week you would have spent. Counts and numbers, not your intuition, tell you where to look.

    Eval score on the golden set, run against the deployed configuration, not your laptop. The deployed system has retries, caching, and edge cases your dev box does not.

    Error rate, split by cause: provider errors, timeouts, output-validation failures, empty retrieval, tool failures. A single "2 percent error rate" hides which is one config change away and which is a design problem.

    So: every one of these four numbers goes in the README with the date and the conditions, because a number without conditions is a rumor.

    span
    one component of a request, like retrieval or generation, with its own latency
    error rate, split by cause
    not one number, but five: how many errors came from each source

    • One "error rate" number without breaking down what kind of error. Fix the wrong problem first.

    • You measure $0.004 per request and three requests per user per week. What is cost per user?

      $0.004 × 3 = $0.012 per user per week, or about $0.6 per user per year.

    • Why does p95 latency breakdown matter more than just the total?

      It shows where your time is going. If generation is 1.9 s of a 2.24 s request, optimizing retrieval saves almost nothing.

    What breaks, how you would know, what you would do

    A playbook is a table you could hand to someone at two in the morning. Three columns: what breaks, how you would know, what you would do. One row for every failure mode you can name.

    The middle column is where the value is. Be honest in it. Half your rows will read "I would not know". That is not an embarrassment — that is the finding. Each of those rows turns into a panel or an alarm, built from the tracing you wired earlier.

    The third column has a rule: it must be a degraded behavior, not a heroic fix. At two in the morning you do not debug. You walk down a short list until something works — serve the cached answer, fall back to the second provider, return the sources without a summary, or turn the feature off behind a flag while the rest of the site stays up.

    Build the playbook by thinking through your system's dependencies. What happens if the provider goes down? If your retrieval database fails? If your code has a bug? If a user sends a poison input? The playbook names each one, the alarm that should catch it, and the graceful way to fail. The graceful ways are usually: use a different provider, serve cached results, return partial results, or disable the feature temporarily.

    The best playbooks learn from real incidents. If your system has ever broken in production, add a row to the playbook for that incident. If a row says "I would not know", that is your signal to add an alarm or a monitoring panel. The monitoring is the difference between a playbook you actually follow and a playbook that sits in a document.

    So: the playbook is not a document about how good your system is; it is the list of smaller promises you can still keep when the big one fails.

    So: the playbook is the contract you can still keep when things break.

    degraded behavior
    a smaller, weaker promise you can keep when the full feature fails
    fail over
    switch to a backup option when the primary fails

    Read, label, count, fix two, re-run

    Error analysis, one more time, because it is the highest-return habit in the whole plan. Dump every failing case — from your golden set and from your real traces. Read them. Actually read them one at a time. Give each one a single line of cause in your own words.

    Now count the causes. This is the step people skip, and it is the only step that matters. The counts tell you what to fix. Your intuition will always nominate the most interesting failure, not the most common one.

    Fix in order of count times harm. And two is a real number — pick the top two clusters, fix them, then re-run the identical golden set so before and after are actually comparable. Change the set and you have thrown away your own evidence.

    Last, promote those cases into the permanent eval set, so the bug cannot come back quietly six weeks from now.

    Here is the sentence you are trying to earn: "Raising chunk overlap from 0 to 80 tokens moved faithfulness from 0.71 to 0.86 on the 30-question set; the remaining failures are all questions that need two documents at once, which is next week's work."

    So: read, label, count, fix two, re-run, promote. That loop, with real numbers behind it, is the thing you will be hired for.

    So: the loop is read, label, count, fix, re-run, promote, and the numbers are what you earn.

    error analysis
    reading every failure, finding what caused it, and counting causes to find the most important one
    cluster
    a group of failures with the same or similar cause

    Where are you on the ladder?

    From testing to understanding to fixing to proving.

    1. I have heard of load testing, the knee, and error analysis.

    Today you write the story about your project, not the code. A reviewer cannot run your code or know which parts were yours. They can only see whether you understand your own choices.     Reasoning is the whole product

    Stop and imagine you are the person on the other side. A hiring manager reads your work for four to eight minutes. They cannot run your code. They cannot tell which parts you wrote, which came from a tutorial, and which came from a model. They have seen two hundred retrieval demos this year, every one of which worked in the screenshot.

    So what can they actually measure in six minutes? Your reasoning. Did you understand the choices in front of you? Did you pick one deliberately? And do you know what it cost?

    Watch two people ship the same assistant. One writes “built with a vector database, a rerank step and a frontier model.” The other writes “dense-only retrieval missed every question with a part number, so I added keyword search and a reranker: recall@5 went from 0.62 to 0.84, and p95 rose 180 milliseconds, which I paid on purpose.”

    Only the second claim is checkable. And only the second claim is impossible to write without actually doing the work—which is exactly why it is believed.

    So: your decisions, your numbers and your failures are the whole product.

    So: the claim is checkable only if you measured it.

    reasoning
    understanding the tradeoffs in your choices, not listing the features
    checkable claim
    a statement that names what was measured, the numbers, and the cost paid

    Six sections, each answering one question

    A write-up has exactly six parts, each doing one job. The reviewer is already asking these questions in order, so the sections answer them without the reviewer having to ask.

    Problem. Who was doing what by hand, how often, and what it cost them? One paragraph. If this paragraph is vague, everything after it reads like a toy.

    Architecture diagram. A box diagram showing the real steps, with model calls marked so a reader can point at where the money and latency go. A Mermaid block is enough.

    Key tradeoffs. Three to five of them. The shape is always the same: I chose X over Y because Z, and it cost me W. Include at least one thing you rejected. You already have data on three: agent versus pipeline, fine-tuning versus prompt plus retrieval, and self-hosting versus per-token.

    What failed and why. This is the section almost everyone skips, which is exactly why it separates you first. Your fine-tuning day belongs here. So does the retrieval approach that lost, the failure mode you decided not to fix, and the reason you decided that.

    Eval results with numbers. Golden set size, how you built it, which metrics and why those ones, before-and-after for your two biggest changes, and how you checked that your judge agrees with a human.

    Cost and latency. Cost per request and per user. P95 latency with the breakdown by step. The one thing you would optimize next. Close with your known failure modes and what you would do with another week.

    So: six sections, each one answering a question the reviewer already has, in the order they will ask them.

    So: six sections, each one carrying a question and an answer.

    architecture diagram
    a box diagram showing the steps of your system and where the model calls go
    tradeoff
    a deliberate choice between two good options, with a measurable cost
    golden set
    a small dataset that you or a human judged, used to measure whether your system works

    Write from the log, keep only what you can source

    You already have twenty-eight days of notes with the numbers in them. The write-up is an edit of raw material you own, not a fresh act of invention. Open LOG.md, pull out every number and every surprise, and sort them into the six sections. Most of the piece assembles itself from there.

    Then run one filter over everything. Can you point at the measurement behind this sentence? If not, cut it today or measure it today. An unsupported number is worse than no number at all, because it is exactly the thing an interviewer will probe first.

    The standard for every sentence is narrow on purpose: it is either a number you measured, a decision you made, or a limitation you know about. No adjective is allowed to do the work of data. “Fast” is not a claim. “p95 2.1 seconds, 78 percent of it inside the generation call” is a claim, and it invites the follow-up question you can answer well.

    So: write from the log, keep only what you can source, and let the numbers carry the adjectives.

    sourced claim
    a statement you can point to a measurement for, with the method and conditions named
    adjective
    a describing word like "fast" or "good" that hides a number you should show instead

    Draw the architecture diagram first

    The architecture diagram is not a detail. It is the piece that reveals what you actually built. When you draw it, the diagram usually shows you which tradeoff is worth explaining in detail and which one is not.

    Do not overthink it. A Mermaid block with five or six boxes is enough. Label the model calls. Draw the cache if you have one. Mark where the latency goes and where the money goes. A reviewer can look at that diagram for fifteen seconds and understand the whole system.

    Now write the tradeoffs section. Your attention is fresh because you just drew the diagram. The easiest tradeoff to explain is usually the one that came up most in your LOG.md.

    So: architecture diagram first, because it reveals everything else.

    Write and assemble the six sections

    Now you have your scratch file with the raw material: numbers sorted into the six buckets, an architecture diagram, and your tradeoffs and failures listed. It is time to assemble the actual write-up.

    Start with the architecture diagram and the tradeoffs section. These are the hardest parts and the most interesting ones. Your attention is fresh at the start of the hour, so do them first. Then fill in eval results from your measurements. The cost and latency section is one paragraph: the cost per request, the P95 latency, and the one thing you would optimize if you had another week.

    Save the problem paragraph for last. Write it when you know exactly what the piece proved. It should be one paragraph that a non-engineer could read aloud without stumbling. If the sentence is long, break it. If a word is fancy, swap it for a plain one.

    Do not polish on the first pass. This is a first draft. The goal is to get all six sections on a page with every claim sourced to a number. Revision comes later.

    So: write the hard parts first, fill in the numbers, and write the opening last.

    first draft
    the unpolished version that has all the information but rough writing
    sourced
    backed by a number you can point to

    Publish once, point everything at it

    Publish the write-up somewhere with a stable link. Then title it with the result rather than the topic. “What 40 golden questions taught me about retrieval” beats “My RAG project” because the first one promises a finding and the second one promises a demo.

    Now distribute, which takes ten minutes and roughly doubles the value of the whole day. Link it from the top of all four of your READMEs. Put it on your resume. Link it from your profile. Put the live link and the repo link on the first screen, before anyone has to scroll.

    Last, send it to two people who work in this area. Ask them one question: what was unclear? The paragraphs they stumble on are the paragraphs that need rewriting, and you will never find those by rereading your own words—you already know what you meant.

    So: one stable link, pointed at from everywhere you exist, checked by two people who are not you.

    So: the write-up is done only when it is pointed at from everywhere.

    stable link
    a URL that will not change, so you can link to it from your resume and keep the link working
    reach
    the people who will see your write-up, determined by where you link it

    Close the page. From memory.

    1. Why title it with a finding instead of a project name?
    2. What is the one question you ask the two readers who review it?

    Your goal: the write-up is live with a stable link, linked from your four READMEs and your resume, and you have sent it to two people for one specific question. Then commit everything.

    Hint 1 — a nudge

    Use your scratch file from Round 2. Assemble it into the six sections in order. Do not polish; this is your first draft. Write the problem paragraph last when you know what the piece proved. Then publish and distribute.

    Hint 2 — the shape of the answer

    Write for one hour: problem (one paragraph), architecture (Mermaid), tradeoffs (three to five, each with numbers), failures (what broke), eval (before-and-after), cost (the one-liner and the latency breakdown). Add links to the four READMEs and your resume. Publish. Send to two readers.

    Still stuck after 10 minutes? The step by step
    1. Take your scratch file from Round 2 and copy it into a document. Add a title that names a finding, not a project.
    2. Order the six sections. Problem, architecture, tradeoffs, what failed, eval, cost.
    3. Paste the Mermaid diagram. One sentence for each tradeoff, with the cost. List the failures.
    4. Copy the before-and-after numbers from LOG.md. Write one line about cost per request and p95 latency.
    5. Write the problem paragraph last. One paragraph that a non-engineer can read aloud.
    6. Publish on a stable URL (a note, a GitHub wiki page, or a Medium post works).
    7. Link from all four READMEs, your resume, and your profile. Test the links.
    8. Send it to two people. Ask: which part did you have to read twice?
    9. Commit. Every day ends with a commit.

    Mix it in. Look at your eval results. Is every number traceable to a day? Can you point at when you ran that test?

    • Explaining the technology instead of the decisions. If a paragraph would fit unchanged in someone else's post, delete it.
    • Hiding failures to look strong. The failures are the evidence that you measured; a write-up without them reads as a demo that was never pushed hard.
    • Waiting for the project to get better first. An unwritten good system loses to a written adequate one, every time.

    • Why title the write-up with a finding instead of the project name?

      The title promises a result, not a demo. "What 40 golden questions taught me about retrieval" tells a reader they will learn something from studying what you did.

    • You link the write-up from your resume. One reader asks, what was unclear? What should that person tell you?

      The paragraph that made them stumble. You cannot find it by rereading your own words; you already know what you meant. Their confusion is the place you need to fill in.

    By tomorrow you can reproduce: the six sections of the write-up from scratch, and the names of the two people who read it.

    Teach it back

    Explain this day to a smart friend who has never written a project summary before. Why does a write-up matter more than the code? What goes into the six sections? Start from the moment a hiring manager reads your work and use four to six sentences.

    Watch for the words “basically”, “something happens here” and “you just”. Each one marks a gap. Go back to that spot in the page, fill the gap, and explain again.

    Where are you on the ladder?

    Four rungs: from understanding the purpose to shipping the proof.

    1. I have seen write-ups that name tradeoffs and failures.
    2. I can say what goes in each of the six sections and why every number needs a source.
    3. Given a project log, I can extract the numbers and sort them into the six buckets.
    4. I can write a complete write-up that proves I understand my own choices, publish it, and link it everywhere.

    Everything is built, measured, and written. Today is packaging: making it possible for a stranger to see in about 60 seconds that you ship AI systems and can defend how they work. By tonight you should be able to say: “A stranger can tell from my resume and profile what I built and what it cost.”

    Your resume is four links

    A resume bullet is a claim someone can check. “Familiar with RAG and vector databases” is a list of rooms you were in. “Built a docs assistant over 12,000 pages: recall at 5 results improved from 0.62 to 0.84 on a 40-question test set, $0.004 per request, p95 2.1 seconds” is a system a stranger can verify in a click.

    So cut the skills section. Every tool that matters moves inside a bullet where it is attached to something real you built. Four repos. Four bullets. One number per bullet. One link.

    You rewrite the top first. The profile headline, the opening paragraph — these should not say “AI engineer,” they should say “shipped a retrieval system that improved from X to Y.” Proof before title. The first line should contain a thing you built and a measured result. Then the hiring manager reads the four bullets and makes a decision in six minutes instead of 60.

    So: four bullets, four systems, four numbers, four links. That is your resume.

    recall
    a measure of whether the system finds the right answer when it exists
    p95
    the time where 95 percent of calls were faster and 5 percent slower
    denominator
    the count under the number; recall on how many test questions

    Your answers come from your own work

    You now know the fifteen standard questions about AI systems. “How do you evaluate this? What failed? How much did it cost? How fast is it?” They are not trivia. Each one has a good answer that starts with “in my capstone project” and continues into a specific measurement.

    So practice saying them out loud. Sixty to ninety seconds each, one time through. The ones where you drift into textbook language are your study list. Not because the textbook is wrong, but because the hiring manager has heard it fifty times already and cannot tell it apart from someone who read a blog post this morning.

    Specific beats general. Every single time. An answer about a problem you solved last month is stronger than an answer about how the world works. Make sure your fifteen answers all come from your own systems. If you find one that does not, that question is your study priority.

    So: the study list writes itself, and it is short.

    blocker
    a question you cannot answer from your own work; your next study topic

    Close the page. Write the answer.

    1. Rewrite this bullet in the new style: “Experienced with prompt engineering and vector search.” Make it specific, with a number and a link.
    2. Why is “I improved recall from 0.62 to 0.84 on my capstone dataset” better than “I understand retrieval systems”?

    Your goal: your resume and LinkedIn profile are rewritten around four shipped systems, not tools. Each bullet says what it did, one number, and has a link. Your fifteen question answers all come from your own work. You have recorded yourself answering them once through.

LinkedIn: update the headline and the opening paragraph the same way. Record audio of yourself answering the fifteen questions, 60-90 seconds each. Mark any answer that does not cite your own work as a study gap.

    Still stuck after 10 minutes? The step by step
    1. Collect your four shipped projects and pick one number per project: eval score, cost, or latency.
    2. Rewrite your resume headline: one system, one number, first line.
    3. Replace your skills section with four bullets. Each: what it does, one number, one link. Delete anything that does not point to a link you own.

    • Waiting for polish. The resume you publish today beats the better one you edit all month.
    • Listing every library you have touched. One system you can defend in depth outranks ten you can only name.

    • What goes in a resume bullet instead of a list of tools?

      What the system does, one number with its denominator, and a link to proof. For example: "Improved retrieval from 0.62 to 0.84 on 40 questions" with a link to the README.

    • You built an agent that costs $0.02 per task and finishes in 2.3 seconds on average. Write a resume bullet.

      Built an agent that completes tasks in 2.3 seconds at $0.02 cost, deployed on [platform], measured on 50 test cases. Live link [here]. Repo [here].

    By tomorrow you can reproduce: four resume bullets with systems instead of tools, each with a number and a link, and your fifteen question answers from memory.

    Depth beats breadth

    From today forward, you pick one path: go deep into one mechanism, or go broad in one domain. Deep means spending the next month on evals, retrieval quality, or inference optimization. Broad means picking a domain where the problems are specific — legal, health, dev tools, finance — where your systems knowledge gives you an edge over people who know the domain but not the tooling.

    Both paths work. What does not work is neither. Reading release notes for a month, peeking at three things, starting nothing — that feels like progress and ships nothing. So you write the choice down today with a deliverable and a date. One month from now, something is done.

    The choice also tells you what to learn next. If you choose depth in retrieval, the next papers you read are about dense retrieval, sparse retrieval, and hybrid search. If you choose a domain, you read three systems papers in that domain. The first week you study; the second week you build; weeks three and four you measure and fix.

    So: choose depth or breadth, pick one deliverable, set one date, and write it down.

    dense retrieval
    finding answers by comparing meaning, using a vector model
    sparse retrieval
    finding answers by matching keywords, like search engines use
    domain depth
    becoming an expert in how systems work for one specific field

    Today you build your personal strategy

    Now you write it down. The choice: depth or breadth? The mechanism (evals, retrieval, inference) or the domain (legal, health, devtools, finance). The deliverable: what will exist in 30 days? The date: when. Write one paragraph. One month from now this paragraph will either say you finished or you got blocked. Either way, you own the number.

    You also decide if you are staying independent, joining a team, or building a company. That matters because the next month is different for each. If you are hiring for a team, you spend time recruiting and interviewing. If you are raising money, you spend time on pitch decks. If you are staying solo, you build full-time. Same mechanism choice, different schedule.

    And: today you take one public action. Write and publish the Day 29 write-up. Open one pull request to an AI tool you actually used. Message three people doing this work — one specific question each, not asking for a job. That is the month. Those are the three anchors.

    So: the choice, the deliverable, the date, and the three actions, all in writing.

    pull request
    a proposal to change code in someone else's project, usually a documentation fix
    anchor
    a visible action that keeps you accountable

    2. Why does choosing depth in one thing beat trying to learn everything?

    Your goal: you have written down the next thirty days. Depth or breadth. The deliverable. The date. The three public actions: published write-up, one PR to open source, three messages to people doing this work. Your choice is in LOG.md and committed.
